_about.purpose: Optional starter pack for a new mx-inv install: generic maintenance library - systems, recurring tasks, checklists and a haul-out project.
_about.scope: STANDALONE UTILITY data - shipped in starter_packs/, never read by the app itself.
_about.architecture: Generated by scripts/release/export_starter_packs.py; loaded on request by load_starter_pack.py through data.py. Safe to load into a database that already has your own boat - existing names are skipped.

notes: All tasks load as never done. hours_meter: 'engine' = main engine hours, 'genset' = generator hours.

tasks.name: AIS - Transceiver Function & Static-Data Check
tasks.description: Confirm the AIS is actually transmitting (have a nearby vessel or a shore AIS site / app confirm your target, or use the maker's configuration tool), holds a GPS fix, and that its STATIC DATA is right - MMSI, call sign, ship name, ship type, length x beam, and GPS antenna offsets. Check the antenna / splitter connections, that the silent-mode switch works, and that the unit is not alarming.
tasks.caution_notes: Two failure modes worth the periodic check: (1) it silently stops transmitting and you think you are visible when you are not; (2) a firmware reset / re-flash can revert the static data - re-verify after any AIS firmware update. If the unit came from a previous boat, confirm it is not still broadcasting that boat's name and MMSI.

tasks.name: Anchor Wash - Diaphragm & Valve Inspection
tasks.description: Unscrew the pump head housing screws to inspect the internal Santoprene diaphragm and check valves for debris punctures or calcium buildup.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the head, inspect the Santoprene diaphragm for pin-holes and the check valves for grit and calcium. Carry one full head/valve service kit per pump type - a split diaphragm is a dockside-unavailable part in most of the cruising world.

tasks.name: Anchor Wash - Electrical Terminal Check
tasks.description: Verify that crimps and connections at the pump, its pressure switch, and its dedicated switch on the Nav Station switch panel (not the main DC breaker panel, which is also at the Nav Station) are clean, corrosion-free, and receiving stable voltage.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the crimps at the pump, its pressure switch and the panel switch, and the supply, for corrosion and stable voltage - a marginal joint makes the pump chatter or run weak and burns the switch contacts. The pump only runs when its panel switch is on AND the deck fitting is pushed and twisted.

tasks.name: Anchor Wash - Inlet Strainer Cleaning
tasks.description: Twist off the clear plastic strainer bowl, pull out the mesh screen, and flush out accumulated sediment.
tasks.caution_notes: Twist off the clear strainer bowl, pull the mesh screen, flush. A blocked strainer starves the pump - it runs hot and loud and diaphragm life drops.

tasks.name: Anchor Wash - Visual Leak & Noise Check
tasks.description: Inspect plumbing fittings for slow drips and check that rubber vibration-damping feet are secure to prevent mounting noise.
tasks.caution_notes: Look for weeping at the head screws and port fittings and confirm the rubber feet are sound - a hard-mounted pump telegraphs through the boat and the vibration eventually cracks a fitting. A pump that cycles on its own with every tap shut has a system leak or a failed check valve.

tasks.name: Arch / Hardtop - Anodized Frame Fastener Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the structural stainless steel mounting bolts and pad-eyes anchoring the aluminum frame to your deck/coaming for bubbling white aluminum oxide.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the stainless bolts and pad-eyes anchoring the arch to the deck - it is a big lever in a following sea and a solar sail in a gust. Cracked gelcoat at the bases or any weeping means re-bed now; a leak here rots the deck core.

tasks.name: Arch / Hardtop - Eisenglass Clarity Polish
tasks.description: Clean the clear vinyl dodger windows to clear away salt-etching and atmospheric grime while laying down a micro-thin anti-static UV shell.
tasks.caution_notes: Clean the clear vinyl with a dedicated marine vinyl cleaner and a soft cloth, then the matching polish - never glass cleaner or paper towel, both haze it permanently. A UV-hazed panel is a canvas-shop replacement.

tasks.name: Arch / Hardtop - Track & Zipper Slide Care
tasks.description: Spray the overhead awning tracks (such as Keder or plastic bolt-rope tracks) and the heavy-duty YKK plastic zippers to ensure smooth installation and removal.
tasks.caution_notes: Dry-lube the bolt-rope / Keder tracks and wax the YKK zippers. A stiff zipper gets forced, the slider distorts, and then the whole panel is off the boat until a canvas shop rebuilds it.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Heading Sensor Re-Calibration
tasks.description: If major steel gear, dive tanks, or spare anchors have been shifted near the autopilot's heading sensor / course computer, run a compass re-calibration swing.
tasks.caution_notes: Re-run the pilot's compass calibration if heavy ferrous gear (dive tanks, spare anchor, tools) has moved near the heading sensor, or if the pilot's heading disagrees with the ship's compass. The sensor drifts with nearby iron and then steers a curve. Know where the sensor is mounted and judge nearby-iron risk against that spot. Hybrid systems (newer control electronics driving an older drive unit) are common - note which part is which.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Actuator Rod Wipe & Seal Check
tasks.description: Wipe down the extending stainless steel actuator ram rod to clear salt paste, and check the rubber wiper boot seal for structural cracks.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe the salt paste off the ram rod and check the wiper boot for splits - grit past the wiper scores the rod and then the internal seal. A Type 2 drive weeping hydraulic fluid, or a mechanical drive throwing grease, is on its way out; a scored rod is the tell.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Clutch Voltage Relay Test
tasks.description: Engage the autopilot to verify the pilot computer is delivering a steady clutch voltage to lock the drive's clutch. If it drops current, the clutch slips under heavy wave loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the clutch-circuit current limit on your pilot computer - an older drive paired with newer electronics can spike past it and cook the board; fit an inline automotive relay if the current climbs. Note where the motor controller is installed.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Drive Arm Structural Bolt Torque
tasks.description: Verify that the structural bolts securing the autopilot drive's backing base to the hull stringers remain tightly torqued.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the bolts through the drive's backing plate into the hull structure - this mount takes a reversing load on every course correction, thousands of times a passage. A backed-off bolt lets the drive rack and then tear out. Wired or nyloc; re-torque quarterly.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Motor Brush Carbon Inspection
tasks.description: Back off the rear cap of the autopilot drive motor to blow out black carbon brush dust before it builds up and shorts the motor.
tasks.caution_notes: Blow the carbon dust out of the drive motor; replace the brushes at the wear line.

tasks.name: Autopilot - Rudder Feedback Alignment Check
tasks.description: Verify your rudder reference transducer (linear or rotary) tracks true without physical linkage binding or loose ball-joints.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the rudder-reference arm moves the full range without binding and reads centre when the rudder is centred - a drifted or stiff feedback unit makes the pilot hunt or hold a permanent few degrees of helm. Re-zero after any steering work.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Air Filter Cleansing
tasks.description: Pull the slide-out mesh filter off the return air grille, wash it down, and dry it to prevent low airflow ice-ups.
tasks.caution_notes: Wash the return-air filter monthly - a clogged filter ices the evaporator and the unit short-cycles on low suction. Never run it without the filter; dust on the coil is a far bigger job than a rinse.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Condensate Drain Flush
tasks.description: Flush the stainless steel collection pan with fresh water and pass a thin wire down the drain lines to prevent blockages.
tasks.caution_notes: Flush the condensate pan and drain line with fresh water and a pan tablet. A slime-blocked drain overflows onto the sole - or in a seaway into the headliner or bilge. No liquid bleach (eats the aluminium pan).

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Heat Exchanger Descaling
tasks.description: Run a closed-loop recirculating flush through the seawater plumbing to clear mineral scaling inside the condenser barrel.
tasks.caution_notes: Recirculate a mild acid (Barnacle Buster) through the seawater circuit to clear barnacle and scale insulation off the cupronickel condenser.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Lithium Battery Voltage Audit
tasks.description: Verify that your 24V house battery bank (ideally LiFePO4) maintains a stable operating voltage under load to prevent compressor efficiency drops.
tasks.caution_notes: The 24V unit draws hard on start and run - log battery voltage under AC load and confirm it holds above the BMS low-cutoff with margin. A sagging bank trips the compressor on low-voltage fault and the AC takes the blame for a battery problem. Check the DC feed lug torque while you are there.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Main DC Terminal Torque check
tasks.description: Verify the heavy-gauge 24V power cables directly into the main control/power board are tightly torqued to prevent resistance heating.
tasks.caution_notes: Torque the main 24V DC terminals to spec - the variable-speed compressor pulls high current and a loose lug overheats.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Pump Controller Connection Check
tasks.description: Inspect the small in-line "black box" pump controller module connections to ensure proper communication between the pump and the main AC unit.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the seawater-pump controller plug and DC connections for corrosion and heat - a marginal joint here under-runs the pump, head pressure climbs, and the unit faults on high-pressure. Reseat and dielectric-grease.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Sea Strainer cleaning
tasks.description:
1. Turn off A-C
2. Shut the seacock, extract the strainer basket, and clear out weed or sediment before it restricts flow and throws a high pressure or water-flow fault.
3. Place a Bromine tablet in it as part of reassembly
4. Reassemble - open Seacock
5. Prime the water pump
tasks.caution_notes: The circulation pump is not self-priming; prime it after any strainer service or it throws an immediate HPF / e8. Never put liquid bleach in the drain pan - it eats the aluminum evaporator fins; use pan tablets.

tasks.name: Berth A/C - Seawater Discharge Check
tasks.description: Confirm a steady ~5 GPM overboard discharge stream to verify the non-self-priming pump hasn’t suffered an air lock.
tasks.caution_notes: No overboard discharge stream means an airlock or blockage - expect an immediate HPF (high-pressure fault) / e8 lockout.

tasks.name: Black Water Pumps - Ezi-Twist Clamping Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the heavy-duty plastic Ezi-Twist locking ring screws to ensure motor vibration hasn't backed off the compression ring.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the heavy Ezi-Twist ring screws - a backed-off ring on a black-water pump leaks the worst thing on the boat into a locker. Tight, halves square.

tasks.name: Black Water Pumps - Hose Odor Permeation Check
tasks.description: Wipe down the incoming and outgoing sanitation hoses with a clean microfiber cloth and sniff the cloth to check for raw sewage odor bleeding through the hose walls.
tasks.caution_notes: Sniff-test the hose runs for odor permeation - once a hose wicks through it must be replaced, not cleaned.

tasks.name: Black Water Pumps - Nitrile Diaphragm & Valve Overhaul
tasks.description: Unbolt the head ring to completely swap out the primary pump head diaphragm and the dual heavy-duty non-return tricuspid valves.
tasks.caution_notes: Use the pump maker's black-water diaphragm/valve kit (nitrile for odor containment). On reassembly the central backing plate's rounded edge must face the diaphragm - a sharp edge slices it open within a month. No 90-degree elbows straight on the barbs. Never run liquid bleach or caustic cleaner through the heads (warps the tricuspid valves).

tasks.name: Black Water Pumps - System Flow Clearance
tasks.description: Flush fresh water through the empty bowl and pump it directly into the tank lines to dilute residual raw sewage sitting inside the pump head.
tasks.caution_notes: After every tank discharge, run fresh water through the empty bowl and pump it to the tank lines - raw sewage left standing in the pump and hose breeds the smell and the hydrogen sulfide that eats stainless from inside. Nitrile kit AK1557 for this pump (odour containment), not Santoprene.

tasks.name: Black Water Pumps - Uric Scale Mitigation
tasks.description: Pump a marine-safe biodegradable descaler or white vinegar through the system to prevent calcium scale from building up and seizing the tricuspid flap valves.
tasks.caution_notes: Hot fresh-water flushes to keep uric scale from locking the valves - no harsh chemicals down the heads.

tasks.name: Black Water Tanks - Run the Black Water Pumps for 1 minute
tasks.description: the tanks are small and will fill up quickly under heavy use
tasks.caution_notes: The holding tanks are small and fill fast with guests - run the black-water pumps a minute at every legal opportunity or pump-out rather than letting a full tank back up into the bowls. Track the fill rate so you know real capacity in hours.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Bonding System Continuity Test
tasks.description: Multimeter on the low-ohms range: confirm under 1 ohm from every bonded fitting (each seacock, shaft brush, engine, genset, tanks, mast step, chainplates) back to the common bonding bus.
tasks.caution_notes: A high-resistance bond is worse than none - it hides a fitting that is corroding alone. Redo the reading after any work that disturbs the bus.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Engine Heat-Exchanger Zinc
tasks.description: Pull and inspect the main engine heat-exchanger pencil zinc (also flagged at 250 h under the engine system).
tasks.caution_notes: Some modern common-rail engines have no HX anode and are bonding-protected (check the exhaust mixing elbow too). If there is none, this task is: confirm the engine bonding strap and inspect the HX / elbow for internal corrosion. The block then relies entirely on the hull bonding-plate anodes and the shaft zinc - so those matter more.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Genset Heat-Exchanger Zinc
tasks.description: Pull and inspect the generator heat-exchanger pencil zinc.
tasks.caution_notes: In warm salt water this can be 50% gone in 3-4 weeks - check it monthly, not by run-hours. Carry a dozen spares and a spare brass plug; any broken zinc fragments must be fished out of the heat exchanger or they block tubes.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Hull Bonding-Plate Anode(s)
tasks.description: Replace the hull-mounted plate / teardrop zinc(s) wired to the green bonding bus. Size and count per the builder's bonding schematic.
tasks.caution_notes: These protect every bronze seacock, the shaft, and the engine/genset from galvanic and stray-current attack. If they are wasted, everything bonded is corroding together - this is the anode that matters most for the thru-hulls.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Reference Electrode / Hull Potential Survey
tasks.description: If a silver/silver-chloride reference electrode is aboard, read hull potential at the dock and adrift.
tasks.caution_notes: -550 to -1100 mV indicates adequate protection for bronze and steel. Over -1100 mV (over-protection - often an isolation-transformer or galvanic-isolator fault) blisters bottom paint and softens wood core around fastenings.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Rudder Stock Bonding & Crevice Check
tasks.description: The rudder carries NO anode (glass blade, foam core, stainless frame + stock). While hauled: confirm the bonding strap from the SS rudder stock to the green bus is intact and reads low-ohms, and inspect the stock where it enters the glass and at the bearing lands for crevice-corrosion staining, pitting or weeping rust.
tasks.caution_notes: With no anode, the bonding strap is the ONLY protection - stray current and galvanic attack find an unbonded stainless part first, and an isolated SS stock crevice-corrodes inside the bearing where you can't see it until it seizes or cracks. Check the strap every haul; redo the ohm reading after any work near the quadrant.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Shaft Anode Replacement
tasks.description: Replace the shaft collar zinc (or prop-nut anode) at haul-out or when more than ~50% wasted; fit on clean bare shaft with both set screws wired.
tasks.caution_notes: Warm salt water eats a shaft zinc in 60-90 days. A missing shaft anode dumps the whole galvanic load onto the prop hub and the cutless-bearing area.

tasks.name: Bosun's Chair & Aloft Gear - Bosun's Chair Condition Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect the bosun's chair: seat board / fabric, all webbing and load straps, every line of stitching, the main lifting ring / shackle and any secondary attachment loop, buckles, and the tool pouches. Check the date - retire UV-aged or shock-loaded webbing.
tasks.caution_notes: You are hanging your whole weight off this 30 m up. Sun-rotted webbing and chafed stitching at the lift ring are the failure points, and they are not always obvious - flex every seam and pull-test. A canvas board-and-strap chair beats a bare plank. If in any doubt, it is a cheap replacement against a fall.

tasks.name: Bosun's Chair & Aloft Gear - Pre-Aloft Rig & Backup Check
tasks.description: Before every trip aloft: inspect the halyard and its shackle end to end, rig an INDEPENDENT backup (a second halyard or a climbing line on an ascender / prusik to the chair), check the winch and its self-tailer, brief the tender and the person going up on stop / lower commands, wear a helmet, and empty loose gear from pockets.
tasks.caution_notes: Most aloft accidents are a single halyard failing (a worn sheave, a corroded shackle, a mis-clutched line) or a winch mistake - the backup line is what saves you, so it must be genuinely independent and tended. Never go up on a snap shackle. Tie into the chair ring with a bowline as well as the shackle. Do not go aloft solo or in a seaway.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Electrical Terminal Service
tasks.description: Check positive and negative wire crimps for salt-air oxidation. Confirm the supply line is protected by its correctly rated fuse.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the pump's voltage and current draw from its label and size the fuse to match. Check the crimps for salt oxidation.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Full Head Rebuild
tasks.description: Open the pump body to pull and replace the cyclical Santoprene diaphragm and the mechanical non-return tricuspid valves.
tasks.caution_notes: Santoprene kit AK1550. On reassembly the backing-plate rounded edge must face the diaphragm or it cuts through within weeks.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Head Ring Alignment Check
tasks.description: Ensure the central Ezi-Twist single-screw locking clamp ring hasn't vibrated loose from engine harmonics.
tasks.caution_notes: The single Ezi-Twist clamp ring is all that holds the pump head together and engine harmonics back its screw off. Check it tight and the head halves square - a creeping ring lets the diaphragm chamber leak.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Hose Joint Check
tasks.description: Verify that the 3/4" reinforced smooth-bore sanitation hoses connected to the dual 45° angle ports are tightly sealed.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the smooth-bore sanitation hose at both 45-degree ports for tight joints - a weeping grey-water joint in a locker smells and grows biofilm. Smooth-bore only; corrugated hose halves the flow of an already low-flow pump.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Inline Float Switch Check
tasks.description: Applies to both the bow and the E/R pump. Lift the linked bilge float or intelligent IC sensor to confirm the pump immediately cycles under full current.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift the float / IC sensor and confirm the pump cycles at full current with no lag. If it is an IC (field-effect) sensor, wipe its face - an oily film makes it false-trigger or miss.

tasks.name: Bow & Engine Room Bilge Pumps - Remote Strainer Clearing
tasks.description: Applies to both the bow and the E/R pump. Clear any hair, lint, or heavy sludge caught in the small-footprint 3/4" remote intake strainer sitting at the lowest point of the bilge.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear the remote intake strainer at the low point - hair and sludge collect there, not at the pump. A blocked strainer makes the pump cavitate and hammer.

tasks.name: Companionway slider - lubricate
tasks.description: the inside bearings are not SS
tasks.caution_notes: If rebuilding the ball-transfer blocks, swap the high-carbon steel balls (they seize in salt air) for captive 5/32" silicon-nitride ceramic balls - ~90-96 per block, ~576 for six blocks - so it runs dry with no grease. Leave one ball's gap per loop to prevent binding; ease the sharp 90-degree rail entry points with fine sandpaper so the ceramic does not chip.

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - Anti-Airlock Vent Clearing
tasks.description: Inspect the small bleed hole molded into the pump's impeller housing chamber to verify it isn't blocked by slime or bilge crust.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear the small weep/vent hole in the volute - blocked, the pump can air-lock after it draws the bilge down and sit spinning dry against a bubble while the water rises. A 1/8" hole in the discharge hose just above the pump is the backup.

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - Centrifugal Impeller Check
tasks.description: Spin the exposed red plastic impeller by hand to ensure it turns freely on the shaft and isn't bound up by tangled fishing line or debris.
tasks.caution_notes: A large crash pump (4000 GPH class) pulls 15-20 A under load - it needs a correctly sized fuse (about 25 A) and 10-8 AWG wire; undersized wiring drops voltage and output badly. Smooth-bore discharge hose only (corrugated costs up to 40% flow).

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - Discharge Hose Hose-Clamp Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the heavy 2-inch ID smooth-bore discharge hose where it fastens to the pump's discharge port.
tasks.caution_notes: Double 316 stainless clamps on every joint below the waterline.

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - Float Switch Manual Trip
tasks.description: Manually lift the associated float switch arm (e.g., Rule 37A or 40A) to ensure the pump instantly kicks on without catching or sticking.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift the float arm - the pump must start instantly with no hesitation. A crash pump you test monthly is one you can trust; if it lags, the switch contacts are pitting - replace the switch, not the pump. Confirm the high-water alarm fires too.

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - High-Amp Marine Wire Inspection
tasks.description: Examine the gas-tight water-blocked marine wire connections. Ensure heat-shrink butt connectors are pristine, as corrosion drops voltage and flow.
tasks.caution_notes: 25 A fuse, 10-8 AWG minimum. Check for voltage drop under load at the pump.

tasks.name: Crash Bilge Pump - Strainer Base De-Trash
tasks.description: Depress the side tabs to pop the pump body off its snap-lock strainer base. Clear out hair, stray zip-ties, limpets, or sludge blocking the intake mesh.
tasks.caution_notes: Pop the pump off its strainer base and clear hair, zip-ties, cans, limpets - a centrifugal impeller loses most of its output to a half-blocked intake, and this pump's whole job is moving a lot of water fast. Check the impeller spins freely.

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Anodizing & Galvanic Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the interface where stainless steel mounting bolts pass through the aluminum tracks for bubbling white powder (aluminum oxide).
tasks.caution_notes: Check where stainless bolts pass through the aluminum track - galvanic corrosion eats the track under the bolt heads unseen. Isolate with Tef-Gel.

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Bearing Integrity Check
tasks.description: Manually roll traveler and genoa cars along their tracks to feel for flat spots, grinding, or missing internal ball bearings.
tasks.caution_notes: Feel for flat spots or grit. The original Delrin balls are 35+ years old and now brittle - they can shatter under shock load; replace proactively with the size specified per car (1/4" or 5/16").

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Deck Organizer Sheave Care
tasks.description: Flush out the stacked deck organizer sheaves near the mast base, checking for axial play or plastic hairline cracks under load.
tasks.caution_notes: Flush the stacked organizer sheaves at the mast base; check each for axial play and hairline cracks. A seized organizer sheave chews the line cover and adds enough friction that a reef won't run under load. Dry-lube only.

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - End-Stop Fastener Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the structural stainless steel screws securing the traveler track end-caps and mechanical line sheaves.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the screws holding the traveler and genoa-track end stops - they take the full shock if a car runs off under load, and a lost end stop means a car and the sail's clew leave the track at speed. Wired or thread-locked.

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Genie/Genoa Car Plunger Lubrication
tasks.description: Clean the spring-loaded pinstop plungers on the genoa cars so they snap cleanly into the track adjustment holes without sticking.
tasks.caution_notes: Clean and dry-lube the genoa-car spring plungers so they seat fully and snap out cleanly - a half-engaged plunger shears under load and then you can't move the car. No wet lube (holds grit).

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Teak & Foredeck Handhold Check
tasks.description: Bare (unoiled) teak on the cockpit and handholds: rinse and gently scrub with a soft brush and mild soap along the grain - no pressure washer. Look for open seams, lifted or missing bungs, cracks and soft or rotted wood. HANDHOLDS: push and pull each one hard; it must not move. Check the fasteners and the bedding under each base for water getting into the deck or core.

tasks.name: Deck Hardware - Track Re-Bedding & Sealing
tasks.description: Pull high-load tracks entirely off the deck, clean away decayed original sealant, and apply fresh marine bedding to prevent deck core rot.
tasks.caution_notes: Pull the tracks fully, remove all old sealant, and re-bed with 3M 4000UV to keep water out of the balsa deck core. New stainless washers and nyloc nuts on reassembly.

tasks.name: Depth, Speed & Temp Transducer - App Calibration & Firmware Check
tasks.description: If the transducer has a maker's Bluetooth app, connect to it to verify attitude pitch/heel calibration and pull internal system logs.
tasks.caution_notes: Verify the pitch/heel (attitude) offsets still match how the transducer sits in the hull, and note the firmware version. A drifted attitude offset throws the speed and depth corrections. Do it hauled or at rest.

tasks.name: Depth, Speed & Temp Transducer - NMEA 2000 Drop Cable Check
tasks.description: Check the Micro-C connector joining the transducer drop wire to your main NMEA 2000 network backbone for stable voltage and tight indexing.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the Micro-C tee and drop cable to the transducer for a tight lock-ring and clean pins - a marginal drop connector browns the pins, the sensor drops off the bus intermittently, and you chase a 'bad transducer' that is really a cheap cable. Confirm the backbone is powered and terminated both ends.

tasks.name: Depth, Speed & Temp Transducer - O-Ring Inspection & Grease
tasks.description: Examine the dual rubber O-rings on the sensor body and the blanking plug for flattening, pinching, or dry-rot.
tasks.caution_notes: Silicone grease on the sleeve O-rings. Push/pull the sensor straight - never twist.

tasks.name: Depth, Speed & Temp Transducer - Paddlewheel Growth Scraping
tasks.description: Soak the pulled sensor head in a jar to dissolve encrusted barnacle rings and use a soft pick to clear the paddle cavity.
tasks.caution_notes: Gen2 paddlewheel + pin kit aboard; clear growth before it binds the wheel.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Aft Deck Tie-Down Eye Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the structural pad-eyes and heavy ratchet/webbing straps on your aft deck to ensure they are secure before lashing the dinghy down for a passage.
tasks.caution_notes: On passage the dinghy lashes flat to the aft deck, clear of the solar array shadow.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Freshwater Washdown
tasks.description: Rinse the entire dinghy and flush the outboard's lower unit / shaft casing with fresh water to clear salt crusting.
tasks.caution_notes: Rinse the whole dinghy and flush fresh water through the outboard's lower unit - salt in the shaft casing corrodes the motor hardware and seizes the tilt. No pressure washer (it drives water past the lip seals).

tasks.name: Dinghy - Hull, Transom & Drain-Plug Inspection
tasks.description:
Inspect the fiberglass hull and keel for gelcoat cracks and impact damage, the tube-to-hull bond seam, the transom and its outboard clamp pad, the tow eye and lifting/D-rings, the rubrail, and the bailer / drain plug and its O-ring.

Drain any water from the inner hull and the raceway from the locker to the stern
tasks.caution_notes: The tube-to-hull glued seam and the transom are where a RIB fails with age and sun - run a fingernail along the seam looking for lifting edges. A missing or perished drain-plug O-ring swamps the dinghy on the painter overnight; carry a spare plug. Check the tow eye and davit rings for elongation or crazing before every offshore leg - a let-go while towing is a lost dinghy.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Hypalon Tube UV Defense
tasks.description: Scrub the dinghy's tubes to remove exhaust soot and buff on a high-grade UV protectant to prevent the fabric from breaking down or getting sticky.
tasks.caution_notes: 303 Aerospace Protectant (or similar) on Hypalon. No pressure washer on an outboard, especially an electric one - it drives water past the lip seals and can flood the motor.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Lifting Tackle Component Check
tasks.description: Inspect the lines, shackles, and hinge pins of the lift array mounted under your solar frame to ensure everything rolls smoothly for night hoisting.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the hoist lines, shackles and hinge pins under the solar frame - this rig lifts the full RIB + motor + fuel every day and a failed shackle drops it (or you) in the water. Mouse every shackle, retire chafed line.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Outboard Propeller Shaft Service
tasks.description: Check the outboard's underwater propeller shaft for tangled fishing line or seaweed wraps that can tear out the internal seals.
tasks.caution_notes: Carry propeller shear pins. Keep the pressure washer away from the outboard casing.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Knock-Apart Anchor Hardware Care
tasks.description: Unzip the storage bag and inspect the knock-apart bolts, structural pins, and hex-wrench tools inside to ensure no moisture is trapped inside the bag casing.
tasks.caution_notes: Coat the knock-apart anchor bolt threads with Tef-Gel or WD-40 before packing it in its bag - damp threads seize from crevice corrosion.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Outboard Idle-Period Run
tasks.description: If the dinghy outboard has not run in ~2 weeks, run it briefly (in a tank or off the transom at the dock) and cycle the tilt.
tasks.caution_notes: An outboard and its tilt mechanism seize from disuse and salt far faster than from running. A short run also keeps the prop-shaft seal wetted and the electrics from sitting damp.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Solar Nav Light Cell Clearing
tasks.description: Wipe the small integrated solar panel on top of the dinghy navigation light to ensure dried salt spray isn't blocking solar cell absorption.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe the solar cell on the dinghy nav light - a salt film cuts the charge and the light will not last the night, which is exactly when you are running back to the boat.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Tube Repair Kit & CSM Adhesive Shelf-Life
tasks.description: Inventory the dinghy repair kit (tube fabric, patches, valve wrench, spare valve) and REPLACE the adhesive annually - it is a consumable with a hard shelf life.
tasks.caution_notes: Know your tube fabric: Hypalon/CSM tubes need a 2-part CSM adhesive and PVC cement will not hold; PVC tubes need PVC adhesive. Two-part glue is dead roughly a year after mixing and weeks in a hot lazarette, so buy fresh and date it. Carry enough fabric and patches for a hand-sized tear on one tube. Practice a dry patch once so you are not learning it in the water.

tasks.name: Dinghy - Valve Service & Tube Pressure Check
tasks.description: Check each tube valve (Halkey-Roberts / Leafield type) for a clean seat and a non-spinning core, replace the valve O-ring, and set each chamber to the printed pressure with a gauge. Confirm the valve wrench is aboard.
tasks.caution_notes: Use the pressure printed on the tube (often about 3.4 psi / 250 mbar) - soft tubes flex the hull joint and pound in chop; over-pressure in the sun splits a seam. Inflate in the shade and top up as it cools. A weeping valve is the most common slow leak and is a 2-minute O-ring fix. Keep spare valve inserts and O-rings in the repair kit.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Annual Jug Count, Condition & Stowage Security
tasks.description: Account for every drinking-water jug plus the bottled-water reserve, confirm each jug is serviceable (no persistent smell, taste or haze that won't clean, no crazing), and check the stowage: a full 5-gal jug is 35-42 lb and a set of them is well over 150 lb - chock and strap them so nothing breaks loose in a knockdown, and keep them out of direct sun.
tasks.caution_notes: Retire a jug on smell, taste or haze - they're cheap against a passage with bad water. A loose full 5-gal jug is a 40 lb projectile below decks; part-filling for handling also keeps the stow lighter. Budget a jug replacement every couple of years in the tropics; translucent jugs are the first to watch.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Bottled-Water Reserve - Stock & Rotation
tasks.description: Confirm at least one case of bottled water per person aboard for the planned passage length, stowed cool, dark and reachable as the emergency / abandon-ship reserve. Rotate oldest-first - drink the near-dated cases down ashore and replace. Check for crushed, swollen or weeping bottles and for a plastic taste.
tasks.caution_notes: Bottled water is a taste-life item, not a safety-life item - warm-stowed PET goes off in flavour in a year or two and the case cardboard collapses in damp. It's the backup for a watermaker failure and part of the grab-bag plan, so it has to be accessible, not buried under the spare anchor. Scale the case count to crew x passage weeks.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Jug Cap, Gasket, Spigot & Body Check
tasks.description: Check each jug's screw-cap threads and the cap gasket/seal for deformation or perishing, the spigot/tap and any vent for cracks, drips and a clean seal, and the handle and body for stress cracks or hazing - translucent jugs especially, and any that have seen sun. Keep a spare spigot assembly with them and carry gasket stock.
tasks.caution_notes: A cap that no longer seals lets air and contamination in and lets water weep out in a seaway. HDPE goes brittle with age and heat and cracks at the handle root and the base corners first. The translucent jug grows algae in any light - keep it boxed or shaded, or make it the first to retire.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Jug Deep Clean & Sanitize
tasks.description: Staggered across the jugs: scrub the interior with a bottle brush, fill with a dilute unscented-bleach solution (about 1 tsp per gallon), cap and let stand ~15 min with a spell on its side to wet the cap and threads, dump, then rinse two or three times with watermaker water and air-dry cap-off. Do the spigot and vent cap too.
tasks.caution_notes: Biofilm builds on the walls and in the cap threads where the brush and the rinse don't reach - that is the source of a taste a plain refill won't fix. Don't use scented or splash-less bleach (additives you can't rinse out). If a jug still smells after sanitizing, retire it. A tank shock treatment is the equivalent job for the ship's tanks.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Jug Fill & Rotation
tasks.description: Keep the jugs in rotation off the watermaker: part-fill each to about 2 gal so it stays liftable, date it as you fill, use the oldest first, and don't let a filled jug sit more than about 2 weeks. When a jug comes empty, take the cap off, invert it to drain, and let it dry fully before the next fill.
tasks.caution_notes: RO permeate has no chlorine residual - anything that gets in grows, and a warm cabin speeds it up. Stale RO water tastes flat and plasticky before it is actually unsafe; a slick feel inside the neck or a musty smell means clean the jug, don't just refill it. Marking the fill date is the whole discipline - an undated jug is an unknown.

tasks.name: Drinking Water - Watermaker Fill-Point Hygiene
tasks.description: Each drinking-water fill: run the watermaker's freshwater flush / product run to spec so the first water isn't stale membrane water, use the dedicated clean hose or funnel (stored capped, drinking-water only), keep the outlet from touching the jug mouth, and wash your hands. Never fill drinking jugs from a dock hose.
tasks.caution_notes: The jugs are only as clean as the last thing that touched them. A shared deck-wash hose, a funnel that lived loose in a locker, or the product hose lying in the bilge undoes the sanitizing. The watermaker's own first draw after a flush carries preservative or stagnant permeate - run it off first. A jug pump's tube and neck seal are a contamination point too - rinse and dry it.

tasks.name: Chart subscriptions - renewal check
tasks.description: Chart-plotter and app chart subscriptions usually renew yearly (often automatically). About 30 days ahead, check the card on file, the price, and whether each subscription is still wanted. Mark done with the renewal date.

tasks.name: Fire Alarms - Exterior De-Salt Wipe
tasks.description: Wipe down the plastic outer shell with a dry or very lightly damp cloth to remove sticky salt residue that acts as a moisture magnet.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe the salt film off the shell - salt is hygroscopic, it holds damp against the electronics and the battery contacts corrode.

tasks.name: Fire Alarms - Manual Test-Button Audit
tasks.description: Firmly press and hold the central test button on each unit until the horn sounds to verify the electronic circuitry, internal horn, and 10-year lithium battery remain perfectly viable.
tasks.caution_notes: Hold the test button until the horn sounds - this proves the horn and circuit, not the sensor. Monthly. Note which units are getting quiet (end of life).

tasks.name: Fire Alarms - Sensing Chamber De-Dusting
tasks.description: Use a tiny blast of clean compressed air to sweep the sensor vents. Dust bunnies, fabric fibers from berths, and micro-salt crystals can block the internal optical sensor, creating false "ghost" alarms or delaying detection.
tasks.caution_notes: A gentle puff of clean air through the sensor vents - berth lint and cooking film in the chamber cause both 3am false alarms and a slow sensor when it counts. No canned-air propellant directly (residue).

tasks.name: Fire Alarms - Ultimate 10-Year Replacement
tasks.description: Look at the date-of-manufacture stamp on the back of the alarm body. Completely retire and replace the units after a decade, as the internal ionization or photoelectric sensors naturally degrade over time.
tasks.caution_notes: Sealed 10-year smoke alarms - replace the whole unit at the 10-year mark, do not just swap batteries.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Aerosol Fire Stick (Element) Check
tasks.description: Check each Element E100 (40100) stick: still within its printed manufacture / replace-by window, strike-cap and safety intact, body undented and uncorroded, mounted and reachable at every quick-grab point (galley, nav, engine access, helm), and that everyone aboard knows you STRIKE the cap - it is not pull-pin-squeeze. Replace any that have been discharged (single use) or heat-cycled hard.
tasks.caution_notes: The Element stick is supplemental fire cover, NOT a USCG-approved extinguisher - it does not count toward the required number, so keep the approved canisters at full strength regardless. Its whole appeal is no gauge / no service, but it does age: check the date and the cap, and swap it out at end of life. One stick is ~100 s of discharge - good for a flare-up, not a developed fire.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Dry Chemical Powder Agitation
tasks.description: Unlatch each dry-chemical (Monoammonium Phosphate) extinguisher, flip it upside down, and vigorously strike the base with a rubber mallet. This loosens packed powder.
tasks.caution_notes: Hull pounding packs dry-chem powder into a solid cake that will not discharge - rap each cylinder with a rubber mallet monthly to keep the powder loose.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Hydrostatic / Ultimate Replacement
tasks.description: Retire standard disposable marine canisters or send refillable commercial units out for hydrostatic pressure chamber testing.
tasks.caution_notes: B-I / B-II replacements on hand; note the hydrostatic/replacement date.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Nozzle & Safety Pin Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the plastic discharge horns for spider webs or salt crusting, and verify the metal pull-pin and plastic tamper seal are unbroken.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear webs and salt from the horn, confirm the pull-pin is seated and the tamper seal intact. A blocked horn back-pressures and can burst; cable-tie the tamper seal, never the pin.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Pressure Gauge Field Check
tasks.description: Scan the dial on every interior canister to ensure the physical needle remains locked dead-center in the solid GREEN zone.
tasks.caution_notes: Needle dead-centre in the green on every canister, monthly, and heft each one - a light bottle has lost charge. A gauge reading low is already partly discharged; swap it now, do not wait for the annual.

tasks.name: Fire Extinguishers - Quick-Release Mount Check
tasks.description: Test the marine retention brackets. They must clamp the heavy canisters securely during pounding seas but release instantly with one hand when pulled.
tasks.caution_notes: Test each bracket - it must hold a heavy bottle through a knockdown but let go with one pull in a smoke-filled cabin. A corroded or paint-locked bracket has killed people; exercise them.

tasks.name: First Aid & AED - AED Battery / Pads Replacement
tasks.description: Replace the AED's consumables (battery and pads - some units use a single cartridge holding both) by the expiry date on the label, often about 4 years. Some suppliers track the expiry and email a reminder; replacements can be scarce, so order early. Read the expiry off the label and set this period to match.

tasks.name: First Aid & AED - AED Status & Pad / Battery Check
tasks.description: Check the AED's status indicator is green, the pads are sealed and in date, and the battery is in date. Note the pad and battery expiry dates on the device notes.

tasks.name: First Aid & AED - Kit Expiry & Restock Audit
tasks.description: Open every kit (primary, heads, ditch bag): check the dates on medications, dressings and sterile items, restock what was used, and record what expires next.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Drag & Line Freshwater Rinse
tasks.description: Back off the drag levers/star wheels completely and hose down the reels, line spools, and rod guides to dissolve salt crusting.
tasks.caution_notes: Rinse after every strike; a thin anti-corrosion film on the reels stops rust bloom in the humid forward cabin.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Line Guide Roller Lubrication
tasks.description: Apply a single drop of high-speed oil to the line guide rollers on the rods and the level-wind worm gears on the reels.
tasks.caution_notes: A drop of reel oil on the roller guides and the level-wind worm - a dry roller flat-spots and saws the line under a run. Oil, never grease (grease collects salt and grit).

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Monofilament / Braid Line Trim
tasks.description: Pull off and discard the first 20 to 30 feet of trolling line to clear away hidden chafe or UV-weakened sections caused by sun exposure in the rod holders.
tasks.caution_notes: Steel-wire top-shots for wahoo at ~6 kn.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Conventional Reel Internal Packing
tasks.description: Open the side plates of conventional (star-drag) reels and pack the gears with thick, salt-blocking reel grease.
tasks.caution_notes: Reel grease/oil and spare carbon drag washers on hand. Store with the drag backed off.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Lever-Drag Reel Service
tasks.description: Strip down the side plates of lever-drag reels to clean the ball bearings and apply a light coat of anti-corrosive grease to the aluminium frames.
tasks.caution_notes: Reel grease/oil and spare carbon drag washers on hand. Store with the drag backed off.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Trolling Holder Fastener Check
tasks.description: Inspect the sub-deck backing plates and sealing washers on your 4 trolling rod holders to ensure heavy strikes haven't stressed the fiberglass gunwales.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the sub-deck backing plates and bedding on the four rod holders - a strike loads them in a direction the deck was not laid up for; a holder that pulls its backing plate takes a chunk of deck and leaks. Re-bed on any weep.

tasks.name: Fishing Gear - Rod Rack Audit
tasks.description: Check the mounting screws of the rod racks to ensure boat slamming hasn't loosened them.
tasks.caution_notes: Back the drag stars/levers to zero before racking rods - stored under tension, carbon drag washers flatten permanently and lose smooth payout.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Pressure Pump - Diaphragm & Valve Inspection
tasks.description: Unscrew the pump head housing screws to inspect the internal Santoprene diaphragm and check valves for debris punctures or calcium buildup.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the head, inspect the Santoprene diaphragm for pin-holes and the check valves for grit and calcium. Carry one full head/valve service kit per pump type - a split diaphragm is a dockside-unavailable part in most of the cruising world.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Pressure Pump - Electrical Terminal Check
tasks.description: Verify that crimps and connections at the automatic demand pressure switch are clean, corrosion-free, and receiving stable voltage.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the crimps at the demand pressure switch and the 24V supply for corrosion and stable voltage - a marginal joint makes the switch chatter (rapid on/off at the tap) and burns its contacts.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Pressure Pump - Inlet Strainer Cleaning
tasks.description: Twist off the clear plastic strainer bowl, pull out the mesh screen, and flush out accumulated sediment.
tasks.caution_notes: Twist off the clear strainer bowl, pull the mesh screen, flush. A blocked strainer starves the pump - it runs hot and loud and diaphragm life drops.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Pressure Pump - Sanitize Water System
tasks.description: Flush the lines with a mild food-grade sanitizing agent to prevent biofilm accumulation in the pump's 5 inner chambers.
tasks.caution_notes: Run a food-grade sanitiser through the whole system, dwell, then flush thoroughly - biofilm in the pump chambers and lines is the usual 'water tastes off'. Isolate the watermaker and the Waterdrop filter first.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Pressure Pump - Visual Leak & Noise Check
tasks.description: Inspect plumbing fittings for slow drips and check that rubber vibration-damping feet are secure to prevent mounting noise.
tasks.caution_notes: Look for weeping at the head screws and port fittings and confirm the rubber feet are sound - a hard-mounted pump telegraphs through the boat and the vibration eventually cracks a fitting. A pump that cycles on its own with every tap shut has a system leak or a failed check valve.

tasks.name: Fresh Water Tanks - Freshwater Loop Chlorination
tasks.description: Sanitize the dual 100-gallon fresh water tanks to kill biofilm without letting localized chlorine concentrations pit the 316 stainless welds.
tasks.caution_notes: Never leave strong chlorine sitting in the stainless tanks more than 4-6 hours - free chlorine drives intergranular stress-corrosion cracking along the 316 weld lines. Dilute heavily and flush promptly.

tasks.name: Fuel / Oil - Hose Material Fatigue Check
tasks.description: Inspect the flexible supply lines connecting the oil pans and fuel manifolds. Look for kinking, stiffness, or heat hardening near engine blocks.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the flexible lines on the fuel-polishing and oil-change manifolds for stiffness, cracking and heat-hardening near the engine - they see suction and are the forgotten hoses. A collapsed suction hose starves the polishing pump; a split pressure hose is a diesel spray. USCG A1/B1 fuel hose only.

tasks.name: Fuel / Oil - Manifold Safety Valve Audit
tasks.description: Verify that all directional selector valves (Port/Starboard fuel or Engine/Gen oil) lock cleanly into their detents without internal cross-bleeding.
tasks.caution_notes: Cycle every selector valve (port/stbd fuel, engine/gen oil) and confirm each locks positively in its detent - a valve that creeps off can cross-feed tanks (overflow out the vent) or draw the wrong sump. Label every position; a mis-set oil-change valve pumps the engine sump into the gearbox.

tasks.name: Fuel Filter / Water Separator - Collection Bowl Deep Clean
tasks.description: Remove the bowl assembly and scrub away internal biological algae slime or asphaltene coatings that resist standard draining.
tasks.caution_notes: Pull the metal bowl and scrub off the asphaltene film and biofilm that draining will not shift. Inspect the bowl seal and the self-vent valve while it is apart.

tasks.name: Fuel Filter / Water Separator - Complete Unit Rebuild
tasks.description: Disassemble the entire casting down to the bare metal body to inspect the internal check-ball seal, centripetal spring, and replace all dried gaskets.
tasks.caution_notes: Full seal/gasket kit - lid, bowl, drain valve, check-ball. Inspect the centrifuge cone and turbine for cracks. Do this at the dock, with a spare filter assembly plumbed in or the boat immobile.

tasks.name: Fuel Filter / Water Separator - Filter Element Replacement
tasks.description: Unscrew the T-handle, remove the lid, pull the filter element out via its wire bail handles, and drop in a new Aquabloc cartridge.
tasks.caution_notes: T-handle off, lid off, element out by the bail. Prime the new element with clean fuel before fitting; smear the lid O-ring with fuel, hand-tighten only. This stage is the 30-micron primary - the 10/2-micron stages are downstream. Carry 3+ elements.

tasks.name: Fuel Filter / Water Separator - Vacuum Gauge Check
tasks.description: Check the optional line vacuum gauge under load. A spike in vacuum pressure (7–10 inHg) flags a restricted filter block.
tasks.caution_notes: Read the restriction gauge at cruise rpm under load. Clean element sits near zero; change at ~7-10 in-Hg, well before the 15 in-Hg where the lift pump cavitates. A sharp jump means an algae slug or cold-fuel wax, not gradual loading.

tasks.name: Fuel Filter / Water Separator - Water & Contaminant Draining
tasks.description: Loosen the bottom drain plug to evacuate water and heavy sludge collected below the internal centrifuge mechanism.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the bowl drain into a jar until clean fuel runs - before every start and daily on passage. Water reaching a common-rail pump is the fastest route to a scrapped HP pump. A fast-filling bowl means the tank has water: polish it.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Cross-Transfer for Trim & Balance
tasks.description: Move fuel PORT<->STARBOARD through the RACOR to correct a list and to keep both tank-sets (and their senders) in a useful range. Log the quantity and reset the selectors to a known state afterward.
tasks.caution_notes: Always transfer THROUGH the RACOR, never tank-to-tank raw - the transfer is a free polish. Set the DESTINATION selector first and confirm it, then the source: a mis-set destination overflows a full tank out the deck vent. Do not walk away from a running transfer.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Fuel Additive Dosing at Fill-Up
tasks.description: At every fuel fill-up, dose biocide (Biobor JF) plus a lubricity/stability additive, calculated to the gallons taken on. Before the passage / fuel run, confirm enough additive is aboard for the fills you expect.
tasks.caution_notes: Dose INTO the tank while filling - the fill turbulence mixes it; adding it after leaves it stratified. Treat every load of dock fuel of unknown quality, no exceptions - the bug grows at the fuel/water interface. If a tank sat untreated or the fuel smells sour, shock-dose at the higher 'kill' rate, then polish. Keep the biocide stocked as a consumable with a real minimum quantity - running out in a remote anchorage is not a quick fix.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Full Polish Cycle (Port & Starboard)
tasks.description: Circulate at least one full volume of each tank-set through the RACOR and back (or cross to the other set). Drain the RACOR bowl before and after; watch the restriction gauge through the run.
tasks.caution_notes: This is the actual polish - distinct from the monthly 'run the pump so it does not gum'. Do a cycle before any passage and after taking on fuel from a questionable source. A gauge that climbs mid-cycle means the tank is dirtier than the last RACOR element showed - change the element and cycle again. Turn the pickup-side stirring up on purpose: run near a full or near a low tank so the return jet agitates the sludge you are trying to catch.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Impeller / Gear Pump Shaft Audit
tasks.description: Examine the oil extraction pump housing and fuel transfer pump shaft seals for fluid tracking or slow weeping.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the transfer pump and oil-change pump shaft seals for weeping - a diesel drip in the bilge is both a fire load and a slow tank leak. Note whether it is the shaft seal (rebuildable) or the pump body (replace).

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Non-Return / Check-Valve Test
tasks.description: Verify the polish-loop check valve(s) (5/16 in. / 8 mm inline one-way): with the polish pump OFF there is no reverse flow / syphon back to the drawing tank, and with it ON the valve is not stuck shut and starving the pump. Check the arrow orientation and the hose clamps.
tasks.caution_notes: A check valve stuck OPEN lets the loop syphon between tanks or lets the pump lose prime; stuck SHUT deadheads the pump and cooks it. These cheap inline valves gum up with fuel varnish - flush or swap on any doubt, they are a stocked spare. Fit it the right way round (arrow = flow) and support the hose so the valve body is not taking load.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Polishing Pump Actuation
tasks.description: Flip the switch on the fuel transfer pump to circulate fuel for 5 minutes. Static fuel pumps are highly prone to vane-seizure or gumming if left dry.
tasks.caution_notes: Run the polishing pump ~5 min monthly even when the fuel looks clean - a gear or vane pump left dry gums and can seize. Monthly circulation also keeps biocide evenly dosed and pulls water to the RACOR before it stratifies.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Racor Vacuum Tracking
tasks.description: Monitor your line vacuum gauge while the polishing loop is active. High-volume polishing pumps will spike vacuum pressure fast if the element is dirty.
tasks.caution_notes: Watch the polisher's own restriction gauge while it runs - a high-flow polishing pump spikes vacuum far faster than the engine will, and that is the early warning that the tank is growing a bug. Rising vacuum run-over-run = shock-dose biocide and change elements.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Selector Valve Exercise & Placard Check
tasks.description: Cycle every source and destination selector through all positions; confirm positive detents and that the placard at the manifold matches the actual plumbing.
tasks.caution_notes: A stiff selector gets forced and cracks or ends up between positions (feeding air). A wrong placard during a night transfer or a tank-switch under way is how you end up with a dry common-rail feed. Photograph the correct valve line-up and keep it at the manifold.

tasks.name: Fuel Polishing - Suspect-Fuel Quarantine & Polish
tasks.description: After fuelling from a questionable source: keep that fuel isolated in one tank-set, draw a sump sample, and polish it 2-3 turnovers through the RACOR before feeding the engine from it.
tasks.caution_notes: Caribbean dock fuel is variable - water, rust and diesel bug are common. Isolating the new fuel means a bad load cannot contaminate your whole supply or strand you mid-passage. A clear jar sample settled 10 minutes tells you most of what you need.

tasks.name: Fuel Tanks - Fuel Sump Water Stripping
tasks.description: Turn on your auxiliary fuel transfer pump or open the dedicated sump petcock to draw a sample from the bottom of the fuel tank. Purge trapped condensed water to prevent microbial growth.
tasks.caution_notes: These are ex-water tanks converted to diesel - the original food-grade EPDM gaskets dissolve into black sludge in diesel and must be swapped to fuel-grade Nitrile (Buna-N) or Viton. Dose Biobor JF hard for the first ~4 fill-ups to kill algae behind the internal baffles.

tasks.name: Galley Water Filter - Bracket Mount Check
tasks.description: Ensure the structural wall bracket or cabinet mounting screws remain secure so the heavy, water-filled canister does not pull on the plumbing lines.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the bracket screws are tight - a full 10UB-CM housing is heavy, and a sagging bracket puts the load on the push-fit plumbing, which then leaks.

tasks.name: Galley Water Filter - Complete Canister Replacement
tasks.description: Twist off the old, exhausted canister and replace it to maintain proper chlorine, chemical, PFAS, and sediment reduction.
tasks.caution_notes: Replace with the filter maker's cartridge - prefer a chloramine-rated one, not just chlorine, which matters when topping up from municipal supplies. Shut the inlet, relieve pressure at the faucet, quarter-turn the old one out, date the housing.

tasks.name: Galley Water Filter - Leak Inspection
tasks.description: Check the 3/8" to 1/2" brass converter valves, the plastic push-to-connect hoses, and the quick-connect black plastic head assembly under the sink for slow drips or fitting fatigue.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the 3/8-1/2" adapter valves, the push-to-connect tubing and the quick-connect head - push-fit joints back out if the tube was not cut square or seated fully. Keep a drip tray under it; a slow leak in a closed cabinet grows mould before you see water.

tasks.name: Galley Water Filter - New Filter Activation Flush
tasks.description: Run cold water continuously through the freshly installed filter to clear manufacturing carbon fines and purge trapped air pockets.
tasks.caution_notes: Run the dedicated faucet cold ~5 minutes after a cartridge change to flush carbon fines and purge air - the first draw sputters and runs grey, that is normal.

tasks.name: Galley Water Filter - Stagnant Line Purge
tasks.description: If the home or vessel has been sitting empty, run the cold faucet to clear out stagnant, unchlorinated water sitting in the core.
tasks.caution_notes: After the boat has sat more than a few days, run the filter faucet a minute before drinking - the carbon block holds unchlorinated water and bacteria bloom in a warm stagnant filter. This is why it feeds a dedicated tap, not the galley supply.

tasks.name: Generator - Air Intake Filter Cleaning
tasks.description: Remove the foam air element from the tuned air intake silencer housing, wash it out, and let it dry completely.
tasks.caution_notes: Foam element in the tuned intake silencer - wash in warm soapy water, rinse, and dry fully before refitting. A damp or oiled element makes the engine hunt under load.

tasks.name: Generator - Belt & Zinc Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect the alternator drive belt tension/wear, and replace the pencil zinc anode inside the heat exchanger.
tasks.caution_notes: Drive belt deflection 3/8"-1/2" at mid-span; replace if frayed or glazed. Glance at the heat-exchanger pencil zinc while you are in there - but the real interval for it is monthly, under Bonding & Cathodic Protection.

tasks.name: Generator - Cooling Loop Flush & Descale
tasks.description: Drain internal antifreeze, flush the internal core tubes of the copper-nickel heat exchanger with a descaling solution, and refill.
tasks.caution_notes: 50/50 distilled water and a diesel-rated antifreeze containing SCAs (supplemental coolant additives) - automotive/IAT coolant lets the wet liners pit. 4.7 L (5 qt) system. At 1000 h also pull the heat exchanger for a professional clean and pressure test.

tasks.name: Generator - Engine Lubrication Service
tasks.description: Extract used engine oil using the built-in sump drain hose and replace the full-flow spin-on oil filter.
tasks.caution_notes: 3.8 L (4.0 US qt) oil, full-flow spin-on filter; use the built-in sump drain hose and drip tray. The 100-hour interval is deliberately short - the 1.3 L industrial block works hard for its output.

tasks.name: Generator - Exercise Run Under Load
tasks.description: Run the genset 30-60 minutes under a real load (salon AC, watermaker, battery charging, water heater) at least monthly - sooner if it has sat more than ~2 weeks.
tasks.caution_notes: An idle diesel deteriorates faster than a working one. Load it to at least 50% so it reaches full operating temperature and burns clean - a genset chronically run at no/low load glazes its bores and wet-stacks (unburnt fuel and carbon in the exhaust elbow). The run also warms off crankcase moisture, keeps the raw-water impeller from taking a set, dries the alternator windings, and circulates fresh fuel through the injectors. Confirm raw-water discharge, no alarms, and clean exhaust after a minute.

tasks.name: Generator - Pre-Start Checks
tasks.description: Verify oil level on the dipstick, look for fuel/coolant leaks, and check the raw water sea-strainer basket for grass or debris.
tasks.caution_notes: Dipstick, no fuel/coolant pooling, sea-strainer clear, seacock open. After start, confirm raw-water discharge at the exhaust within ~15 s - no stream means a dry impeller, shut down. Max operating heel: 15 deg continuous, 30 deg intermittent.

tasks.name: Generator - Primary & Secondary Fuel Service
tasks.description: Change out the primary fuel/water separator filter, then replace the secondary spin-on engine filter.
tasks.caution_notes: Replace the primary fuel/water separator element and all its sealing O-rings, then the secondary spin-on. System is self-bleeding - run the 12V lift pump to purge. Supply and return lines 1/4" ID minimum.

tasks.name: Generator - Raw Water Impeller Swap
tasks.description: Open the raw water pump faceplate, extract the rubber impeller, grease the chamber, and install a new element to prevent overheating.
tasks.caution_notes:
Gear-driven pump, neoprene impeller - keep an impeller kit (impeller + cover gasket) aboard at all times. Grease the chamber on reassembly with glycerine or soap, not petroleum. Recover every vane of the old impeller.

The galley sink drain outlet sits just forward of the engine/genset raw-water inlet, so water leaving it flows aft past the inlet when underway. With the impeller out, look for grease or food debris in the vanes and strainer, not just sand and salt.

tasks.name: Generator - Valve Clearance Adjustment
tasks.description: Measure and adjust the mechanical valve-to-rocker clearances while the engine cylinder head is completely cold.
tasks.caution_notes: Intake and exhaust 0.25 mm (0.0098"), engine dead cold. Re-torque the head bolts to spec first, then set the valves. Wrong clearance shows as hard starting, low power and a tapping top end.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Bow Roller Chafe Guard Check
tasks.description: Check the contact point where the anchor is tensioned against the bow roller. Ensure no sharp metal edges are grinding into the Dyneema loop.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the roller and cheeks where the rode and the snubber bridle bear - any sharp edge or worn roller saws Dyneema and nylon, and a worn roller lets the chain jump the gypsy under load.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Chain Locker Drain Clear-Out
tasks.description: Clear mud sludge, biological debris, and rope fibers from the locker drain holes to ensure the compartment drains completely dry.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear the locker drains of mud, weed and rope fibre so the compartment dries fully between uses - standing water in a sealed locker is the anaerobic condition that pits stainless chain. A blocked drain also keeps weight in the bow.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Fortress Anodizing & Thread Care
tasks.description: Unpack the disassembled Fortress, clean the precision interlocks, and treat all structural assembly bolts to prevent seizing.
tasks.caution_notes: Aluminum Fortress: coat the knock-apart assembly threads with Tef-Gel before stowing it broken-down, or crevice corrosion freezes them.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Galvanized Chain Re-Zincing / Swap
tasks.description: Monitor the backup galvanized chain for raw, brown rust bleeding. Once the zinc coating fails completely, re-galvanize or replace the links.
tasks.caution_notes: Watch the galvanized backup chain for through-rust and brown bleed. Once the galv is gone the links work-harden and lose strength fast - re-galvanize or replace, do not run another season.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Locker Pad-Eye & Bitter End Check
tasks.description: Verify that both cutaway rope tails are completely free of rot, and check that the structural pad-eyes have zero rust cracking.
tasks.caution_notes: Both bitter ends made off to structural pad-eyes with a lashing you can cut fast (not a shackle needing a wrench), pad-eyes free of rust weep or crazing. You must be able to slip the rode in seconds to abandon an anchorage.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Nylon-to-Chain Splice Service
tasks.description: Inspect the chain-to-rope splice on the backup rode for structural stiffness, inner strand unlaying, or hard friction spots.
tasks.caution_notes: Typical: 8-plait nylon spliced to chain; 316 cotter pins or seizing wire on the shackles.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Rode Reversal (End-for-Ending)
tasks.description: Lay the full chain (and any nylon rode) out on a dock. Swap it end-for-end so the heavily worn anchor-end section gets a rest in the deep locker.
tasks.caution_notes: Flake all the chain and nylon rode on the dock, inspect every link, swap end-for-end so the working end rests. Caliper a sample against new - retire the chain at ~10-12% diameter loss or first crack.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Soft Shackle Friction & UV Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the Dyneema soft shackle for structural fuzzing, flat spots, or color-fading from direct UV exposure on the bow cleat.
tasks.caution_notes: When stowed, take the chain off the gypsy and hold the boat on a Dyneema soft shackle to a bow cleat - do not leave load on the windlass.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Stowage Shackle Replacement
tasks.description: Retire and replace the Dyneema soft shackle to prevent structural failure that could drop the anchor while bashing into a head sea.
tasks.caution_notes: Replace the Dyneema soft shackle holding the boat to the bow cleat on a fixed cycle regardless of looks - UV and cyclic load degrade it invisibly, and it is the only link between boat and anchor while you sleep.

tasks.name: Ground Tackle - Swivel & Shackle Weld Check, seizing wire
tasks.description: Inspect your primary anchor swivel and backup shackles for thread backing, micro-cracks, or bent pins.
tasks.caution_notes: All-stainless chain piled deep in a damp, low-oxygen locker is prone to hidden crevice-corrosion pinholes, so aggressive fresh-water flushing is mandatory. A stainless swivel on a galvanized anchor or chain is a strong galvanic cell that strips zinc from the shackle and top links - inspect those closely.

tasks.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Acrylic Micro-Scratch Cleansing
tasks.description: Clean the thick acrylic lenses to clear away atmospheric UV hazing and salt etching.
tasks.caution_notes: Clean the acrylic with a plastic polish (Novus 1/2, Meguiar's PlastX), soft cloth, no dry wiping. A 35-yo crazed lens is a structural item - it can fail inward under a wave. Budget replacements.

tasks.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Dogs & Adjuster Arm Lubrication
tasks.description: Apply a drop of dry-film lubricant to the rotating quick-dogs, thumb screws, and telescoping hatch adjuster arm slide tracks to prevent binding.
tasks.caution_notes: Dry-lube the quick-dogs, wing screws and the telescoping friction arm - a stiff dog gets over-torqued and cracks the cast frame ear; a seized arm lets a hatch slam and shatter the lens. Never wet lube on deck.

tasks.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Frame Re-Bedding & Lens Seal
tasks.description: Pull aging hatches off the deck or replace crazed acrylic lenses if the original structural bedding compound begins to shrink and weep water into the cabin.
tasks.caution_notes: When the original structural bedding shrinks and weeps, or a lens crazes through: pull the hatch, remove every trace of old sealant, re-bed frame (butyl) and lens (structural sealant) separately. A weeping hatch frame rots the deck core and the beam under it.

tasks.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Hinge Pin Galvanic Isolation Check
tasks.description: Inspect the heavy stainless steel hinge pins passing through the cast aluminum hatch frames. Look for white, bubbling aluminum oxide powder (galvanic corrosion).
tasks.caution_notes: Look for white bubbling powder where the stainless hinge pins pass through the cast-aluminium frames - galvanic corrosion swelling the casting, which eventually cracks the ear or seizes the pin. Tef-Gel on reassembly.

tasks.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Portlight & Hatch Gasket Wipe
tasks.description: Wipe down the thick internal neoprene sealing rings to remove grit, and apply a thin layer of protectant to keep the rubber from checking or sticking to the frame.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe the neoprene seals and treat with a rubber protectant (303, not silicone spray) - a hard or grit-imprinted gasket leaks under a boarding sea. Replace one that will not rebound; hatch gasket stock is a good spares item on an older boat.

tasks.name: Headsail Furling - Bearing Rinse & Full-Cycle Function Check
tasks.description: Fresh-water flush the furling drum and the halyard-swivel races (many furlers use un-greased Torlon bearings - rinse only, no oil unless the manual says otherwise). Furl and unfurl each sail through its full range and feel for notchiness, grinding or a tight spot; check the drum line is fair on the drum and the foil feeds cleanly.
tasks.caution_notes: Salt-locked bearings load up the furling line until something parts at the worst moment; for sealed Torlon races the rinse is the whole maintenance plan.

tasks.name: Headsail Furling - Foil Joint, Connector & Torque-Tube Inspection
tasks.description: Go up each foil: check every foil-connector set screw is present, seated and staked; the luff groove is fair across each joint with no lifted edges; the torque tube and its link at the drum are tight; the halyard swivel and its restrainer are sound. Check the deflector / halyard-wrap angle at the masthead.
tasks.caution_notes: A foil-connector screw that backs out chews the sail luff tape and can jam the sail half-furled in a blow - the classic offshore headsail emergency. With new foils, re-check after the first hard season.

tasks.name: Hot Water Heater - Heating Element Inspection
tasks.description: Isolate power, drain the tank, and back out the single heating element screw thread to inspect for fractures or severe scale encrustation.
tasks.caution_notes: Never energize the element with the tank dry or air-locked - run every hot tap until flow is steady first; trapped air burns the element out in seconds. Replace with the heater maker's element (match wattage and voltage on the label).

tasks.name: Hot Water Heater - Sacrificial Anode Rod Check
tasks.description: Remove the top access cap and unscrew the hex-head magnesium anode rod. Replace it if it has degraded by more than 50% or if core wire is exposed.
tasks.caution_notes: Typically a short 3/4" NPT magnesium anode taking a 1-1/16" socket - confirm the right part for your heater. Check often - once the anode is gone the tank corrodes.

tasks.name: Hot Water Heater - Sediment Flush & Agitation
tasks.description: Attach a hose to the drain valve, isolate power, shut off the intake, and flush out accumulated hard-water minerals before they encrust the element.
tasks.caution_notes: Point-of-use heater accumulates sediment fast - flush and agitate on schedule or the element buries and burns out.

tasks.name: Hot Water Heater - TPR Valve Manual Test
tasks.description: Manually lift the lever on the Temperature & Pressure Relief (TPR) valve to ensure water discharges cleanly, clearing lime scale and verifying the drain pipe isn't blocked.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift the T&P-relief lever briefly (bucket ready) and confirm it passes water and reseats. No shut-off valve between it and the tank; it must terminate at a drain. If it weeps repeatedly the cause is thermal expansion on a check-valved supply - fit a small (~1.5 gal) expansion tank or a 125 PSI supply-line relief, not a new T&P valve.

tasks.name: Hot Water Heater - Thermostat & Electrical Audit
tasks.description: Turn off power and check the internal ECO (Emergency Cut-Off) high-limit switch wiring underneath the front access panel for loose connections.
tasks.caution_notes: Thermostat range 50-140 F, ships in the OFF position - keep it at/below 125 F for scald safety. Check the element terminals for heat discoloration; a loose terminal on the 12 A load is a classic hot-spot fire. Confirm the circuit is dedicated.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Below-Waterline Fitting Bedding Re-check
tasks.description: For the first two hauls after relaunch following below-waterline work, re-verify the bedding and seals of every thru-hull, the shaft log / cutless housing, and every transducer (antifouling, depth/speed) for weeping or a chalky seal.
tasks.caution_notes: Below-waterline hull work disturbs everything. A fitting re-bedded during a refit can still weep as the sealant cures and the laminate re-stabilises - the first two seasons are when it shows.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Bilge Dryness Discipline
tasks.description: Keep the bilge dry. Trace and fix any persistent inflow rather than just pumping it - check the stuffing box, keel bolts, mast step, tank fittings and thru-hull hoses in turn.
tasks.caution_notes: Standing fresh water against the inside of a freshly-dried laminate reintroduces moisture from the wrong side, and the bilge is where the mast heel and keel bolts live. A rising dry-bilge water level is a diagnostic signal, not a nuisance.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Blister & Barrier-Coat Inspection
tasks.description: At every haul, walk the whole bottom for new blistering, weeping or barrier-coat lift - closest attention to the old remediation area and the keel-to-hull joint.
tasks.caution_notes: Photograph and mark anything suspect for comparison next haul. Small isolated blisters in the barrier coat (not the laminate) can be opened, dried and filled; a spreading field means the barrier is failing.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Bulkhead Tabbing & Structural Grid
tasks.description: Check the glass tabbing where the main bulkheads, the mast-step bulkhead and the floors join the hull for cracking, delamination or a hollow 'tick' when flexed - especially around the mast step and the chainplate bulkheads.
tasks.caution_notes: Tabbing that has released transfers rig and grounding loads into a smaller area and the failure accelerates. Small cracks at tabbing edges are a watch item; a bulkhead you can move relative to the hull is a haul-now item.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Chainplate Structural Inspection
tasks.description: Beyond the rigging deck-leak check: rotate through the chainplates over a few years, pulling each to inspect for crevice corrosion at and below the deck line, and check the tie-rod lower terminals, backing plates and the bulkhead/knee they land on.
tasks.caution_notes: Crevice corrosion hides exactly where you cannot see it - at the deck slot and under backing plates. This is the classic hidden failure on a boat this age; a chainplate lets go under load with no warning.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Coppercoat Surface Reactivation
tasks.description: Before launch (or by diver mid-season) lightly abrade the Coppercoat with a Scotch-Brite pad or 400-grit wet paper to strip the oxidised patina and expose fresh copper.
tasks.caution_notes: Coppercoat is a copper-loaded epoxy - it works by slow copper release, so a polished or slimed surface stops antifouling. Never hard pressure-wash or scrape with metal; that removes the epoxy itself. A gentle soft-pad wipe through the season keeps it active.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Hull-to-Deck Joint Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect the hull-to-deck joint under the aluminium toe rail for weeping, movement, or backed-off fasteners; re-bed any section that leaks.
tasks.caution_notes: Persistent leaks here rot the deck core and the tops of the bulkheads below. A joint that works in a seaway also shows as gelcoat cracking along the sheer.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Keel Bolt & Keel Joint Check
tasks.description: Check the external keel bolts for torque to spec and the keel-to-hull joint for an opening seam ('smile'), rust weep, or movement. Sound the bilge sump around the bolt heads for water.
tasks.caution_notes: On a 35-year-old bolted keel, budget for an eventual drop-and-re-bed. Weeping rust at the joint or bolts that keep needing torque means the bedding has failed and water is tracking to the bolts - do not defer past one more haul.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Mast Step / Compression Post Check
tasks.description: Keel-stepped rig: inspect the mast step in the bilge for standing water and aluminium corrosion/pitting at the heel, and check the deck collar/partners and the compression structure below for any sign of compression.
tasks.caution_notes: Standing bilge water at an aluminium mast heel is a slow structural killer - keep that area bone dry. Corrosion at the heel eats section where the whole rig load lands; catch it while it is surface pitting.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Post-Osmosis Moisture Log
