tasks.description: Take moisture-meter readings at fixed, marked points on the topsides and bottom and log them; compare season over season.
tasks.caution_notes: A peeled-and-dried laminate keeps giving up water for a season or two - you want the trend flat or falling, never rising. Set the baseline at the first haul after relaunch and read the same spots every time, same meter, hull surface-dry.

tasks.name: Hull & Structure - Rudder Structure & Moisture Check
tasks.description: Sound the rudder blade for delamination and voids, check for weeping at the lower bearing and the trailing edge (waterlogged foam), and inspect the stock-to-blade weld/armature area.
tasks.caution_notes: A 35-year-old rudder can waterlog silently until it freezes at a bearing or the blade splits in a seaway. Drill-and-drain plus a winter dry-out buys time; a blade that keeps taking on water needs rebuilding. Separate from the bearing overhaul under Steering.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - AIS MOB Satellite Sync Test
tasks.description: Step outside on deck and trigger a full AIS/DSC/GPS test run to confirm the beacon acquires satellites and drops a "MOB Test" target directly onto your cockpit chartplotter.
tasks.caution_notes: On deck with clear sky, run the beacon self-test - confirm GPS acquisition and a test position message. A failed self-test is a dead beacon. Note the battery replacement date.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - Complete Lithium Battery Overhaul
tasks.description: Send the internal MOB beacons to an authorized service partner to completely pull and replace their internal long-life batteries.
tasks.caution_notes: Send the AIS MOB units to an authorized service partner at the battery end-of-life date - the sealed lithium pack is not user-replaceable and an expired beacon may not transmit long enough to be found. Stagger replacements so you are never without one.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - Hydrostatic / Bobbin Expiry Check
tasks.description: Check the stamped manufacturing or expiration dates on the internal Hammar Hydrostatic caps or standard bobbins.
tasks.caution_notes: Mustang/Hammar hydrostatic caps have a hard 5-year expiry from the manufacture date, not from first use. Rearm kits: Mustang Hydrostatic Rearm Kit E or B.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - MOB Beacon Self-Test
tasks.description: Run a basic functional self-test on the integrated beacon (e.g., Ocean Signal or ACR) to verify battery health and circuit routing without transmitting a live alert.
tasks.caution_notes: Route the auto-inflator ribbon with zero twists inside the vest folds - a snagged ribbon can fire the 161.975 MHz AIS MOB beacon live inside a closed locker.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - PFD 16-Hour Bladder Test
tasks.description: Unpack the vest fabric cover and orally inflate the internal yellow or orange bladder until completely firm. Let it sit overnight.
tasks.caution_notes: 16-hour hold test on each bladder. Never dry a bladder in direct sun through a hatch - UV micro-porosity breaks down the coating.

tasks.name: Inflatable PFDs - Survivor Strobe Light Audit
tasks.description: Test the integrated water-activated survival lights via their test contacts to verify brightness and battery storage voltage.
tasks.caution_notes: Test the water-activated light on each vest - contacts wet, confirm a bright strobe. In a night MOB the light is how the boat finds you; a dead one halves the odds. Log battery expiry.

tasks.name: Jacklines & Tethers - Jackline Inspection & Passage Rig
tasks.description: Inspect the jacklines for chafe, UV degradation and stitching / splice condition, check the bow and stern attachment points, and confirm they rig so a clipped-on crew stays on deck and out of the water - run inboard of the shrouds, tensioned, ends that cannot unhook. Rig them before every passage; strike and stow in the sun-off when in port.
tasks.caution_notes: Webbing jacklines chafe through where they cross a toe rail or stanchion base and go brittle from UV - a jackline that parts under load is worse than none. Dyneema jacklines do not stretch (good) but roll underfoot (bad) - flat webbing is the usual choice. The point of a jackline is to keep you ON the boat, not to drag you alongside: route so the tether cannot reach past the rail.

tasks.name: Jacklines & Tethers - Tether Inspection & Retirement Check
tasks.description: Inspect every safety tether: webbing for UV fade, fuzzing and cuts, all stitching, the snap-hook / carabiner gates and springs, the overload (load-limiting) indicator not tripped, and the age. Also a hands-on check before each offshore leg.
tasks.caution_notes: Tether webbing is a life-safety consumable with a service life - World Sailing / manufacturers retire it around 5 years, sooner in hard tropical UV or after any shock load. A tripped overload flag means that tether took a fall and is done. Prefer a double tether with a mid-length short leg, and snap hooks that cannot roll open against a jackline. Store out of the sun.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Bonding Wire Integrity Audit
tasks.description: Verify the heavy-gauge green ground wire runs continuously from the Keel Cooler hull studs directly to the main engine battery negative block.
tasks.caution_notes: Verify continuity of the green bonding wire from each keel cooler to the bus (under ~1 ohm) - the no-zinc coolers depend entirely on it. A broken bond leaves the sintered-bronze block unprotected and it dezincifies fast in warm salt water.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Compressor Area Ventilation Check
tasks.description: Clear stored gear away from the Danfoss compressor footprint and inspect the electronic controller box connections for salt corrosion.
tasks.caution_notes: The compressor and its Danfoss/Secop controller need free air in and hot air out - a sealed or dust-blocked cabinet makes the controller cut out on thermal overload, which looks like a gas fault. Clear the intake, confirm the module fan runs (its terminals are limited to 0.7 A - a stalled fan cannot be forced). Keep the keel-cooler filter/drier vertical, arrow down.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Evaporator Box Defrosting
tasks.description: Turn off the system to let frost layers melt naturally. Thick ice blocks heat transfer and forces the compressor to run continuously.
tasks.caution_notes: Never use a knife or screwdriver to clear ice - a pierced evaporator wall destroys the unit. Let it thaw or use warm water.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Keel Cooler Chemical Descale
tasks.description: Soak the external porous bronze matrix in a mild acid solution during a haul-out to dissolve deeply embedded micro-calcium deposits.
tasks.caution_notes: Hauled out only: brush on a 20% muriatic mix or Barnacle Buster to dissolve calcium in the bronze pores, then flush with fresh water once the fizzing stops. Never put automotive leak sealer or antifreeze in the loop.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Keel Cooler Growth Scraping
tasks.description: Gently clear barnacles, tube worms, and algae off the porous exterior bronze plate to prevent thermal insulation.
tasks.caution_notes: Never run the compressor while hauled out - it destroys the system almost immediately. No bottom paint on the sintered-bronze keel-cooler face (kills thermal exchange). Plastic scraper only, never metal.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Refrigerant Flow & Frost Test
tasks.description: Turn on the compressor and track the frost line. Frost must cover at least 85% of the evaporator panel within 20 minutes to prove correct charge.
tasks.caution_notes: Box warm, start the system and feel the evaporator: frost should march evenly across the plate within minutes. Frost only at the inlet corner = low charge or a restriction; no frost and a hot compressor = lost charge. R134a; a gauge check and top-up is a refrigeration-tech job, not dockside.

tasks.name: Keel-Cooled Refrigeration - Sacrificial Zinc Replacement
tasks.description: Swap out the small streamlined pencil zinc anode attached directly to the underwater Keel Cooler body to prevent galvanic pinking.
tasks.caution_notes: Some keel coolers have no pencil/collar anode; protection is then a bonding wire from each cooler to the ship's bonding grid plus the hull bonding-plate anode. For those, this task = verify each cooler's bond is intact and reads under ~1 ohm to the bus, and that the hull anode protecting them is not wasted. Where there is a zinc, replace it at ~50% wasted.

tasks.name: Lifelines - Inspection (wire or cover, terminals, gates, lashings, stanchion bases)
tasks.description: Run the whole length by eye and by hand: broken strands or cracked cover, corrosion at swages and terminals, chafe where the line passes through stanchions, gate latches that open and close freely, lashings intact, and every stanchion solid at its base (no movement, cracks or leaks). Also part of the pre-passage rig check.

tasks.name: Lifelines - Tension & Terminal Check
tasks.description: Check tension and that every turnbuckle / tensioner is locked (locknut, cotter or wire) and the terminal threads and toggles are sound. Confirm the lifeline type on the device first - the right tension depends on it.

tasks.name: Liferaft - Authorized Station Recertification
tasks.description: Return the raft to a service station authorized by the raft maker for full pressure tests, gas cylinder weighing, and survival pack consumable replacement.
tasks.caution_notes: Maker-authorized station: full inflation/pressure test, cylinder weigh, expiry replacement of flares/rations/water, repack. Book early - stations back up before hurricane season, and an out-of-cert raft is not one you can rely on or clear a rally with.

tasks.name: Liferaft - Canister Shell & Binding Band Check
tasks.description: Visually check the fiberglass shell for spider cracks from deck work and verify the white binding bands are unbroken.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the fibreglass canister shell for spider cracks (usually from someone standing or working on it) and confirm the white binding/breaker bands are intact. A cracked shell lets water in and can foul deployment; broken bands mean it may already have tried to open. Never tape or lash the shell.

tasks.name: Liferaft - Cradle Structural Fastener Torque
tasks.description: Verify the stainless steel bolts securing the low-profile aluminum or steel cradle to your deck or cabin top remain tight against hull vibration.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the bolts holding the cradle to the deck - it must hold a ~90 lb canister through a rollover and then release it. Loose or weeping bolts (a core leak here is common) need re-bedding, not just re-torque.

tasks.name: Liferaft - HRU Replacement Reset
tasks.description: Discard the expired automated hydrostatic cutter mechanism and swap in a fresh unit to guarantee automatic depth deployment.
tasks.caution_notes: Hammar H20 HRU; log the hard expiry date - it is not serviceable past it.

tasks.name: Liferaft - Hydrostatic Release Unit (HRU) Check
tasks.description: Examine the expiration date stamp on your Hammar H20 Hydrostatic Release Unit. If the date has passed, the raft will not auto-deploy if the boat sinks.
tasks.caution_notes: The container painter must run through the Hammar H20 hydrostatic release weak link - never tie it straight to a deck cleat, or the raft cannot float free if the boat sinks.

tasks.name: Liferaft - Painter Line Shackle Check
tasks.description: Ensure the high-tensile painter line loop exiting the container is securely tied to your cradle's weak-link bypass node.
tasks.caution_notes: The painter must lead through the Hammar H20 hydrostatic-release weak link.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Floating Line Deployment & Wash
tasks.description: Flake out all 150 feet of the yellow floating polypropylene line on a dock. Wash away embedded salt crystals, check for hard knots, and ensure the line isn't stiff or brittle from UV exposure.
tasks.caution_notes: Flake all 150 ft on the dock, wash out the salt, inspect the full length for UV embrittlement and chafe - the yellow polypropylene floating line is the weak point (poor UV life). Stiff or powdery surface = replace; it has to take a person's shock load.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Rope-to-Boat Attachment Audit
tasks.description: Trace the bitter end of the line down to where it ties to your boat. Verify the knot is secure around a high-load structural stern cleat or heavy-duty pad-eye.
tasks.caution_notes: Tie the bitter end to a structural deck cleat only - never to a stanchion base, it will rip out.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Soft Case / Storage Bag Swap
tasks.description: Replace the exterior fabric storage bag once UV radiation rots the stitching or fabric, which leaves the inner rope exposed to sun damage.
tasks.caution_notes: Replace the outer bag once the stitching or fabric sun-rots - a failed bag exposes the line to UV and it then fails on deployment. Cheap part, critical function.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Storage Case Integrity Check
tasks.description: Inspect the rail-mounted case buckles, straps, and fabric for tearing or sun-rotting to ensure the case won't blow open or fall off the boat in a storm.
tasks.caution_notes: The yellow polypropylene floating line has poor UV resistance - if the case is torn or sun-bleached the rope may be brittle enough to snap under a person's weight. Replace the case and check the line.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Survival Strobe Light Test
tasks.description: If you have a water-activated survival light attached to the collar webbing, test its contacts to verify the battery isn't dead.
tasks.caution_notes: If a water-activated light is on the collar, wet the contacts and confirm it fires bright - a night MOB with no light on the sling is nearly hopeless. Note the battery expiry.

tasks.name: Lifesling - Yellow Foam Collar Inspection
tasks.description: Open the case and inspect the high-buoyancy collar. Check the retro-reflective tape panels for peeling and ensure the heavy lifting rings/webbing straps show zero fraying.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the case: check the collar foam is not waterlogged or crushed (lost buoyancy) and the reflective tape is not peeling. A sun-baked collar degrades even unused - it has a life.

tasks.name: Propeller - Line Cutter Dive Check
tasks.description: Between haul-outs, dive the shaft: confirm the line cutter's blades are still sharp and undamaged, the body has not shifted on the shaft, and (if fitted) the cutter anode still has metal. Clear any line, weed or barnacle growth from the cutter and the prop gap.
tasks.caution_notes: In the tropics the cutter fouls and the anode (if any) wastes between hauls - a growth-jammed or shifted cutter is the same as no cutter, and you find out at 2 am wrapped on a pot warp.

tasks.name: Propeller - Line Cutter Service
tasks.description: At haul-out: dress or replace the rotating line cutter's blades (sharp, no chips), check the blade bolts and the body clamp screws are tight and wired, confirm the body is clocked so the blades clear the strut and cutless bearing, and check the cutter's integral zinc - renew it if it is past ~50%.
tasks.caution_notes: Cutter blades chip on wire and hard debris and go dull; a dull cutter wraps line instead of slicing it. The cutter zinc wastes fast in warm salt water - check it every dive, not just at haul-out, and keep a spare blade/zinc kit unopened. Record the cutter size and part numbers on the prop card.

tasks.name: MOB Recovery Gear - Ring Buoy & Horseshoe Condition & Deploy Check
tasks.description: Check the Jim-Buoy GW-20 ring and the horseshoe buoy for UV cracking and water-logging, their grab lines and drogues, any attached light and its battery, and that each pops cleanly out of its rail bracket one-handed. Confirm the throwing line is flaked, not knotted.
tasks.caution_notes: This gear lives in the sun on the stern rail and is forgotten until the one moment it matters. UV-hardened foam and a perished light are the common finds. The bracket must release with one hand under load - a MOB recovery is single-handed by definition while someone else steers. Keep it rigged to throw, not lashed down.

tasks.name: MOB Recovery Gear - Throw Bag Repack & Rope Inspection
tasks.description: Pay out the NTR throw bag's full 50 ft, inspect the rope for UV fade, glazing and abrasion, rinse and dry it, then re-stuff (not coil) so it pays out cleanly. Do a practice throw once a season.
tasks.caution_notes: Rescue throw-line goes stiff and weak in tropical UV faster than you expect - a line that will not pay out, or snaps on the shock load, is worse than nothing. Re-stuff loosely; a coiled or damp-packed bag birds-nests on the throw. Everyone aboard should have thrown it at least once.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Anode Inspection
tasks.description: Check and scrape away surface build-up on heat exchanger zinc sacrificial anodes; swap out if degraded beyond 50%.
tasks.caution_notes: Some modern common-rail engines have no heat-exchanger pencil zinc and rely on bonding instead - check the engine manual (and the exhaust mixing elbow). If there is none, this task becomes: verify the engine's bonding strap is intact and inspect the HX end tanks and mixing elbow for internal corrosion - the block then relies on the hull bonding-plate anodes and the shaft zinc.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Belts & Controls Adjustment
tasks.description: Inspect and retention the engine alternator V-belt and check for optimal travel on throttle/gear shift cables.
tasks.caution_notes: Alternator V-ribbed belt deflects 8-9 mm under a 100 N push at mid-span, checked after 5 min idle; keep all oil off it. Set throttle and shift cables for full travel to the pump and gear stops with a little spring-back each end.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Break-In Oil & Filter Swap
tasks.description: Drain initial factory oil and change the filter to capture microscopic metal shavings shed as the engine components seat together.
tasks.caution_notes: 50-hour break-in change - the first oil carries the most seating debris. Use the oil grade in the engine manual (commonly API CD or higher, SAE 10W-30 or 15W-40). Oil filter: hand-tight to seal contact then about +3/4 turn. Change the transmission gear oil at the same time if the gearbox manual calls for a break-in change.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Coolant Loop Flush
tasks.description: Completely drain and refresh the closed-circuit freshwater cooling loop to prevent scale buildup and heat transfer issues.
tasks.caution_notes: Use the engine maker's long-life coolant on its stated cycle (typically 2 years; 1 year for conventional coolant). Cooling-system corrosion is behind a large share of diesel failures - do not stretch it. Refill slowly with the thermostat housing highest, run to temp with the cap off to purge air, then top up.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Idle-Period Run
tasks.description: If the boat has sat and the main engine has not run in ~3 weeks, run it up to full operating temperature (thermostat open, ~20-30 min) - under load if you can motor, or in gear against a dock line.
tasks.caution_notes: Same reasons as the generator: condensation in the crankcase and exhaust, fuel gumming in the injection system, the raw-water impeller taking a set, a damp alternator. A common-rail engine especially does not like stale fuel sitting on the injectors. Get it hot enough that the thermostat opens - a short cold run leaves more water behind than it burns off.

tasks.name: Main Engine - New Mount & Alignment Check
tasks.description: Verify tight engine mount nuts and physically check shaft alignment to compensate for fiberglass hull flexing under initial propulsion loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Re-check engine-mount nuts and shaft alignment once the hull has settled under load - a new install and new mounts compress through the first season. Align to 0.05-0.1 mm at the coupling on all four quadrants, boat afloat with tanks at normal level.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Primary/Secondary Fuel Service
tasks.description: Drain water from the primary separator daily, then fully replace both fuel filters to safeguard high-pressure common-rail fuel injectors.
tasks.caution_notes: Common-rail injectors will not tolerate water or dirt - drain the primary separator daily and replace both the primary element and the engine secondary filter at the manual's interval (commonly 250 h). Bleed with the filter-mounted hand primer until fuel runs bubble-free; never crack a line at the rail.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Routine Lubrication Service
tasks.description: Extract used engine oil and install a fresh filtering block to preserve the internal common-rail engine protections.
tasks.caution_notes: 250-hour oil + filter (API CD+, 10W-30 / 15W-40; filter +3/4 turn past contact, 20-24 N.m). Shorthanded: pre-stage pan, bagged filter and rags before you start so a warm-oil change stays a 15-minute job.

tasks.name: Main Engine - Seawater Impeller Replacement
tasks.description: Extract the raw-water pump cover to swap the flexible impeller blades before rubber fatigue causes cooling loss.
tasks.caution_notes: Carry 2+ spare impellers plus cover gaskets/O-rings and spare screws. Count the vanes of the old impeller - any missing piece is downstream in the heat exchanger and must be recovered. Fit the new one with glycerine or dish soap, never petroleum grease. If a sink drain outlet sits forward of the raw-water inlet, look for grease or food debris in the vanes and strainer, not just sand and salt.

tasks.name: Mast & Nav Lighting - Mast Wiring Loom & Base Connector Check
tasks.description: At the mast base open the junction box / deck plug: check for green corrosion, water tracking, sound strain relief, and that the loom is still tied off inside the extrusion so it cannot slap. Continuity / insulation check each circuit (lights, VHF, wind, AIS if run). Reseal.
tasks.caution_notes: A keel-stepped mast sits its base in the bilge zone - the loom and its connector are the first things to corrode, and a high-resistance joint there dims the nav lights and raises VHF SWR.

tasks.name: Mast & Nav Lighting - Navigation, Anchor & Steaming Light Test
tasks.description: Switch through every exterior light in turn - masthead tricolour, lower running lights (port/stbd/stern), steaming/foredeck light, all-round anchor light - and confirm each strikes, shows the right colour over the right arc, and the lens/gasket is sound. Part of the pre-passage checklist as well as the 90-day cycle.
tasks.caution_notes: COLREGS and the insurer both assume these work: a dark boat offshore at night is the classic collision setup, and a mis-wired tricolour/anchor pair (both on, or the wrong one) is a common post-refit fault - check it explicitly. Carry spare modules/bulbs and know the mast-base junction. If the masthead anchor light has a daylight sensor and won't switch off by day or won't strike at dusk, suspect the photodiode/sensor, not the LED.

tasks.name: Masthead - Windex Vane Inspection
tasks.description: At the annual rig check / next trip aloft: confirm the Windex XL vane spins freely with no wobble, the vane and reference arms are straight and aligned, the counterweight and sail-shaped tab are intact, and the masthead bracket and its light (if fitted) are secure. Also give it a binocular check from the deck before every offshore leg.
tasks.caution_notes: The Windex is the primary wind reference for short-tacking, picking up a mooring and sailing in light air - a bent vane or a seized bearing quietly costs you boat-handling. Birds and a wrapped halyard are the usual killers. It is a fragile aluminium part you cannot fix at sea, so carry a spare vane (or a whole spare unit).

tasks.name: Mooring Lines - Line Desalting Soak
tasks.description: Submerge the entire rope sets in fresh water to clear out trapped salt crystals that slice internal core fibers under high surge loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Soak and flush the hidden salt crystals from inside the line and any chafe sleeves - dried salt abrades the fibers from within.

tasks.name: Mooring Lines - Line Retirement
tasks.description: Replace both lines completely. Mooring lines undergo intense, localized cycling because they are typically shorter than anchoring snubbers.
tasks.caution_notes: Retire nylon the moment it has stiff, hard or glazed patches - that is rope past its thermal yield point from storm-load friction heat; the stretch is gone and will not return.

tasks.name: Mooring Lines - Line Rotation / End-for-Ending
tasks.description: Swap the lines end-for-end so the center loop area that handles the pennant eye friction gets shifted to the protected cleat beds.
tasks.caution_notes: Swap the lines end-for-end so the section that has been taking the pennant-eye friction moves to a fresh part - the eye and the first few feet do all the work and glaze first.

tasks.name: Mooring Lines - Pennant Eye Chafe Check
tasks.description: Inspect the midpoint of each line leg where it passes through the mooring pennant eye for friction fuzzing or glazing.
tasks.caution_notes: Return-to-boat mooring uses four separate lines through the fairleads. Never run one continuous line out through the mooring eye and back - the multi-directional shear saws through 5/8" nylon in hours.

tasks.name: Mooring Lines - Toe Rail Fairlead Check
tasks.description: Verify your fire-hose chafe guards are perfectly aligned inside the toe rail fairleads, as you now have four line leads exiting the bow instead of two.
tasks.caution_notes: With four lines through the fairleads, check each fire-hose chafe guard is centred in its chock and has not crept - an exposed spot of nylon in a chock saws through in a blow. Re-seize daily on a mooring in wind.

tasks.name: Oil Change System - Sump Valve Leak Check
tasks.description: Inspect the brass or stainless steel ball valves threaded directly into the engine and generator oil pan drain ports to verify zero seal weeping.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the ball valves in the engine and genset oil-pan drains for weeping at the stem and the joint - they live hot and vibrating, and a drip is a bilge oil sheen and a slow loss of sump level. A knocked-open handle drains the sump - wire the handles closed.

tasks.name: PFDs - Inherently Buoyant - Annual Condition Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect all 7 foam PFDs (6 adult Type II orange + 1 juvenile): fabric and stitching, straps, buckles and D-rings, buoyancy foam not compressed or waterlogged, whistle attached, reflective tape intact, USCG label legible, no mildew or rot.
tasks.caution_notes: Foam PFDs fail from UV, mildew and crushed foam, not from a mechanism. A jacket stored wet in a damp locker is dead in a season. Squeeze the foam - hard lumps or a jacket that no longer floats a full water jug gets binned. The juvenile PFD must still fit the child it is for - check the weight range and the crotch strap.

tasks.name: PFDs - Inherently Buoyant - Stowage, Count & Accessibility Check
tasks.description: Confirm the full count is aboard (6 adult + 1 juvenile foam, plus the 3 offshore inflatables), that they are in a labelled, dry, quick-to-reach location known to all crew and guests, and that the throwable and its count still meet the requirement for the number of people aboard.
tasks.caution_notes: The regulation is one wearable per person plus a throwable - crew and guests change the number you must carry. Guests never know where the PFDs are unless you show them; a locker no one can open in a hurry is the same as not having them. Keep the inflatables and the foam PFDs in separate, obvious places.

tasks.name: CBP user-fee decal - renew for the calendar year
tasks.description: The annual CBP user-fee decal (bought through DTOPS for the vessel's documentation number) is a calendar-year decal: it expires Dec 31 and is needed before re-entering the US from foreign waters. About 60 days before the year ends, buy next year's decal, then mark this task done with its effective date and note the sticker number.

tasks.name: EPIRB registration (NOAA) - renew
tasks.description: NOAA 406 MHz beacon registrations must be renewed every 2 years, and updated whenever boat or contact details change. Mark done with the date the registration was confirmed. Note the beacon battery expiry date as well.

tasks.name: Ship Station Licence - renew
tasks.description: Renew the ship radio station licence where your flag requires one (e.g. a 10-year FCC licence); start about 90 days ahead. Mark done with the new grant date.

tasks.name: Passports - renew
tasks.description: Many countries require 6 months' passport validity on arrival, so the real deadline is about 6 months before expiry; set this reminder about 3 months before that. Mark done with the new issue date.

tasks.name: Vessel documentation / registration - renew
tasks.description: Renew the vessel's documentation or state registration before it expires (e.g. a USCG Certificate of Documentation runs 5 years); start about 90 days ahead. Check every printed detail (name, numbers) for errors and get them corrected at renewal. Mark done with the new issue date.

tasks.name: Yacht insurance - renew
tasks.description: Start about 60 days before the policy period ends. The renewal may need signed proof that the last survey's recommendations were complied with. Mark done with the new policy's effective date.

tasks.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Condenser Vent Vacuuming
tasks.description: Vacuum the exterior metal slot grilles on the compressor side of the box. Dust and pet hair accumulation over the cooling fins will force the swing motor to run hotter and longer.
tasks.caution_notes: Vacuum the condenser grille and coil. A swing compressor shrugs off heel and rough use but not a heat-blanketed condenser - a blocked coil makes it cut out on thermal overload. If the unit was carried over from a previous boat, factor its real age into service expectations.

tasks.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Dual-Voltage Socket Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the rear 110V AC plug port and the secondary 12V/24V DC thermal fuse socket for loose indexing or salt-air green copper corrosion.
tasks.caution_notes: Many portable fridges auto-prioritize AC over DC when both are present. Keep the DC plug and socket contacts clean - voltage drop here stops it cycling.

tasks.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Internal Basket & Sump Clean
tasks.description: Pull out the wire food baskets and wash down the internal plastic/aluminum walls to prevent stagnant water or food spills from breeding bacteria.
tasks.caution_notes: Pull the wire basket and wipe the sump - spills pool under the basket and freeze. Baking soda and warm water, dry before re-powering.

tasks.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Lid Gasket & Tension Check
tasks.description: Wipe down the continuous rubber lid gasket. Inspect the heavy-duty stainless steel locking latches to ensure the lid clamps down perfectly air-tight.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the lid gasket and the over-centre latches - the seal and latch tension do the sealing. A soft latch or a compressed gasket lets the box sweat and it runs non-stop. Adjust the strike; carry a spare strike plate.

tasks.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Manual Defrost Protocol
tasks.description: Turn off the system to let structural ice build-up melt away naturally. Ice layers on the interior walls act as thermal insulation, dropping cooling speed.
tasks.caution_notes: No sharp tools in the box - a pierced evaporator wall is fatal to the unit.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - BatteryProtect Relay Test
tasks.description: Trigger a low-voltage test state to verify the BatteryProtect safely detaches your non-essential DC loads before your house bank sustains damage.
tasks.caution_notes: BatteryProtect is unidirectional - never connect a charger or inverter to its output side; back-feed destroys the MOSFETs and is a fire risk.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - Firmware Update
tasks.description: Use the manufacturer's app or remote portal to pull firmware updates for the monitoring hub, inverter-charger and solar controllers to patch communication bugs.
tasks.caution_notes: Update the solar controllers, converters and inverter-charger first; update the monitoring hub last - updating the hub mid-sequence can drop its data buses. Re-check the main DC fuses afterward.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - Remote Monitoring Sync Audit
tasks.description: Open the power system's remote monitoring dashboard (the monitoring hub's cloud portal, if you have one) and check for unprompted device disconnects, tracking errors, or historical low-voltage alarm logs.
tasks.caution_notes: Scan for device drop-outs, comms errors and gaps in the history graphs - an inverter or solar controller that keeps falling off its data bus is usually a loose data cable or a failing RJ45, and you want that fixed before it is the reason the batteries did not charge on passage. Confirm the alarm and generator auto-start logic still test-fire.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - High-Amp Fuse Link Audit
tasks.description: Open the Lynx Distributor or Lynx Power In cover plates to inspect the LED fuse indicators and confirm all MEGA fuses are seated tightly with zero heat discolouration.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the Lynx MEGA fuses are seated tight - vibration backs them off and they arc.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - Inverter & Solar Controller Fan Cleaning
tasks.description: Use compressed air to blow accumulated dust or lint out of the cooling fans on the inverter-charger and high-amperage solar charge controllers to prevent thermal throttling.
tasks.caution_notes: Blow the dust out of the inverter-charger and solar controller cooling fans - a fouled fan derates the unit under load (you lose inverter output or charge current exactly when you are pushing it) and the bearing eventually seizes. Confirm the fans spin up under load.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - Main DC Terminal Torque Check
tasks.description: Use a calibrated torque wrench to verify that all heavy M8/M10 connection studs (bus bars, inverter-charger inlets, battery-protect poles) remain tight.
tasks.caution_notes: Torque every main DC lug to spec with a calibrated wrench and insulated tools.

tasks.name: Power Electronics - DC-DC Converter Thermal Clearout
tasks.description: Inspect the aluminium heat-sink fins on the DC-DC converters. Isolated converters run hot - clear away any surrounding gear that blocks passive convective airflow.
tasks.caution_notes: Passively cooled DC-DC units can run >140F; keep about 4" vertical clearance and clear the dust.

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Prop Hub Anode Check
tasks.description: Inspect / replace the feathering prop's hub anode (the primary task lives under the Propeller system) - listed here so the whole anode set is checked together.
tasks.caution_notes: Do every anode on one dive or one haul-out so nothing is missed. The hub anode is the smallest and goes first.

tasks.name: Propeller - Anode Replacement
tasks.description: Replace the feathering prop's cone/hub zinc (or aftermarket collar zinc) at haul-out or when more than ~50% wasted.
tasks.caution_notes: A feathering prop with no anode dezincifies the bronze hub gears - an expensive rebuild. Warm salt water can consume the small hub anode in 6-8 weeks, so dive and check it between haul-outs. Also tracked under Bonding & Cathodic Protection.

tasks.name: Propeller - Blade Backlash / Gear Wear Check
tasks.description: At haul-out or launch, rock each blade by hand through its full arc and feel for play at the blade tip.
tasks.caution_notes: More than slight tip play means the bevel gears inside the hub are worn - send it to the prop maker or its service agent before it strips at sea. Check every blade; wear is usually uneven.

tasks.name: Propeller - Hub Grease Service
tasks.description: Pump the prop maker's waterproof grease into the hub zerk until fresh grease purges past the blade seals.
tasks.caution_notes: On a feathering prop this is THE maintenance job. A hub that runs dry seizes, loses feathering and wears the gears. Every haul-out minimum; more often in the tropics. Use the maker's grease or a fully water-resistant marine grease - never a lithium/EP grease that emulsifies.

tasks.name: Propeller - Pitch Verification
tasks.description: Confirm all blades are set to the same pitch and that it matches the last prop service sheet.
tasks.caution_notes: A drifted or mismatched pitch shows as prop walk, vibration, or the engine not reaching rated rpm (over-pitched) / over-revving with no thrust (under-pitched). Record the current setting on the boat's prop card.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Condenser Coil De-Dusting
tasks.description: Clean the compact aluminum fins or wire condenser grids at the back or base of the cabinet to prevent high head pressures and compressor cycling.
tasks.caution_notes: Vacuum or blow out the condenser coil; keep the DC connections clean - voltage drop here stops it cycling.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Door Gasket Cleaning
tasks.description: Wipe down the magnetic rubber door seals to remove food residue or sticky spills that compromise the air-tight seal.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe the door gasket and dollar-bill-drag-test the seal all round. A stiff, torn or grit-fouled gasket lets warm humid air in, the box sweats and ices and the compressor never rests. A smear of protectant keeps the rubber supple.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Drain Line & Port Clear-Out
tasks.description: Clear out the small internal condensation weep hole and drain tube to prevent stale water from pooling in the bottom of the cabinet food bay.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear the interior defrost drain and its through-cabinet port - a blocked drain pools water in the box bottom and it freezes into a block. Pipe cleaner or a warm flush.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Interior Defrosting
tasks.description: Turn off the system to let structural frost layers melt away, which restores optimal heat transfer efficiency across the cooling plate.
tasks.caution_notes: No sharp tools on the evaporator - a puncture destroys the unit.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Ventilation Grille Clear-Out
tasks.description: Ensure external cabinet ventilation slots and the integrated 12V/24V/120V cooling fan are completely clear of dust, pet hair, or loose items.
tasks.caution_notes: Keep the condenser intake and exhaust grilles clear - a blocked grille traps heat around the compressor and it runs non-stop or cuts out on overload. Vacuum, do not poke.

tasks.name: Refrigerator - Voltage & Contact Inspection
tasks.description: Check power supply terminal connections to verify there is zero corrosion or resistance-induced voltage drop.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the DC connections at the fridge and the fuse/breaker for corrosion and voltage drop under compressor load - a marginal joint under-runs the compressor and the box will not hold temperature. 7.5 A / 15 A blade fuses per the spares list.

tasks.name: Rigging - Aloft Hardware Inspection
tasks.description: Go aloft to check tangs, spreader tips, rivets, boom vang attachments, and the gooseneck assembly for stress cracking, loose fastners, or severe corrosion.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect tangs, spreader tips, rivets, vang attachment and gooseneck for cracks or loose fasteners. On an older spar treat these as fatigue points even when the wire is new - re-rigging does not renew the tangs, spreader bases or extrusion.

tasks.name: Rigging - Chainplate Leak Isolation
tasks.description: Inspect the sub-deck chainplate tie-rods and the deck pass-through points inside the saloon cabinetry for moisture tracks or weeping rust.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the sub-deck chainplate tie-rods and the saloon cabinetry pass-throughs for weeping rust or moisture tracks. Any stay deck collar tied down below deck (e.g. an inner forestay) is another deck penetration; check it for weeping / movement at the same time.

tasks.name: Rigging - Full Un-Stepped Rigging Overhaul
tasks.description: Un-step the mast completely. Strip down all terminal fittings, pull all wires/rods, non-destructively test (NDT) structural tangs, and replace all standing components.
tasks.caution_notes: Retirement wall: ~10 years for wire, 5-7 for solid rod. New wire resets this clock; the spar does not. Non-negotiable for blue-water safety.

tasks.name: Rigging - Hydraulic Backstay / Vang Service
tasks.description: Check the oil level on the Navtec/Seatec cockpit hydraulic panel, bleed trapped air, and inspect the ram piston seal for hydraulic fluid seepage.
tasks.caution_notes: Check fluid level at the Navtec/Seatec panel, bleed trapped air, and inspect the ram piston seals for seepage. ISO 32 or system-spec hydraulic fluid.

tasks.name: Rigging - Masthead Sheave Lubrication
tasks.description: Go aloft to verify that the main, genoa, and spinnaker halyard sheaves rotate smoothly without binding or friction flat-spots.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the main, genoa and spinnaker halyard sheaves turn freely with no binding or flat spots.

tasks.name: Rigging - Turnbuckle Flush & Thread Check
tasks.description: Back off turnbuckle body threads slightly under calm conditions, clean out gritty salt paste, inspect internal threads, and apply fresh anti-seize coating.
tasks.caution_notes: In calm conditions back the threads off slightly, clean the salt paste, inspect the internal threads, and re-apply Lanocote/Tef-Gel anti-seize before re-tensioning and re-securing the locking. Include any below-deck rigging screws (e.g. an inner-forestay deck tie-down) - same routine.

tasks.name: Rigging - Visual Stay & Wire Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the lower swage terminals, mechanical fittings (e.g., Sta-Lok/Norseman if updated), and look for tiny individual broken wire strands ("meat-hooks") or rod rust bleed.
tasks.caution_notes: Check lower swages for hairline cracks and single broken strands ('meat-hooks'); look for rust bleed weeping from any fitting. Mechanical (Sta-Lok / Norseman type) terminals are the field-serviceable ends - know which of your terminals they are. Any insulators in a stay (e.g. an SSB backstay) sit in the structural load path: inspect them as structural terminals every time this audit runs, and give them a deeper check with the rig slack at haul-out - a cracked insulator core still drops the stay.

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Block & Sheave Bearing Care
tasks.description: Clean internal ball/roller bearings and apply a dry lubricant that won't attract airborne salt, dust, or sand.
tasks.caution_notes: Flush the bearing races with mild soapy water, dry fully, then apply only dry-film Teflon (McLube Sailkote).

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Complete Line Replacement
tasks.description: Completely retire old, stiff, faded, or structurally compromised halyards and sheets to prevent line breakage under heavy offshore sailing loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Retire halyards and sheets on a schedule, not just on visible failure - a core-shot halyard looks fine in the cover right up until it parts under a loaded genoa in a squall. Stiff, faded, fuzzed or clutch-flat-spotted = done. Keep one full-length spare halyard aboard. Re-used line of uncertain age: retire on condition, not on the age clock.

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Deep Rope Wash & Softening
tasks.description: Remove all running rigging from the spars using messenger lines. Soak them to extract embedded salt crystals and restore flexibility to stiff, sun-baked lines.
tasks.caution_notes: Front-loader only - never a top-loader with an agitator. Cold gentle cycle, Woolite, mesh bags; air-dry in shade, never with heat.

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Line Chafe & Splice Audit
tasks.description: Inspect high-wear entry points—such as where halyards exit the masthead sheaves, rope clutch grip zones, and Genoa sheet car splices—for fuzzing or jacket wear.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the masthead exits, rope-clutch grip zones and genoa-sheet car splices; inspect the lock-stitches on every splice. Line re-used from an earlier boat or refit carries prior service hours - retire it on condition (stiffness, fuzz, core-shot, clutch flat-spots), not on the age clock. Keep a written line plan (which line, where it runs, new vs re-used, approximate age).

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Line Reversal (End-for-Ending)
tasks.description: Pull lines through the system and swap them end-for-end. This shifts the primary chafe zones (like the rope clutch bite points) to an fresh, unworn section of the line.
tasks.caution_notes: Shift the clutch bite points and deck-organizer wear zones onto fresh, unworn line.

tasks.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Rope Clutch Cam Service
tasks.description: Open rope clutch housings (e.g., Lewmar or Spinlock) to inspect the teeth on the gripping cams and clear away packed aluminum or synthetic salt dust.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the Lewmar/Spinlock housings, clear the salt dust, and replace cams whose teeth have worn flat (causes the line to slip).

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - Automation Relay Continuity
tasks.description: Test the terminal contacts on the FireBoy discharge relay to ensure that if the extinguisher triggers, the circuit cleanly shifts state to command engine/blower shutdown.
tasks.caution_notes: Wire the sensor loops Normally-Closed - a cut or corroded wire then reports a fault instead of failing silent.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - FireBoy Cylinder Gauge Audit
tasks.description: Check the physical pressure dial on your engine room FireBoy tank to ensure the needle remains locked inside the solid GREEN operating field.
tasks.caution_notes: The fire-suppression discharge relay must cut power to the main engine fuel solenoid and the generator stop circuit mechanically, independent of any software - a running diesel inhales the clean agent and renders it useless.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - Flow Sensor Internal Clean
tasks.description: Unbolt the internal plumbing ports of the raw water flow sensors to clear away micro-marine scaling or grass blades that can jam the paddle flag.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the raw-water flow sensor ports and clear scale, grass and weed off the vane - a fouled sensor lags or sticks, then it either nuisance-alarms or misses a real cooling failure. Do it with the impeller service.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - Heat Sensor Contact Check
tasks.description: Inspect the wiring blocks on the engine room heat sensor to ensure no vibration loosening or terminal corrosion at the screw terminals.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the wiring blocks at the ER heat sensor for vibration-loosened or corroded terminals - a heat sensor with a bad connection just reads 'no alarm' forever. Wiggle-test with the engine running.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - High Water Float Actuation
tasks.description: Manually lift the levers on both Aqualarm bilge float switches to confirm the automation core registers the true digital high state.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift both Aqualarm bilge float levers and confirm the panel shows a real high-water alarm (not just the test lamp). This is the last warning before the boat floods faster than the pumps - test it like you mean it, monthly.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - Raw Water Flow Run-Test
tasks.description: Start the main engine and the generator to confirm each raw-water flow sensor drops its alarm state once cooling water moves the internal paddle.
tasks.caution_notes: Start each engine and confirm the flow sensor drops its no-flow alarm within seconds - and at the dock, close a seacock and confirm it RAISES the alarm. A flow alarm that only ever shows OK may be failed the wrong way. Check the sensor is sized for your plumbing.

tasks.name: Safety Sensors - Smoke Sensor Chamber Sweep
tasks.description: Use a tiny blast of clean air to sweep the Aqualarm engine room smoke detector chamber to remove diesel dust or belt fibers that create false alarm triggers.
tasks.caution_notes: Gentle clean air through the Aqualarm ER smoke detector - diesel soot and belt dust blind it, and an ER smoke alarm slow by 60 seconds is the difference between an extinguisher and a liferaft.

tasks.name: Sails - Corner Ring Webbing Check
tasks.description: Inspect the high-load tack, clew, and head stainless steel rings to ensure the heavy structural webbing loops aren't chafed or rotting.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the tack, clew and head rings and their webbing loops for chafe and rot.

tasks.name: Sails - Exhaust Soot / Oil Removal
tasks.description: Dissolve dark, greasy diesel exhaust stains near the leech panels by hand-scrubbing with a specialized citrus degreaser or solvent.
tasks.caution_notes: Hand-scrub diesel soot near the leech with a mild citrus degreaser or solvent; avoid sharp creases when folding.

tasks.name: Sails - Mildew & Black Spot Soak
tasks.description: Submerge or saturate affected panels in a broad wash bay to kill black mold spores feeding on organic dirt inside the weave.
tasks.caution_notes: White Dacron tolerates a 1:10 bleach dilution for mildew; never bleach if there are Aramid/Kevlar/Technora patches. Ease halyards and leech lines at the dock so the soak does not set a distorted draft.

tasks.name: Sails - Professional Loft Inspection
tasks.description: Send to a sail loft for an industrial wash, hot-knife thread trimming, patch reinforcements, and draft-shape evaluation.
tasks.caution_notes: End-of-season loft service: industrial wash, hot-knife thread trim, patch reinforcement and draft-shape analysis.

tasks.name: Sails - Salt Crystallization Rinse
tasks.description: Hose down both sides of the sails with fresh water to clear embedded salt crystals, which act like sandpaper to fiber weaves when dry.
tasks.caution_notes: No pressure washers - they strip the resin finish and blow out the designed shape. Never roll or bag a sail wet.

tasks.name: Sails - Seam & Stitching Audit
tasks.description: Drag a finger along the high-wear horizontal panels and batten pockets to check for broken, frayed, or UV-rotted stitching.
tasks.caution_notes: Check horizontal seams and batten pockets for broken, frayed or UV-rotted stitching. Restitch with V-92 / V-138 UV-bonded polyester thread. A sail that has spent a long time folded in storage also needs a check of fold-line creases and mildew in addition to the usual UV/age wear.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Condensate Drain Pan Clearing
tasks.description: Flush out the stainless steel/composite base pan to clear away organic slime buildup before it plugs the drains and overflows into the cabin.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear the pan and both drain paths - pan tablets, not bleach. Confirm the pan slopes to the drain at the boat's rest trim; a pan that pools grows slime and corrodes through.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Cupronickel Condenser Descaling
tasks.description: Pump a mild acid recirculating loop through the seawater circuit to dissolve insulating barnacle growth and calcium scale inside the heat exchanger.
tasks.caution_notes: Recirculating mild-acid loop (Barnacle Buster) through the seawater side to dissolve barnacle growth and scale off the cupronickel condenser.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Electrical & Bonding Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the high-voltage electrical box terminal screws and verify the green chassis bonding wire is perfectly clean to avoid galvanic rot.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the 120V connections at the unit and breaker for heat, confirm the green bond to the chassis and seawater circuit is intact, and verify the GFCI/ELCI trips. A self-contained AC with a failed bond can energise the seawater and eat the bronze.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Evaporator Coil Fin Dusting
tasks.description: Gently clear away dust particles embedded deep in the aluminum air fins to ensure proper thermal exchange.
tasks.caution_notes: Vacuum / soft-brush the evaporator fins and comb out any bent ones - a dust-matted coil loses capacity and runs the compressor hot. Do this before the seawater-side descale so you are not chasing two faults at once.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Return Air Filter Cleaning
tasks.description: Pull the mesh filter off the front of the evaporator air intake grille to wash away dust, salt-fuzz, or pet hair that restricts airflow.
tasks.caution_notes: Monthly wash of the return-air filter. A blocked filter freezes the coil and the unit ices up and stops cooling - the number-one 'my AC died' cause. Dry fully before refitting.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Reversing Valve Exercise
tasks.description: Cycle the system on the digital display from "Cooling" mode over into "Heating" mode for 5 minutes to keep the internal sliding valve slider from freezing up.
tasks.caution_notes: If it is a heat pump, run it in heat mode a few minutes each quarter even in season - a reversing valve that never moves sticks, and then there is no heat when you want it. Listen for the changeover clunk.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Sea Strainer Cleaning
tasks.description: Shut the intake seacock, pull the internal mesh basket out of the glass sea strainer, and dump out trapped weeds, mud, or jellyfish.
tasks.caution_notes: Pump is not self-priming; an airlock throws an immediate high-pressure fault. No liquid bleach in the condensate pan - it corrodes the aluminum fins; use pan tabs.

tasks.name: Salon A/C - Seawater Flow Verification
tasks.description: Visually confirm that a steady, robust stream of seawater is discharging out of the side of the hull to prove the pump isn't airlocked.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm a strong overboard discharge within ~30 s of the pump starting. Weak or no flow = airlock, blocked strainer, growth in the intake, or a tired pump, and the unit faults on high-pressure within a minute or two. Marine AC pumps do not self-prime - clear the airlock at the pump or the strainer lid.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Backflow Check-Valve Flush
tasks.description: Clear slime out of the small inline rubber check-valve or flapper to prevent dirty discharge water from draining right back into the sump pit.
tasks.caution_notes: Clear slime from the inline check valve - fouled, it either sticks open (discharge drains back, pump short-cycles) or sticks shut (pump runs, nothing moves). If it won't clean up, replace it - they are cheap.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Discharge Hose Clamp Check
tasks.description: Verify the stainless steel hose clamp securing the 3/4" ID smooth-bore discharge pipe is perfectly tight and rust-free.
tasks.caution_notes: Double 316 stainless clamps on the discharge below the waterline.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Float Switch Check
tasks.description: Lift the integrated or external inline float switch to ensure the small pump instantly hums to life without delay.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift the float, confirm instant start. This one lives in a shower sump or shallow bilge and gets soap scum on the switch - a sticky switch here means a wet sole.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Impeller Cavity Audit
tasks.description: Look up into the exposed base cavity and manually spin the plastic centrifugal impeller to verify it isn't choked by hair or dental floss.
tasks.caution_notes: Match the fuse to the float switch: legacy 25D takes 2.5 A, the newer 25DA takes 4.0 A.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Strainer Base Clean-Out
tasks.description: Press the red side tabs to pop the white pump body out of its red snap-lock base. Clear out accumulated hair, soap scum, or debris from the mesh intake.
tasks.caution_notes: Monthly on a shower/galley sump pump - hair and soap scum choke it fast. Pop the body off the base, clear it, check the impeller spins.

tasks.name: Salon Bilge Pump - Wiring & Contact Service
tasks.description: Inspect the 12V positive and ground crimps. Because these smaller units sit deep in damp sumps, ensure waterproof heat-shrink joints remain air-tight.
tasks.caution_notes: These small pumps sit in the wettest spot on the boat - every joint must be adhesive-lined heat-shrink or a sealed connector, tinned wire, up out of the water. A green crimp here is why the pump 'died'. Fuse to the switch variant (25D = 2.5 A, 25DA = 4.0 A).

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Air Intake Filter Inspection
tasks.description: Pull the paper/foam element from the primary air intake assembly. Tap away grit or swap if salt-crusted.
tasks.caution_notes: Pull the intake element, tap out grit, replace if salt-crusted or oil-fouled. A restricted intake starves stage 1 and every stage downstream runs hot; site the intake in clean air, upwind of every engine exhaust.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Breathing Filter Swap
tasks.description: Replace the active carbon/molecular sieve cartridge. Fused salt/humidity drops its filtering efficiency, risking toxic air.
tasks.caution_notes: MCH-6 breathing-filter cartridge on the 20-hour interval.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Complete Lubrication Overhaul
tasks.description: Unbolt the bottom drain plug to flush and replace the complete crankcase synthetic oil volume.
tasks.caution_notes: The maker's synthetic compressor oil; filter cartridges; a spare drive V-belt.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Condensate Water Purge
tasks.description: Crack open the manual condensate separator and filter housing discharge valves to blast out trapped water and moisture slurry.
tasks.caution_notes: The 10-minute moisture purge is mandatory - water past the separator corrodes the 3rd/4th-stage HP piston sleeves. Max 1 hour run, then 1 hour rest.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Drive Belt Tension Audit
tasks.description: Check for flat spots on the drive belt and measure the deflection play between the motor sheave and the compressor flywheel.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the V-belt for glazing and flat spots and set deflection per the manual between the sheaves. A slipping belt loses fill rate and its dust fouls everything - a spare belt is a must-carry.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Exhaust/Toolroom Ventilation
tasks.description: Ensure your workroom's overhead hatch is open or an active fan runs while compressing to guarantee the machine pulls cool, clean oxygen.
tasks.caution_notes: A single-phase 110V compressor motor can pull ~30 FLA - it needs a dedicated 30-40 A breaker on 10 AWG, never a shared 15 A cabin outlet. Start it with the generator online or on 30 A shore power; the inductive surge may not start off batteries.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Idle-Period Run & Purge
tasks.description: If the compressor has not been used in ~a month, run it 10-15 minutes (venting, not filling) with the moisture drains cycled, then pickle per the layup note if it will sit longer.
tasks.caution_notes: Standing moisture in the stages and separator corrodes the HP piston sleeves and the check valves. A short monthly run keeps the internals oiled and dry; if you are leaving it weeks, follow the full layup procedure instead.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Safety Valve Pressure Test
tasks.description: Run the unit up to its maximum cut-off pressure to verify the physical spring safety valve pops open reliably to vent over-pressure.
tasks.caution_notes: Run to cut-off and confirm the final-stage spring safety valve lifts and vents at its stamped pressure and reseats. A stuck safety valve on a 300-bar machine is a bomb - if it does not lift cleanly, replace it, never adjust it.

tasks.name: Scuba Compressor - Visual Crankcase Oil Check
tasks.description: Verify the synthetic oil level sits precisely between the MIN and MAX lines on the dipstick.
tasks.caution_notes: Level between MIN and MAX before each session and every 5 running hours - a small dive compressor works hard for its size and a low level cooks the upper stages. Use only the maker's specified synthetic oil. Darkening fast = blow-by; milky = moisture past the separator.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Cylinder Hydrostatic Test
tasks.description: DOT/TC 5-year hydrostatic re-test of each cylinder; new date stamp on the crown.
tasks.caution_notes: A cylinder past its 5-year hydro cannot legally be filled. Hydro facilities are scarce in many island chains - schedule this for a stop with a test facility and stagger the tanks so you are never grounded. Budget that an aluminium 80 may fail and need replacing at ~20-25 years.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Cylinder Visual Inspection (VIP)
tasks.description: Annual internal/external visual inspection of every cylinder (PSI/PCI standard); fresh VIP sticker applied.
tasks.caution_notes: No current VIP sticker = no fills, in the US and almost every Caribbean shop. Look for internal corrosion (steel: rust/tumble; aluminium: white oxide), neck cracks, and valve-thread damage. Any pre-1990 aluminium 6351-T6 alloy tank also needs an eddy-current neck test. Store tanks with ~200-500 psi (never bone dry - lets moisture in), valve shut, upright and secured, out of the sun.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - DSMB, Reel & Spool Check
tasks.description: Inspect each delayed SMB for pinholes and a working oral/LP inflator and dump; check the reels/spools for cracks, line condition and a smooth ratchet; re-tie worn line.
tasks.caution_notes: A DSMB is your 'here I am' to the boat and to traffic on every ascent - a leaker that will not stand up is a real safety gap on a cruising boat where you may be diving off the tender. Rinse and dry fully after use; talc lightly before long stowage so the fabric does not stick.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Dive Computer & Light Care
tasks.description: Charge the dive computers, lights and the air-transmitter; check seals; offload logs / update firmware. Also do this before every dive trip.
tasks.caution_notes: Li-ion self-discharges and hates being stored flat - top up every ~90 days on the shelf, not just before a trip. Open the battery hatch, check the O-ring and sealing face for grit and hairs, re-grease lightly with silicone. Wipe salt off the charge contacts. A user-replaceable computer battery (some Suunto/Shearwater) - carry the spare cell and the O-ring kit.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Exposure Suit, Mask, Fin & Snorkel Check
tasks.description: Check wetsuits/skins for seam and zipper condition, mask skirts and straps for perishing, fin straps/buckles (carry spare fin straps or spring straps), and snorkel keepers.
tasks.caution_notes: Rubber straps and mask skirts perish fast in heat and sunscreen - a snapped fin strap ends a dive. Rinse gear in fresh water, dry out of the sun, store the mask in its box so the skirt keeps its shape. Keep a save-a-dive kit (straps, buckles, mouthpieces, zip ties, O-rings, silicone).

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Regulator & BCD Annual Service
tasks.description: Service the first + second stages, octopus, SPG and BCD per the manufacturer's schedule (annual, or 2-year with a logged dive count).
tasks.caution_notes: First/second-stage rebuild kits and dynamic O-rings; carry a spare mouthpiece and LP/HP hose. After a bench service, breathe and check every reg in the water before you rely on it. Daily: rinse in fresh water after every dive with the dust cap ON and dry - never press the purge while rinsing (drives water into the first stage). Store the BCD partly inflated so the bladder does not stick.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Tank Valve & O-Ring Check
tasks.description: Check each cylinder valve for smooth operation, the burst disc, and the yoke/DIN O-ring; replace tired O-rings.
tasks.caution_notes: A weeping valve O-ring wastes a fill overnight and a failed one on a boat passage empties the tank. Keep a pot of the correct yoke and DIN O-rings. Do not over-tighten a DIN reg into the valve.

tasks.name: Scuba Tanks & Dive Gear - Weight System & Save-a-Dive Kit Audit
tasks.description: Account for all soft/hard weights and pouches, check the BCD/belt quick-release weight pockets and buckles, and restock the save-a-dive kit.
tasks.caution_notes: A jammed or missing ditchable-weight release is a serious problem in an emergency ascent - cycle every buckle and QR yearly. Rinse lead and pockets (salt cakes and abrades the fabric).

tasks.name: Bonding & Cathodic Protection - Strut Clamshell Zinc
tasks.description: Replace the 4-in clamshell zinc on the bronze strut at haul-out or when more than ~50% wasted; bed clean, wire the fasteners. Confirm the strut's bonding wire back to the green bus is attached and low-resistance.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirmed: bronze strut, 4-in clamshell anode. Warm salt water eats a clamshell zinc fast - dive and check it between haul-outs. If the strut ever runs anode-less it dezincifies (pink casting) and the cutless-bearing area corrodes; a broken bonding wire does the same quietly. Carry spare 4-in clamshells + fasteners.

tasks.name: Shaft Seal & Stern Tube - Dripless Seal Inspection & Post-Launch Burp
tasks.description: Inspect the dripless prop-shaft seal: bellows for cracks, checking or soft spots; the two hose clamps doubled, tight and rust-free; the carbon flange face and the stainless rotor seating clean and square; the rotor set-screws / collar tight and safety-wired. Confirm bellows compression is to the maker's spec. After EVERY haul or launch, burp the seal (lift the bellows or open the vent) to purge trapped air before the engine runs.
tasks.caution_notes: A dripless seal that runs dry - unburped after launch, or a collapsed / split bellows - cooks the carbon face in minutes, scores or cracks it, then weeps or lets go and floods the boat. The bellows is age-limited: replace it on the maker's schedule (about 6 years for several makers) regardless of how it looks. Record the seal make and model - it sets the bellows interval and the spare part number.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Complete Head Rebuild
tasks.description: Back out the clamping screw, open the head housing, and completely replace the internal Santoprene diaphragm and tricuspid flap valves.
tasks.caution_notes: Santoprene kit AK1550 for grey/bilge duty. Backing-plate rounded edge faces the diaphragm. No caustic cleaners.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Electrical Line Verification
tasks.description: Test terminal joints for corrosion or resistance drops. Confirm the correctly rated fuse is fitted.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the pump's voltage and fuse rating from its label. Check terminal joints for corrosion and voltage drop under load.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Ezi-Clamp Ring Inspection
tasks.description: Check the single structural screw holding the patented Ezi-Clamp locking ring to ensure the multi-directional pump head has not vibrated loose.
tasks.caution_notes: The one structural screw on the Ezi-Clamp ring holds the multi-port head together - vibration backs it off and the head weeps or comes apart.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Hot Water Flush
tasks.description: Dump hot water down the shower or galley drain to melt body oils, soap film, and hair mats caught in the diaphragm chamber.
tasks.caution_notes: Run hot water down the drain the pump serves for a minute monthly - it melts the body-oil, soap and hair mat that cements the diaphragm chamber and the tricuspid valves. A diaphragm pump passes solids but not a grease plug.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Inlet Strainer Clearing
tasks.description: Clear the hair, soap film and lint caught in the shower sump pump's inlet strainer.
tasks.caution_notes: The shower pan is the heaviest hair-and-soap load on the boat, and it collects at the strainer, not the pump. A blocked strainer makes the pump cavitate and hammer.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Line Hose-Clamp Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the 3/4" (19mm) or 1" (25mm) smooth-bore reinforced intake and discharge hoses for tight sealing.
tasks.caution_notes: Smooth-bore 3/4" or 1" reinforced hose, clamps tight - relaxed new hose and vibration both loosen them. Double-clamp any run that could siphon.

tasks.name: Shower Sump Pump - Manual Switch Check
tasks.description: The pump is switched manually (no float switch): confirm the switch starts the pump and stops it when switched off.
tasks.caution_notes: Manual switching means nobody is watching it - a switch that sticks on runs the pump dry. Check the switch and its terminals for corrosion.

tasks.name: Snubber - Complete Snubber Line Retirement
tasks.description: Completely replace both nylon legs to ensure maximum energy absorption. Nylon naturally loses its elastic memory after thousands of cyclical loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Retire on any stiff or glazed section - friction-heat damage to nylon is permanent.

tasks.name: Snubber - Fire Hose Under-Wrap Inspection
tasks.description: Peel back or look underneath the fire hose wrap on the cleat eyes to check for hidden rope fuzzing or trapped salt crystals that harden the nylon weave.
tasks.caution_notes: Peel back the fire-hose sleeves at the cleat eyes and look underneath - salt crystals and hidden fuzzing collect where you cannot see, and the sleeve hides a failing splice. Flush and re-inspect.

tasks.name: Snubber - Salt-Cyst Removal Soak
tasks.description: Submerge both nylon legs in a fresh water bucket to flush out embedded salt crystals that slice internal core fibers under cyclical loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Push the hose nozzle right inside the fire-hose chafe sleeves to flush trapped salt.

tasks.name: Snubber - Thimble Rotation & Throat Audit
tasks.description: Check the hook-end eye splices. Ensure the nylon rope hasn't stretched out or loosened around the SS thimbles, which can cause the thimble to twist or cock sideways under heavy surge loads.
tasks.caution_notes: Heavy-duty gusseted thimbles. Watch the throat for elongation and micro-sawing at the Suncor hook.

tasks.name: Snubber - Toe Rail Fairlead Chafe Check
tasks.description: Inspect the newly added chafe gear at the toe rail. Ensure the wrap hasn't slipped out of the fairlead chock and check the aluminum or stainless rail edges for burrs.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the toe-rail chafe gear daily on the hook - the bridle legs work back and forth with every yaw and the wrap creeps out of the chock. An exposed leg saws through in a chop in hours.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Arch & Frame Fastener Torque
tasks.description: Verify the stainless steel bolts, U-clamps, and tilt-mechanisms securing the heavy 300W bifacial panels to your arch remain tight against engine harmonics.
tasks.caution_notes: Re-check every mount bolt, U-clamp and tilt-pin on the arch - the panels are big sails in a gust and the arch flexes underway. A backed-off clamp lets a panel lift, tear its wiring, or leave the boat. Nyloc or wired.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - CIGS Delamination & Bubble Check
tasks.description: Run your hand across the surface of the CIGS panels to check for localized lifting, edge un-bonding, or trapped moisture bubbles under the top layer.
tasks.caution_notes: Flexible CIGS panels wick saltwater through any un-bonded edge and permanently short the copper-selenide layer. Re-seal a lifting edge immediately with marine edge tape.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Inspect Connections
tasks.caution_notes: Walk every MC4 pair and junction for heat discoloration, water in the connector and UV-cracked insulation. A high-resistance MC4 is a rooftop-fire cause and silently kills a string's output. Confirm the inline blocking diodes.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - MC4 Connector Insulation Audit
tasks.description: Inspect the high-voltage MC4 connection joints behind the arrays. Ensure they are elevated out of pooling deck water and showing zero signs of UV cracking.
tasks.caution_notes: Check any inline MC4 blocking diodes. Keep rigid and flexible (CIGS) strings on separate solar controllers so one string does not bottleneck the other.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - MPPT Terminal Heat Check
tasks.description: Re-torque the high-current DC output terminals on the solar charge controllers to prevent terminal arcing from cyclical heating expansion.
tasks.caution_notes: Re-torque the controller DC terminals to that unit's spec (small controllers are often around 2.4 Nm; larger units differ). Cyclical heating backs a lug off over a year and it then arcs under charge current. Hand-feel or thermal-scan the terminals after an hour of good sun.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Salt & Bird Debris Rinse
tasks.description: Wash down all panels. Even a tiny speck of dried bird dropping or salt crusting can drop an entire string's output by 50% via cell shading.
tasks.caution_notes: Rinse bird strikes and salt crust off the same day - a partly-shaded cell drags its whole series string down and cooks the bypass diode. Shading is not linear: 10% shade can be 50% loss.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Thermal Camera Scanning
tasks.description: Use a cheap smartphone thermal camera to scan the arrays under full noon sun. A single localized "hot spot" flags a failing cell or blown bypass diode.
tasks.caution_notes: Scan the arrays under full noon sun with a phone thermal camera. A hot single cell = a failing cell or shorted bypass diode; a hot whole panel = a bad junction-box connection. Cheapest early warning for a panel about to fail open.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Wash
tasks.description: Clean off salt, dust and dirt.
tasks.caution_notes: Weekly fresh-water rinse - salt film alone costs several percent and etches the surface over time. Low pressure, soft cloth; flexible (CIGS) panels do not tolerate scrubbing.

tasks.name: Solar Panels - Bifacial Panel Clean
tasks.description: Clean the underside of bifacial panels and polish the white deck or arch surfaces below them to maximize rear-side bounce light reflection.
tasks.caution_notes: Bifacial panels harvest off the underside - keep wiring, antennas and shadows off the back face.

tasks.name: Steering System - Autopilot Linear Drive Check
tasks.description: Inspect the mounting bracket of your under-deck autopilot hydraulic ram or mechanical drive arm where it pins to the auxiliary tiller arm.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the autopilot drive-arm bracket and the clevis where it pins to the tiller arm for elongation and cracking - this bracket takes every autopilot correction for thousands of miles. Keep the dedicated pin-drop wrench zip-tied to the bracket.

tasks.name: Steering System - Cable Tension & Swage Check
tasks.description: (If Wire/Chain system) Inspect the stainless steel steering wires for broken "meat hook" strands, and verify the tension nuts at the rudder quadrant are tight.
tasks.caution_notes: Wire/chain: run a rag over the wires for meat-hooks, check the chain-to-wire links, and set quadrant tension so there is no slack at centre but the chain still seats on the sprocket. Carry a spare cable made up to length. After new cables are fitted, re-tension and re-check the swages after the first season of use, then on the normal cycle.

tasks.name: Steering System - Emergency Tiller Drill
tasks.description: Physically unpack and fit the manual bronze/aluminum emergency tiller onto the rudder stock head to ensure the access hatch clears and the arm moves freely.
tasks.caution_notes: Keep the lazarette path to the emergency tiller and linear drive clear of loose gear at all times - you may need it in seconds.

tasks.name: Steering System - Mamba Universal Joint Service
tasks.description: (If Mamba torque tube system) Crawl into the aft lazarette to clean and heavily pack the universal joints, bevel gearboxes, and splined end fittings with grease.
tasks.caution_notes: Into the lazarette: clean and heavily grease the torque-tube U-joints, bevel boxes and splined ends. Highest-value steering job on a shorthanded boat - a seized U-joint offshore means the emergency tiller for the rest of the passage. Keep the path to it permanently clear.

tasks.name: Steering System - Pedestal Needle Bearing Care
tasks.description: Remove the compass housing from the top of the pedestal. Apply a small amount of grease to the main wheel shaft needle bearings.
tasks.caution_notes: Lift the compass off the pedestal head and grease the wheel-shaft needle bearings with waterproof marine grease, sparingly. A dry bearing here feels like notchy steering and slowly wears the shaft.

tasks.name: Steering System - Quadrant Stop Bolt Check
tasks.description: Ensure the heavy rubber-padded structural stop bolts (which prevent the rudder from over-rotating and jamming against the hull) are secure.
tasks.caution_notes: The padded stop bolts absorb the shock when a following sea slams the rudder - confirm they are tight, pads intact, and that the rudder meets them before the quadrant can foul the hull or gear. This is what keeps a broach from bending the stock.

tasks.name: Steering System - Rudder Bearing Overhaul
tasks.description: Drop the rudder during a haul-out to inspect the upper and lower rudder stock bearings for ovaling, structural looseness, or composite degradation.
tasks.caution_notes: Drop the rudder at haul-out to check upper and lower bearings for ovalisation and play and the stock for crevice corrosion at the bearing lands. On an older hull, budget for this - a failed lower bearing lets the blade wander and can crack the tube.

tasks.name: Steering System - Rudder Stock Gland Inspection
tasks.description: Check the packing gland or lip seals at the top of the rudder trunk for seawater weeping while underway or backing down under power.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the rudder-trunk packing / lip seal for weeping when backing hard under power (worst-case load). A few drops is acceptable on a stuffing type; a stream is not. Know where the gland-adjusting tool lives. After a repack, early weeping usually means the new packing has bedded in and wants a nip, not that it is worn.

tasks.name: Stern Wash - Diaphragm & Valve Inspection
tasks.description: Unscrew the pump head housing screws to inspect the internal Santoprene diaphragm and check valves for debris punctures or calcium buildup.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the head, inspect the Santoprene diaphragm for pin-holes and the check valves for grit and calcium. Carry one full head/valve service kit per pump type - a split diaphragm is a dockside-unavailable part in most of the cruising world.

tasks.name: Stern Wash - Electrical Terminal Check
tasks.description: Verify that crimps and connections at the pump, its pressure switch, and its dedicated switch on the helm switch panel are clean, corrosion-free, and receiving stable voltage.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the crimps at the pump, its pressure switch and the panel switch, and the supply, for corrosion and stable voltage - a marginal joint makes the pump chatter or run weak and burns the switch contacts. The pump only runs when its panel switch is on AND the deck fitting is pushed and twisted.

tasks.name: Stern Wash - Inlet Strainer Cleaning
tasks.description: Twist off the clear plastic strainer bowl, pull out the mesh screen, and flush out accumulated sediment.
tasks.caution_notes: Twist off the clear strainer bowl, pull the mesh screen, flush. A blocked strainer starves the pump - it runs hot and loud and diaphragm life drops.

tasks.name: Stern Wash - Visual Leak & Noise Check
tasks.description: Inspect plumbing fittings for slow drips and check that rubber vibration-damping feet are secure to prevent mounting noise.
tasks.caution_notes: Look for weeping at the head screws and port fittings and confirm the rubber feet are sound - a hard-mounted pump telegraphs through the boat and the vibration eventually cracks a fitting. A pump that cycles on its own with every tap shut has a system leak or a failed check valve.

tasks.name: Tank Monitoring & Senders - Tank Sender Calibration (first fill / after tank work)
