tasks.description: Multi-point calibrate every fuel and water tank sender: fill from a known-low or empty state in measured increments, record the raw sender value against actual gallons at each step, and enter the calibration curve in the tank monitor.
tasks.caution_notes: Tanks with sloped bottoms make a 2-point (empty/full) calibration badly wrong in the middle, which is exactly where you make decisions on passage. Take at least 5-6 points per tank. Do it on the FIRST fill (or after any sender/tank work) and log the curve so it can be re-entered if the monitor is replaced. Note total usable capacity vs nameplate - the pickup does not reach the last few gallons.

tasks.name: Tank Monitoring & Senders - Level Sender Cross-Check
tasks.description: Compare the tank monitor's readings against a physical dip or sight tube, and against fuel actually burned (engine + generator hours x consumption). Investigate any tank that has drifted.
tasks.caution_notes: Resistive senders corrode, float arms stick, and reed-switch senders lose segments - the failure mode is a reading that looks plausible but is stuck or offset. The burn-rate cross-check is the one that catches a slowly-lying sender. Keep a manual dipstick calibrated to each tank as the backup of record.

tasks.name: Tank Monitoring & Senders - Sender & Wiring Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect each tank sender flange, gasket and the sender wiring / ground for corrosion, chafe and loose terminals. Confirm the tank grounds tie to the common bus.
tasks.caution_notes: A weeping sender flange on a diesel tank is a fuel leak and a fume source; on a water tank it is contamination. A bad sender ground reads erratic or full-scale. Viton/Nitrile gasket on the diesel-converted tanks - never the original EPDM.

tasks.name: Tanks (General) - Inspection Port Sealing
tasks.description: Open the sub-floor access boards to check the gaskets on the large circular stainless tank inspection ports for compression tracking or slow weeping.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspection-port seals must be fuel-grade Buna-N or Viton - the original EPDM fails in diesel. Match the return-fuel line to the active tank selector or fuel overflows the deck vent.

tasks.name: Tanks (General) - Isolation Block Inspection
tasks.description: Check the heavy neoprene or high-density rubber strips underneath the aluminum/stainless hold-down tank straps. If the rubber slips, crevice corrosion forms.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the neoprene strips under the tank hold-down straps - compressed or rotted, the tank works against bare metal and chafes through a corner, or the strap goes slack and the tank shifts in a seaway. A full tank adrift is a serious problem.

tasks.name: Tanks (General) - Tank Grounding Wire Check
tasks.description: Verify the copper static grounding strips connecting the fuel fills and tank bodies to the main ship grounding bus are tight to avoid static electrical risk.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm the static-bonding straps from the fuel fills and metal tank bodies to the ship's ground bus are tight and unbroken - fuel through a hose builds static and an ungrounded deck fill is a spark risk while fuelling. Diesel is forgiving; the outboard's gasoline is not.

tasks.name: Temperature Sensors - CR2477 Battery Replacement
tasks.description: Unscrew the enclosure and swap out the internal coin-cell battery. Cold environments (like freezer boxes) will drain battery capacity significantly faster than ambient cabins.
tasks.caution_notes: Fresh CR2477 yearly, sooner for freezer tags where cold roughly halves usable capacity and a marginal cell reads erratically before it dies. Use the high-capacity CR2477 (spares list, 6-pack) - do not substitute a CR2450.

tasks.name: Temperature Sensors - Casing De-Salt Wash
tasks.description: Wipe down the sensor housings with a dry cloth to clear away sticky salt crusting that can block or attenuate the 2.4 GHz radio signal.
tasks.caution_notes: Wipe salt crust off the tag housings - a heavy salt/dirt layer attenuates the BLE signal and traps moisture against the seal. Dry cloth, no solvents on the plastic.

tasks.name: Temperature Sensors - Gasket & Condensation Inspection
tasks.description: Open the weatherproof enclosure of any sensors deployed in harsh areas (like the freezer box or deep bilge) to ensure there is no internal condensation.
tasks.caution_notes: Open the tags in the harshest spots (freezer, deep bilge) and check the seal and for internal condensation - a wet PCB corrodes and the humidity channel goes wild first. Re-seal, or move to an external probe if a spot keeps killing tags.

tasks.name: Temperature Sensors - Signal & Data Audit
tasks.description: Open the monitoring dashboard (app or monitoring hub) and check for any wireless temperature sensor disconnects or low-battery warnings.
tasks.caution_notes: Check every wireless tag is still reporting and none flags low battery - a dropped tag is flat, out of Bluetooth range of the receiver, or shut inside a metal box (the freezer) attenuating 2.4 GHz. These are the early warning for a fridge / freezer / bilge problem, so a silent tag matters.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Bronze "Pinking" Inspection
tasks.description: Scratch the surface of the 3 bronze thru-hulls with a knife. If the metal looks bright gold, it is healthy. If it looks dull red/pink, it is zinc-depleted.
tasks.caution_notes: Look for pink or coppery patches on the bronze valves - dezincification from stray current or a broken bond. A pinked valve can fail under light pressure.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Bronze Valve Bonding Check
tasks.description: Inspect the green bonding wire attached to the 3 bronze thru-hull backing collars to ensure zero wire corrosion or loose screws.
tasks.caution_notes: The 3 remaining bronze thru-hulls must stay on the green bonding grid or stray current will 'pink' (de-zincify) them.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Emergency Bung Audit
tasks.description: Verify that a correctly sized tapered soft-wood or foam emergency plug is tethered directly to every single thru-hull valve.
tasks.caution_notes: A correctly-sized soft-wood plug tethered at every through-hull, plus one oversized plug at the largest intakes. Soft pine or fir, not hardwood - it swells to seal. Re-check the tethers; that is what fails, not the plug.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Hose Clamp Tension Audit
tasks.description: Verify that all hoses attached to the valves are double-clamped with high-grade stainless steel bands facing in opposite directions.
tasks.caution_notes: Two AWAB or all-316 clamps per barb below the waterline, screw heads opposed. Reject any clamp with a slotted (perforated) band - they crevice-corrode and shear. Nip them up; new hose relaxes in the first months.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Marelon Valve Lubrication
tasks.description: For Marelon ball valves, disassemble the hose tail (or flush via the thru-hull while hauled) and apply a specialized grease to keep the ball turning smoothly.
tasks.caution_notes: Marelon/composite valves: pure silicone grease only (the valve maker's lubricant). Petroleum grease, white lithium and WD-40 swell and split the composite. Composite valves are electrically inert - keep them off the bonding circuit. Bronze valves with a grease path: service them with this task too.

tasks.name: Thru Hulls - Valve Actuation (Exercise)
tasks.description: Fully close and open all bronze and Marelon valves several times to scrape away internal barnacles and marine growth before they seize.
tasks.caution_notes: Full open-close-open on every seacock monthly, afloat and hauled. A composite ball valve that has not moved in months needs real force - that is when a handle snaps. Keep the boat's whole thru-hull count and locations on a card at the companionway. Include any hard-to-reach valves (e.g. cockpit scupper seacocks) - they are the most likely to seize unnoticed and the easiest to skip.

tasks.name: Toilets - Internal Mechanism Lubrication
tasks.description: Add marine toilet lubricant to the bowl and pump it through to keep internal rubber, leather parts, and chambers running smoothly.
tasks.caution_notes: Pump a marine head lubricant (or a spoon of vegetable oil) through monthly - the piston cup, joker valve and flap valve are rubber/leather and run dry and stiff otherwise, then they leak and the pump gets hard to work.

tasks.name: Toilets - Piston Rod Greasing
tasks.description: Unscrew the top seal housing and apply grease directly to the vertical piston rod to maximize the lifespan of the top seal.
tasks.caution_notes: Unscrew the top seal housing and grease the piston rod - a dry rod scores the top seal, then the pump weeps at the top of every stroke and draws air. Waterproof grease, thin film.

tasks.name: Toilets - System Flush & Conditioning
tasks.description: Flush water through to clear the lines. Use marine holding tank treatments to dissolve sludge and debris.
tasks.caution_notes: Pump ~15-20 strokes of clean water through after every use to clear the discharge line to the tank - waste left in the hose is 90% of head odour. Dose the holding tank, not the bowl, with treatment.

tasks.name: Toilets - Uric Scale Clear-out
tasks.description: Dissolve mineral and scale buildup inside the small intake/discharge valves and wastewater lines.
tasks.caution_notes: Uric scale (hard white crystal) builds in the discharge elbow, joker valve and vented loop and chokes the line - the tell is progressively harder pumping. White vinegar overnight, or dismantle and pick it out. Never a drain acid - it destroys the rubber.

tasks.name: Tools - Canvas & Sleeve Salt Wash
tasks.description: Take the tools down and wash the canvas wrench rolls and bucket sleeves in fresh water. Fabric fibers collect airborne salt mist, which will actively draw moisture straight onto the steel if not laundered.
tasks.caution_notes: Launder the tool-roll canvas yearly - the fabric holds airborne salt and dampness against the steel.

tasks.name: Tools - Craft Box Desiccant Refresh
tasks.description: Check the sealed plastic craft boxes organizing your specialized gear. Regenerate or swap the small desiccant packs inside.
tasks.caution_notes: Store DeWalt 20V batteries detached from tools, inverted, in gasketed dry-boxes with VCI blocks - salt-moisture bridging the open terminal slots causes a high-resistance short and thermal runaway (battery fire). Unplug 110V chargers when leaving the boat.

tasks.name: Tools - Door Mounting Screw Check
tasks.description: Inspect the wood screws and grommets holding the sliced bucket sleeves to the doors to ensure hull pounding hasn't stripped the fiberglass/wood threads.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the screws and grommets holding the cut-bucket tool sleeves to the locker doors - hull pounding works them loose, a sleeve dumps its tools in the bilge, and a heavy loose sleeve swinging on a door in a seaway wrecks the door. Nyloc or thread-lock, oversized washers.

tasks.name: Tools - Exposed Tool Barrier Wipe
tasks.description: Spray a clean cloth and wipe down the handle shafts of the wrenches in the canvas sleeves and tools on the doors to keep a micro-thin anti-rust shell active.
tasks.caution_notes: Contact cleaner then dielectric grease on exposed terminals; VCI coins in the boxes.

tasks.name: Transmission - Break-In Oil Change
tasks.description: First gear-oil change with the engine 50-hour break-in. API CD or higher, SAE #20 or #30, about 2.0 L, pumped out via the dipstick tube.
tasks.caution_notes: The break-in oil carries the most cone and gear seating debris - do it on time. Inspect the drained oil for bronze glitter.

tasks.name: Transmission - Cone Clutch Function Test
tasks.description: Under load against a dock line, confirm firm engagement ahead and astern with no slip, and zero creep in neutral.
tasks.caution_notes: A cone clutch (common on small marine gearboxes) is not field-adjustable like a band clutch - slip or creep means worn cones and a haul-out rebuild. Catch it early from the oil and the feel, not after it fails leaving a dock.

tasks.name: Transmission - Damper Plate & Coupling Check
tasks.description: Listen at idle in neutral for the rattle/growl of a failing damper (drive) plate between the flywheel and the gear input. Check the output-coupling bolts and set screws are tight, wired, and free of fretting rust.
tasks.caution_notes: A failed damper plate strands the boat and is a common wear item - carry a spare. A loose or fretting coupling flange throws the shaft alignment out and chews the cutless bearing.

tasks.name: Transmission - Routine Oil Change
tasks.description: Use the gear oil in the transmission manual (commonly API CD+ SAE 20 or 30 straight-grade, 15W-40 often acceptable), filled via the dipstick tube. Many small marine gearboxes are splash-lubricated with no oil filter.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the drained oil: bronze glitter = clutch-cone wear, milky = water past a seal, black and burnt = the cone has been slipping. Any of those means haul and open the gear.

tasks.name: Transmission - Shift Linkage & Detent Check
tasks.description: At the gear-end shift lever, confirm the cable drives fully into the forward, neutral and reverse detents with a little over-travel, and the lever springs back to centre.
tasks.caution_notes: A gear that does not fully engage rides the cone clutch and burns it. Set the cable at the gear end, not just the pedestal.

tasks.name: Transom Shower - Cover, Seal & Mount Check
tasks.description: Check the hinged cover, its latch and gasket, the drain path behind it, and the housing-to-deck bed for leaks into the locker below.
tasks.caution_notes: A failed cover gasket or a blocked drain lets the recess fill and sit; a weeping deck bed rots the core around the cut-out. UV embrittles the ABS cover and latch - carry the fact that this whole unit is a cheap replacement rather than a repair.

tasks.name: Transom Shower - Function, Hose & Mixer Check
tasks.description: Run hot and cold, check the mixer for smooth action and no cross-flow, check the spray head and trigger, and inspect the 7 ft hose and both fittings for leaks, kinks and chafe where it retracts into the housing.
tasks.caution_notes: The retracting hose chafes at the housing lip and at its swivel - that is where it splits and dribbles into the lazarette / transom locker. A stiff or cross-flowing mixer sends hot water back down the cold line. If the boat has sat, flush the line through - stagnant fresh water in the hose grows biofilm you then rinse yourself with.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - Acoustic Dampening Clearance
tasks.description: Verify that no loose heavy gear, toolboxes, or anchor chain coils are directly contacting the hull sections right over the transducer mounts, as this dampens the ultrasonic frequency.
tasks.caution_notes: Confirm nothing heavy rests on the hull directly over a puck - a toolbox, spare anchor or chain pile absorbs the ultrasound and leaves that hull patch unprotected. Mark the puck locations inside.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - Bilge Fluid Clearance Sweep
tasks.description: Ensure the bilge areas where the 6 transducers are glued remain dry. While the pucks are fully submersible, sitting under oily bilge water degrades the casing plastics over time.
tasks.caution_notes: Keep the bilge under the six transducer pucks dry - oily bilge water degrades the casing plastic and the epoxy bond, and an internal oil film damps the ultrasound. Fix the source of any bilge oil.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - LED Status / App Heartbeat Audit
tasks.description: Check the controller faceplates (or the maker's smartphone app, if it has one) to verify the units are actively pulsing.
tasks.caution_notes: Ultrasonic antifoul only deters new larval settlement - it cannot remove existing growth. Never switch off the controller breakers while away; keep the solar charging live to carry the 24/7 draw.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - Main DC Terminal & Fuse Integrity Check
tasks.description: Inspect the direct-to-battery or distribution panel power connections. Ensure wire junctions are free of green copper corrosion.
tasks.caution_notes: Spare inline fuses aboard; check the DC feed and fuse holders for heat.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - Out-of-Water "Tick" Audio Verification
tasks.description: While the boat is hauled out on the hard, place an ear to the outside of the hull to listen for the faint, intermittent "chirping/clicking" signature sound to confirm output.
tasks.caution_notes: Hauled: ear to the hull outside, listen for the faint intermittent tick over each puck - confirms the transducer is driving. Silent puck + lit controller = a broken transducer or a cracked epoxy bond.

tasks.name: Ultrasonic Antifouling - Transducer Epoxy Tap Test
tasks.description: Physically wiggle each of the 6 pucks and tap the casing. If the epoxy bond has fractured due to structural hull flexing or foot-steps, the acoustic waves cannot pass into the fiberglass.
tasks.caution_notes: Tap-test each transducer puck for a solid bond; re-epoxy any that sound hollow. No anchor or gear resting on the hull over a puck - it dampens the acoustics.

tasks.name: Underwater Imaging - Battery, Contact & Storage Care
tasks.description: Charge camera, strobe and video-light batteries on the shelf, clean the housing bulkhead/hot-shoe and sync-cord contacts, and store the housing OPEN with the O-rings out.
tasks.caution_notes: Li batteries hate being stored flat; salt creep on the sync contacts is the usual strobe-misfire cause. Storing the housing sealed compresses the O-rings into a set - store it open, O-rings bagged separately.

tasks.name: VHF Radios - Antenna Coaxial Connection Audit
tasks.description: Unbolt the PL-259 coaxial antenna connector at the back of each fixed VHF radio to check for white salt oxidation on the copper pin.
tasks.caution_notes: Unmake the PL-259 at each fixed radio and at the antenna base, check for green/white oxidation and water ingress, remake with fresh connectors and self-amalgamating tape over the joint. Corroded coax raises SWR, the radio folds back power to protect its finals, and your range quietly halves. After a refit check both ends - a new masthead run may still meet old deck-to-radio tails.

tasks.name: VHF Radios - Cockpit Plug Compression Care
tasks.description: Inspect the waterproof screw-on cap where the cockpit CommandMic plugs into the deck bulkhead plate to ensure salt air isn't penetrating the precision multi-pin jack.
tasks.caution_notes: PL-259 spares; keep the cockpit connector sealed and 303-treated.

tasks.name: VHF Radios - MMSI / GPS Integration Sync
tasks.description: Verify that your unique Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) is registering correctly on both fixed radios, and ensure they are pulling accurate GPS/GNSS data from your NMEA 2000 network for emergency DSC dispatch.
tasks.caution_notes: Program every fixed radio with the vessel's 9-digit MMSI. If an AIS or radio was re-used from a previous boat, CONFIRM its static data (MMSI, ship name, ship type, LxB dimensions, GPS antenna offsets) was re-programmed for this boat and is not still broadcasting the old one. See the AIS task.

tasks.name: VHF Radios - Masthead Antenna SWR Check
tasks.description: Use an SWR (Standing Wave Ratio) meter while transmitting to verify your masthead VHF antenna whip or coaxial line hasn't suffered internal water-wicking or structural degradation.
tasks.caution_notes: Never key a mic to transmit with no antenna connected - reflected RF melts the PA output transistors instantly. Record a baseline SWR reading when the antenna is new. If AIS shares this antenna through a splitter, an SWR problem hits both.

tasks.name: VHF Radios - Mobile VHF Battery Lifecycle Test
tasks.description: Discharge your handheld VHF battery completely and recharge it to verify full capacity, and apply silicone grease to its casing seals.
tasks.caution_notes: Keep a charged spare handheld battery. On an older handheld the battery is the weak point; run the capacity test on schedule and price a replacement before a long cruise.

tasks.name: Ventilation Fans - Blade & Shroud Deep Clean
tasks.description: Remove the front grille screws. Use a toothbrush and damp cloth to scrub sticky salt-dust grime off the plastic fan blades and casing.
tasks.caution_notes: Grille off, wash the salt-dust film off the blades and shroud - a dirt-loaded blade runs out of balance and that vibration is what finally kills the bearing.

tasks.name: Ventilation Fans - Grille Blow-Out
tasks.description: Use compressed air to blow accumulated dust and lint out of the protective front grille and motor vents before it cakes up.
tasks.caution_notes: Blow the dust and lint out of the grille and motor vents monthly - a blanketed motor runs hot and the sleeve bearing dries faster. A minute per fan; there are ten.

tasks.name: Ventilation Fans - Spindle Bearing Lubrication
tasks.description: Pull off the front assembly and apply a drop of light machine oil directly onto the central motor shaft seam to stop the fan from squealing.
tasks.caution_notes: A drop of light oil on the front bearing seam quiets a squeal for a while, but a squealing fan motor is near end of life - keep spare units aboard rather than nursing them; many small fan motors are not really serviceable. Quarterly lube fits between a monthly grille blow-out and a six-monthly deep clean.

tasks.name: Washing Machine - Clean lint filters, check hose connections
tasks.description: GENERAL BEST PRACTICE, not sourced to a manual for this specific unit (none found - see device notes). Clear lint from both tubs' filters; check inlet and drain hose connections (including the temporary berth-sink/shower-pan hookup - see device notes) for wear, kinks or leaks.

tasks.name: Water Maker - Charcoal Carbon Filter Service
tasks.description: Swap the carbon block pre-filter which catches traces of chlorine during freshwater flushes. Chlorine will chemically melt an RO membrane instantly.
tasks.caution_notes: Dock and municipal water will melt the polyamide membrane layer - always flush through a fresh charcoal filter and change the carbon block on schedule.

tasks.name: Water Maker - Freshwater Flush
tasks.description: If the unit sits unused for short periods, run a freshwater loop to clear salt brine from the high-pressure chambers.
tasks.caution_notes: On return, flush at 0 PSI for 15-20 min, then dump the first full hour of product water before collecting to the tank.

tasks.name: Water Maker - High-Pressure Pump Oil Change
tasks.description: Unbolt the high-pressure pump head from its mounting pad, drain the crankcase via the Allen plug, and refill with fresh oil.
tasks.caution_notes: ISO 60 pump oil; drain via the Allen plug.

tasks.name: Water Maker - Membrane Core Replacement
tasks.description: Swap out the two central RO cores if total dissolved solids (TDS) stay high or product flow rates permanently drop.
tasks.caution_notes: Many small watermakers use 2.5 x 40 in seawater RO elements - confirm the size and count in your watermaker manual. RO elements typically last 2-5 years.

tasks.name: Water Maker - Pre-Filter Element Swap
tasks.description: Replace the 20-micron and 5-micron spun-poly sediment pre-filters to prevent restriction at the boost pump inlet.
tasks.caution_notes: Typical prefilters: 10" spun-poly, 20 micron then 5 micron. Change monthly or when the boost-pump gauge shows restriction - the prefilters are sacrificial and cheap; a starved boost pump and a fouled membrane are not. Prime the new housings with product water, never raw seawater.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - Annual Seam & Pressure-Retention Test
tasks.description: Once a year, inflate each SUP and the dock, mark the pressure, and leave 24 hours. More than ~20% loss overnight (temperature-corrected) means a valve or seam leak - soap-test to find it.
tasks.caution_notes: Drop-stitch fabric and welded/glued seams fail slowly and from the inside; this is the test that catches it before a trip. A failing valve reads the same as a seam leak - always check the valve first (swap the valve O-ring, snug the valve wrench). Log the retention figure so you can watch the trend.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - Electric SUP Pump Care
tasks.description: Charge the electric pump's 13500 mAh battery, run it briefly, clear the intake filter/screen of grit and salt, and check the hose and fittings. Also charge before any trip.
tasks.caution_notes: The Li pack self-discharges and degrades if left flat between uses - top up every ~90 days on the shelf. A clogged intake screen makes the pump overheat and cut out short of pressure. Carry the manual backup pump (the SUP bundle's hand pump) - the electric one WILL die mid-trip eventually.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - Pre-Use Pressure & Rig Check
tasks.description: Before a run of use: inflate both SUPs and the dock to the printed working pressure with a gauge, check fins, leashes, D-rings and the dock's connection points, and confirm they hold pressure through the session.
tasks.caution_notes: Drop-stitch boards want their full rated PSI (typically 15-18) or they flex and delaminate; a soft board in chop is also unsafe. Inflate in the shade - a board pumped hard in the sun then left out can burst as it heats. Check the Halkey-Roberts valve is finger-tight and the core is not spinning.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - Repair Kit & PVC Cement Shelf-Life
tasks.description: Inventory the patch kit that came with each board (patches, valve tool, spare valve) and REPLACE the PVC/contact cement annually - sooner once opened.
tasks.caution_notes: The glue in the bundled repair kit is almost certainly dead already - single-part PVC cement has a shelf life around 1 year sealed and weeks once opened, and a bad-glue patch fails in the water. Buy fresh two-part inflatable adhesive (e.g. Polymarine / Bostik) and store it cool. Keep enough fabric and patches for a palm-sized puncture on each hull type aboard.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - UV, Rinse & Stowage Discipline
tasks.description: After use: fresh-water rinse, dry fully, and stow out of direct sun. For passages or long layup, deflate, roll loosely (not tight creases) and bag. Recurring reminder, not a fixed job.
tasks.caution_notes: In the tropics UV is the number-one killer of PVC and drop-stitch - a board left rigged on deck in Caribbean sun ages years in months. Salt left in the fabric and valves accelerates it. Do not store tightly folded on a sharp crease or under heavy gear - the coating cracks there first.

tasks.name: Watersports & Inflatables (SUP / Dock) - Valve Service & O-Ring
tasks.description: Check each Halkey-Roberts valve for a spinning core, cracks and a clean seat; replace the valve O-ring; confirm the valve wrench is aboard.
tasks.caution_notes: A weeping valve is the most common inflatable failure and is a 2-minute fix with the right O-ring and wrench. Do not over-tighten - you crack the flange. Keep spare valve inserts and O-rings in the repair kit.

tasks.name: Winches - Powered Winch Power & Control-Bus Inspection
tasks.description: On powered winches, check that the heavy motor power lines and the thin control-bus cables plugged into the winch control unit are tight and corrosion-free.
tasks.caution_notes: The winch power supply may step the house voltage up for the motor; supply, control unit and buttons often talk over their own bus, which must NOT be spliced to the boat's NMEA 2000. Check the time-delay fuse on the feed, the power cables for tight lugs and heat, and read the status LEDs. Confirm the supply's input voltage against its label.

tasks.name: Winches - Pawl & Spring Replacement
tasks.description: Swap out the small mechanical directional flappers and springs to prevent dangerous back-winding failures.
tasks.caution_notes: Replace pawls and springs on a schedule (4 + 4 per Size 40 winch, plus circlips) - a weak spring lets the pawl skip under shock load and the drum runs backwards. Cheap kit, keep spares.

tasks.name: Winches - Stripping & Degreasing
tasks.description: Lift off the drum, remove the roller bearings, and completely wash away old, hardened grease from the internal gears.
tasks.caution_notes: Annual strip: drum off, roller bearings out, wash all hardened grease out with white spirit, inspect the gear teeth, bearings and ratchet gear. Old grease turns to grinding paste and the pawls stop springing.

tasks.name: Winches - Topworks Lubrication
tasks.description: Apply fresh grease to the gear teeth/bearings, and apply thin machine oil strictly to the pawls so they do not stick.
tasks.caution_notes: The winch maker's gear grease on gear teeth and bearings ONLY. Light machine oil on the pawls and springs - NEVER grease the pawls; a greased cold pawl sticks and the winch back-winds under load, throwing the handle.

tasks.name: Winches - Waterproof Seal Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect the base seals and O-rings where the motor pack driveshaft passes through the deck to ensure no saltwater penetrates the 48V motor housing.
tasks.caution_notes: Inspect the base seals / O-rings where the motor-pack driveshaft passes through the deck - a failed seal floods the below-deck motor and MCU, which is a winch-plus-electronics replacement. Any weeping = pull and re-seal now.

tasks.name: Wind Sensor - Aloft Debris Cleansing
tasks.description: Go aloft to ensure spider webs, salt crusting, or bird droppings aren't freezing the wind cups or blocking the twin-fin vane orientation.
tasks.caution_notes: Aloft: clear spider web, salt and bird mess from the cups and vane - a sticky cup reads low and a fouled vane hunts. Check the masthead connector seal and that the unit is firmly seated while you are up there.

tasks.name: Wind Sensor - Field Installable Connector Check
tasks.description: Open the mast-base junction box where the bare mast wires are terminated. Check for loose or shorted wire-to-terminal crimps.
tasks.caution_notes: Carry a spare field-installable connector. Push/pull connectors only - never twist.

tasks.name: Wind Sensor - Gateway Firmware Update
tasks.description: Update the wind gateway's firmware via an NMEA 2000 chartplotter or the maker's PC software to patch communication bugs.
tasks.caution_notes: Makers push fixes for translation bugs that cause intermittent wind drop-outs. Note the version. Never twist push/pull connectors.

tasks.name: Wind Sensor - Gateway LED Status Check
tasks.description: If the wind sensor reaches NMEA 2000 through a gateway / bridge, verify its indicator lights show healthy network traffic (typically slow, steady green).
tasks.caution_notes: A fast flash or amber usually means the bus is not seeing the masthead unit or is not terminated. A dead wind instrument on the first night of a passage is a watch-keeping problem.

tasks.name: Wind Sensor - Masthead Connector Flush
tasks.description: Disconnect and clean the masthead wind connector at the arm base to prevent salt air tracking.
tasks.caution_notes: Check the gateway's port current limit before adding devices to it. Push/pull connectors must never be twisted - twisting snaps the pins.

tasks.name: Windlass - Clutch Check & Adjust
tasks.description: Release and re-engage the clutch mechanism using the windlass handle to ensure smooth progressive friction control.
tasks.caution_notes: Drop and re-set the clutch a few times to feel for smooth progressive grip. If it slips loaded or will not free-fall, strip and clean the cones - do not just tighten the clutch nut, that masks worn cones and shears keys. Dual-chainwheel windlasses: both chainwheels and the warping drum often share one common shaft, each coupled by its own clutch. Before powering one chainwheel (or the drum), back the OTHER chainwheel's clutch nut off - a clutch left tight is still coupled and will pay out or haul in that rode uncontrolled. Confirm against your windlass manual.

tasks.name: Windlass - Complete Gearbox Overhaul
tasks.description: Remove the gearbox from the spacer tube, flush the casing, replace old seals, and change the fluid completely.
tasks.caution_notes: Pull the gearbox off the spacer tube, flush, renew all seals and O-rings, refill. Do this at the dock - a windlass gearbox failure at anchor in a blow is a real emergency.

tasks.name: Windlass - Deck Foot Switch(es) & Control Inspection
tasks.description: Inspect the up/down deck foot switch(es), the hinged covers and rubber boots, and the hand remote / panel: positive make-and-break, no corrosion or green on the terminals, sealing intact, drain path clear. Exercise each control through the windlass.
tasks.caution_notes: The foredeck foot switch lives under boarding seas and anchor mud and is the usual windlass 'dead' cause - water tracks past a split boot and corrodes the contacts or shorts the low-current side. Keep a spare switch aboard (stocked). A stuck-closed switch runs the windlass away - know where the breaker / isolator is.

tasks.name: Windlass - Electrical Inspections
tasks.description: Check tightness, integrity, and cleanliness of terminals at the motor, foot switches, and solenoids.
tasks.caution_notes: Check and clean the main lugs at the motor, the solenoid/contactor and both foot switches - the windlass pulls hundreds of amps and a high-resistance joint here overheats or drops out mid-hoist. Confirm the deck breaker holds current without nuisance trips.

tasks.name: Windlass - External Component Protection
tasks.description: Spray external, below-deck, and electrical connections to mitigate corrosion and salt buildup.
tasks.caution_notes: Corrosion-block the below-deck body, the motor and every electrical connection - the motor and solenoid sit in a wet locker and terminal corrosion is the usual 'windlass won't run' cause.

tasks.name: Windlass - Gearbox Oil Check
tasks.description: Inspect the gearbox oil level through the inspection sight glass and top off if necessary.
tasks.caution_notes: Check level at the sight glass; top up with the windlass maker's specified EP gear oil (typically SAE 90). A dropping level means a shaft seal is weeping - track it before the box runs dry.

tasks.name: Windlass - Topworks / Clutch Servicing
tasks.description: Strip down the running gear (capstan/clutch nut, upper/lower clutch cones, chainwheel), clean away grease and salt, and re-grease.
tasks.caution_notes: Full strip of the running gear - capstan, clutch nut, upper/lower cones, chainwheel - clean off old grease and salt, inspect the cones and drive key, re-grease with waterproof marine grease (not lithium). Carry spare keys/keyways and cone springs.

checklists.name: Abandon Ship Procedure
checklists.caution_notes: The SEQUENCE for abandoning ship; the companion 'Ditching / Abandon Ship Grab List' is the list of things to have in hand. Edit it to match your boat.

items.name: Call it - muster
items.caution_notes: The skipper calls "Abandon ship". Everyone to the cockpit in PFDs; inflatables on and clipped in if the sea is up.

items.name: Send distress while there is still power
items.caution_notes: VHF (DSC radios): lift the cover, hold DISTRESS for about 3 seconds, wait for the acknowledgment, then MAYDAY on channel 16. Use a laminated VHF radio card with the MAYDAY script, kept at the nav station. Activate the EPIRB (know whether yours has a hydrostatic float-free release that self-activates if the boat sinks). Send a satellite-messenger SOS if you carry one. Give position, souls aboard, raft. Message template: MAYDAY - [vessel name] - [Lat/Lon] - Abandoning ship - [# people] - [raft type + colour] - [time UTC].

items.name: Grab the ditch bag and the grab list
items.caution_notes: Use the 'Ditching / Abandon Ship Grab List' checklist. Everyone should know where the ditch bag lives. Satellite messenger; phones in waterproof cases; PFD-mounted MOB devices and personal beacons.

items.name: Water and meds
items.caution_notes: Four fresh-water jerry cans are aboard but no abandon-ship water is designated yet - the likely home for the emergency grab can is the dinghy while it rides in its cradle on the aft deck (to be decided). Take medications; drink water now.

items.name: Launch the raft
items.caution_notes: Know your raft's capacity, where and how it is mounted, and its canopy colour (for the MAYDAY). Keep the painter attached and secure to the boat; DO NOT cut it until the vessel is going down and below deck level. Keep a knife near the raft and know where the others are.

items.name: Final shut-offs - only if time and safe
items.caution_notes: Fuel shut-offs. If fire is the reason: the four master switches under the nav seat (house battery disconnect, house loads, solar, inverter/charger) and the start-charger disconnect in the aft-berth battery compartment. The start batteries CANNOT be isolated from the motors (no switch between them), so the start circuits stay live in an engine-room fire. Seacocks are not part of this sequence: if a through-hull is the source of the flooding, closing it is damage control and belongs before the decision to abandon - do not spend time closing seacocks once the call is made. The boat is all-electric: no gas to close.

items.name: Record time and position (UTC)
items.caution_notes: In the log / on the raft's waterproof pad; note the last message sent.

items.name: Board the raft and secure it
items.caution_notes: Set a watch. No sea anchor or drogue is carried at present (both planned before an ocean crossing) - add "stream the sea anchor" here when one is bought.

items.name: Once in the raft - reminders
items.caution_notes: Leave the cabin lights on. Hatches and ports are the skipper's judgement: open for fire or grounding (visibility, nobody trapped), shut for flooding (slows the water, floats longer). Photograph damage if possible. Keep everyone clipped in / tethered to the raft. Hourly position updates by satellite messenger. Ration water.

checklists.name: Anchoring / Raising Anchor Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: Raising and setting the anchor - the same procedure, up and down.

items.name: [SAFETY] Check the OTHER chainwheel's clutch before powering the windlass
items.caution_notes: On a dual-chainwheel, single-shaft windlass both chainwheels (and any warping drum) share one shaft, each with its own clutch. Before running EITHER chainwheel (raising or setting), back off the OTHER chainwheel's clutch nut until it stops. If you leave it tightened, it is still coupled to the shaft and will get driven too - paying out or hauling in that anchor/rode uncontrolled while you are trying to work the one you actually intend to use. Skip if your windlass has a single chainwheel.

items.name: Raising - anchor wash system
items.caution_notes: Power up the anchor washdown pump; clear mud/grass from the chain before it reaches the chain locker.

items.name: Raising - maneuvering throttle
items.caution_notes: Maintain low-RPM forward gear under engine power to absorb strain and prevent windlass motor overheating while hauling.

items.name: Raising - retrieve the chain/anchor
items.caution_notes: Snubber retrieval: idle forward slowly under propulsion to ease tension, unhook and clear the chain snubber line from the bow deck cleats. Keep the bow pointed toward the anchor with the chain slack. Wash the chain as necessary to keep the chain locker clear.

items.name: Raising - standard comms calls (reference)
items.caution_notes: "Up and down" - chain vertical, bow over the anchor, anchor still on/in the seabed. "Anchors aweigh" - anchor broken loose and clear of the bottom; vessel is officially underway. "Anchor in sight" - anchor visible near the surface. "Clear anchor"/"Foul anchor" - clean vs. wrapped in its own chain/cable/debris. "Anchor home" - fully secured in the hawsepipe.

items.name: Raising - secure from anchor retrieval
items.caution_notes: Secure chain in place via the soft shackle to the bow cleat. Remove chain from the gypsy. Close up the deck hatches. Unpower the anchor wash pump.

items.name: Setting - pick the spot
items.caution_notes: Pick a safe spot for the boat with appropriate bottom conditions.

items.name: Setting - deploy anchor
items.caution_notes: Deploy anchor / lock windlass / back down.

items.name: Setting - verify the set
items.caution_notes: Dive the anchor to verify proper set.

items.name: Setting - monitor swing
items.caution_notes: Monitor swing diameter over the first 15 minutes to guarantee absolute clearance from shoals, obstructions, or neighboring hulls.

items.name: Setting - snubber
items.caution_notes: Confirm the chain snubber line is securely cleated to the bow chocks, entirely isolating mechanical strain off the windlass gear.

items.name: Setting - anchor alarm
items.caution_notes: Activate the anchor alarm - confirm it transitions to the Engaged state.

items.name: Ground Tackle - Freshwater Mud & Salt Flush
items.description: Blast out the bow rollers, chain locker compartments, and active rode with fresh water to clear salt crystals and abrasive mud.
items.caution_notes: Flush the whole chain, not just the visible part - salt trapped in the locker pile drives crevice corrosion on the stainless.

items.name: Snubber - Suncor Slot Engagement Check
items.description: Inspect the structural throat and gate of the Suncor chain hook for metal bending or hair-line fracture stressing.
items.caution_notes: Inspect the Suncor hook throat and gate for bending or hairline cracks before every deploy - a hook shock-loaded in a blow can be cracked and still hold until the next gust. A snubber hook failure at 2am in 30 kn is why you are awake.

checklists.name: Arrival & Immigration Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: Approach, clearance and the legal paperwork on arrival.

items.name: Hoist the Q flag
items.caution_notes: Immediately upon crossing the 12 NM territorial boundary, hoist the Yellow Q (Quebec) "Man in Boat" flag on the starboard spreader - signals the vessel is healthy and requesting clearance.

items.name: Arrange arrival
items.caution_notes: Contact the arrival dock and arrange actual arrival. If required, contact the follow-on anchorage/mooring for the initial part of the stay.

items.name: Prepare the boat for arrival
items.caution_notes: Stow loose passage gear. Inflate fenders as required (dock, mooring ball, or anchoring). Rig dock lines or snubber. Move the boat hook to the bow. Bring out the "Marriage Saver" headsets before finalizing the approach.

items.name: Launch the dinghy
items.caution_notes: Launch and fit the motor after mooring or anchoring, if not going to a dock.

items.name: Crew quarantine
items.caution_notes: Keep all crew and guests aboard. No physical contact with land or other vessels is permitted until Customs and Immigration officially grant "Pratique" (free clearance).

items.name: Assemble the legal shipboard document binder
items.caution_notes: Ship's documentation/registration certificate (original); certified crew list & passenger manifest (5 printed copies); valid passports for everyone aboard (expiration > 6 months); outbound clearance certificate from the last port; up-to-date vaccination records/yellow cards if regionally required; inventory of restricted items to declare (alcohol, funds, etc.); funds to cover check-in costs.

items.name: Captain to Customs/Immigration/Port Master
items.caution_notes: Clean up and dress respectfully. Arrange transportation if required. Clear in and pay fees at each location, get copies of all signed documents. Ensure you have all the boat's and crew's original documents before departing each office.

items.name: Official Pratique granted
items.caution_notes: Once cleared by authorities, drop the Yellow Q flag and hoist the courtesy flag of the host nation on the starboard spreader (pulled from inventory).

items.name: Notify the host marina/ port authority
items.caution_notes: Notify of imminent arrival.

items.name: Settle marina bills, if shore facilities were used
items.caution_notes: Settle all local dockage, electricity, and port fees. Secure a physical, zero-balance receipt from the marina office.

items.name: Clear Customs / Immigration
items.caution_notes: Present passports and your original inbound ship's papers as required. Secure your official Outbound Clearance Certificate (Zarpe). Check that every passport has received its official, legible outbound stamp before leaving the immigration facility.

items.name: Local courtesy flag removal
items.caution_notes: As you slip your lines or hoist anchor, drop the foreign courtesy flag from your rigging. Keep your home port ensign flying cleanly from the stern.

checklists.name: Departure Day - Systems & Prep Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: See the separate Departure Safety Briefing, Preparing to Sail, and Engine Start checklists for the rest of departure day.

items.name: AIS
items.caution_notes: Confirm it's on and actively updating our position and receiving data - confirm with other vessels or the Marine Traffic app. Update destination port and ETA in the AIS interface or via the PC interface.

items.name: VHF - cockpit, salon, portable
items.caution_notes: Cockpit: plug in handset, verify function. Salon: power up, verify function. Portable: ensure fully charged. Arrange a radio check on the units (not on Channel 16).

items.name: Navigation data verification
items.caution_notes: Confirm the chart plotters are exchanging data and showing all data expected: navigation; engine data once the motor is running; the course plot line showing.

items.name: Tracking
items.caution_notes: Ensure the satellite tracker / messenger is mounted and reporting the vessel's position.

items.name: Internet access
items.caution_notes: If going offshore, switch the satellite internet plan to its offshore / ocean mode if it needs one.

items.name: Marriage-saver headset system
items.caution_notes: Bring it out and ensure it's completely charged.

items.name: Stow the dinghy and SUPs
items.caution_notes: Bring the dinghy onboard, load SUPs and the floating dock on top, and lash down prior to departure.

items.name: Boat hook
items.caution_notes: Retrieve from pole storage and preposition at the bow for quick deployment.

items.name: Spotlight charged and in place
items.description: Check the rechargeable spotlight is fully charged and back in its place in the cockpit. It is also on the Ditching / Abandon Ship Grab List.

items.name: Sound the mast horn from the helm switch
items.description: Press the helm switch and confirm the horn sounds.
items.caution_notes: Warn the crew and any close neighbours first - it is very loud.

items.name: Test the hailer through the cockpit VHF
items.description: Confirm the hailer works through the cockpit VHF: switch to hail mode, speak, and check it can be heard outside. Then switch back to normal VHF operation.

checklists.name: Departure Safety Briefing
checklists.caution_notes: The captain's pre-departure briefing to crew. Each step is a topic group to cover, not a physical task.

items.name: Vessel safety basics
items.caution_notes: No alcohol while underway. Drug use/possession is prohibited. Location of thru-hulls & strainers. Bung locations/mallets. Alarm panel procedures.

items.name: Reefing policy
items.caution_notes: Reef above 15° of heel. Reef if a squall is expected. When in doubt, reef.

items.name: PFD & tether policy
items.caution_notes: Mandatory while underway and not below. Extra PFD locations. Life sling. Tether use mandatory if out of the cabin. Must have someone in the cockpit if someone leaves it. 3-point contact rule at all times - be deliberate, know where your 3 points are and how to get to the next ones. Watch footing inside and outside; wear footwear if in doubt.

items.name: Emergency equipment - where it is
items.caution_notes: Fire extinguishers (confirm the count at the boat - there may be one more): aft berth (not yet mounted); galley, in the doorway between galley and berth; salon, above the door between the nav station and the shower; one inside each of the port and starboard berths, above the doorways; Fireboy in the engine room. The fire stick is not yet mounted. Two fire blankets: one in the galley, one on the bulkhead opposite the nav station. No flares aboard (they expire): the Coast Guard-accepted light beacon is in the starboard net in the cockpit. The EPIRB is on the solar arch (hydrostatic-release case); MOB devices and personal beacons are fitted to each person's Type V PFD. First aid: the primary kit (expanded crew-level kit, OTC meds, AED, trauma kit) is in the aft cabinet in the port berth; a much smaller kit is in the cabinet in the master head. Dive knives: bow (base of the inner forestay), helm, and stern (starboard scuba-cylinder strap, below the raft).

items.name: Engine and power shut-offs
items.caution_notes: Show the crew the engine STOP control, the generator breaker, the raw-water seacock and the hydrolock rule (see the Engine Start checklist), and where the battery master switches are (house bank, house loads, solar, inverter/charger, start batteries). Never turn off a battery switch while an engine is running.

items.name: Galley safety
items.caution_notes: To kill the induction hob: the cooktop and the microwave each have a dedicated breaker, and the galley outlets a third, all on the master AC panel at the nav station (below the DC panel, above the master alarm panel). Fire blanket in the galley; the nearest extinguisher is in the doorway between the galley and the berth.

items.name: Head and fresh water
items.caution_notes: Explain how the heads work (manual or electric, and that only waste and toilet paper go in), where black water goes and how the tanks are emptied, how the fresh-water pump and water heater are run, and any water-conservation rules aboard.

items.name: MOB procedure
items.caution_notes: Immediately use the closest chart plotter to activate a MOB location. All crew on deck. Assess the best possible way to retrieve the crew member. Know the ditch bag, EPIRB, binoculars, and spotlight locations.

items.name: Hydration
items.caution_notes: Water & Propel locations.

items.name: Comms briefing
items.caution_notes: Internet usage (email, weather, emergency calls) - offshore data may be metered. Download entertainment content before departure. VHF radio - use AIS to monitor approaching traffic, initiate calls if we'll pass close. The satellite tracker is our tracking mechanism - checked at watch handover.

items.name: Duty roster / watch schedule
items.caution_notes: Watch length (e.g. 6-hour shifts). Cleaning. Food prep. Passage plan including weather forecast. Designated shore agent has the passage/float plan. Periodic reporting via the satellite tracker.

items.name: Captain's orders & the Golden Rule
items.caution_notes: If you are unsure, worried, or in doubt about any situation, wake the captain immediately - no crew member will ever be criticized for calling or waking the captain, no matter how minor the issue turns out to be. When in doubt, reef. Do not take chances. Monitor AIS/radar for other vessels or weather that might impact the passage.

items.name: Watchstanding discipline
items.caution_notes: If you are primary on watch, you are not sleeping - that means actively scanning the horizon 360° every 10-15 minutes, not just looking at the plotter screen. All deck hatches and portholes must remain closed and locked while underway unless explicitly permitted by the captain.

items.name: Wake the captain - vessel condition
items.caution_notes: Any unusual noise, vibration, or smell (especially burning or electrical odors). High bilge water alarms or a sudden increase in bilge pump activity. Any equipment failure impacting propulsion, steering, navigation, or safety. Any doubt about the vessel's position or navigation instruments.

items.name: Wake the captain - navigation & traffic
items.caution_notes: Any CPA with another vessel expected under 2 NM where positive contact hasn't been made and a passing plan explicitly coordinated via VHF. A vessel on a steady bearing failing to show signs of altering course. Unable to maintain the planned course/track. Unexpected sightings of land, navigation markers, or unlit objects.

items.name: Wake the captain - weather & sea state
items.caution_notes: A sudden/unexpected wind speed change of 10+ knots. A persistent wind direction shift of 30°+. A significant barometric pressure drop (2+ millibars in 3 hours). Any sudden drop in visibility (squalls, fog, heavy rain).

items.name: Non-standard sail configurations
items.caution_notes: Notify the captain before using: wing-on-wing, asymmetric, code zero, storm sails.

items.name: Hostile-approach protocol
items.caution_notes: If overtaken by a vessel with ill intent, do NOT fight back - surrender immediately if clearly outnumbered/outgunned/outrun. Call a Mayday on VHF, activate SOS on the satellite messenger and AIS, then cooperate with the boarding party. Agree the boat's policy (firearms, valuables) with the crew before departure.

checklists.name: Ditching / Abandon Ship Grab List
checklists.caution_notes: Grab list, not a sequential procedure - each step is one item to have in hand.

items.name: Dinghy bag (bow locker)
items.caution_notes: Copies of the dinghy's paperwork sealed in a baggie; cheap plastic space blankets and rain ponchos; handheld flares and a signal mirror; tiny flashlight, chem light sticks, and whistle; mini first-aid kit, bug repellent, and sunscreen; small handheld VHF radio; multitool; PFDs for users; anchor, chain and line; lock and cable.

checklists.name: Dive Preparation
checklists.description: This is the checklist for prepping all of the Scuba Related stuff for use
checklists.caution_notes: run this checklist to prepare the boat and gear for diving - this is NOT the individual pre-dive checklist prior to getting in the water

items.name: Prep Camera Gear if being used
items.caution_notes:
1. Verify all batteries are charged
2. Silicon Grease all O-Rings
3. Load memory cards
4. Assemble Housing/ Camera
5. Take a picture to confirm function

items.name: Tanks
items.caution_notes:
1. Ensure Cylinders are full
2. Inspect O-Rings
3. If using the Pony bottle verify holder is serviceable, tank is full, O-ring is serviceable

items.name: Personal Gear
items.caution_notes:
1. Determine which BCs are being used - inspect for use
2. Determine which regs are being used - inspect for use
3. Dive computers - ensure charged and configured

items.name: Underwater Imaging - Housing O-Ring Service & Pre-Dive Leak Check
items.description: Before every dive: inspect and lightly grease the main housing and port O-rings, check the sealing groove for a single hair or grain, close up and run the vacuum/leak alarm if the housing has one; watch it on descent.
items.caution_notes: One hair on the O-ring floods the housing and the camera is gone. Never dive a housing you have not personally sealed and vacuum-checked that day. Carry spare O-rings and silicone grease for every housing and port.

items.name: Slip/dock lines
items.caution_notes: Double-up spring, bow, and stern lines for local surges. Deploy hull fenders clear of fixed dock hardware.

items.name: Shore power hookup
items.caution_notes: Connect the shore power cable to the dock pedestal FIRST, then the boat inlet. Turn on the pedestal breaker, then the internal main AC breakers. Confirm proper polarity.

items.name: Inverter/charger confirmation
items.caution_notes: Ensure the inverter/charger transitions to its charging state.

items.name: GeoFence alarm
items.caution_notes: Set the GeoFence alarm trigger to guard against vessel theft.

items.name: Engine cooldown
items.caution_notes: Allow the motor to idle and cool off so the turbocharger can safely cool.

checklists.name: Engine Start / Shutdown Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: Covers both the main engine and the generator.

items.name: ⚠️ Critical System Rules
items.caution_notes: Know your boat's own rules - e.g. if the engine and generator share a fuel system or raw-water strainer, never run both at once. Alternator safety: never turn off a battery switch while an engine is running, or you will destroy the alternator diodes. FAILED START - hydrolock: see the two Start steps for the cranking limits and the close-the-seacock procedure, and check the numbers against your own manuals.

items.name: Check oil level
items.caution_notes: Know where the dipstick is on the main engine and on the generator.

items.name: Fuel system - select source tank
items.caution_notes: Check the tank level via the chart plotter, tank monitor or sight gauge first, then set the tank-select valve.

items.name: Fuel system - select fuel filter element
items.caution_notes: If you have a dual (switchable) primary filter, select the element to use. Verify the bowl is clean and no water is present before starting.

items.name: Fuel system - set the destination valve
items.caution_notes: Main engine: select the main engine. Generator: select the generator.

items.name: Fuel system - set the fuel tank return valve
items.caution_notes: Under the sole by the nav station. Select the SAME tank as the source tank chosen above.

items.name: Fuel system - ensure the system is primed
items.caution_notes: See the fuel filter element change procedure if it needs priming.

items.name: Raw water - confirm the seacock is open
items.caution_notes: Forward and SB of the engine, outside the stringer. Yellow handle should be UP.

items.name: Raw water - check the strainer
items.caution_notes: Aft wall of the engine room. Clear of debris; shut the seacock first if it needs cleaning.

items.name: Belts - inspect tension and condition
items.caution_notes: Check for fraying as well as tension.

items.name: Coolant - verify level
items.caution_notes: Top off if not full.

items.name: Engine bay inspection (pre-start)
items.caution_notes: Shaft area clear of wire/hoses/entanglement hazards. No excessive water under the engine. No fuel, water, or coolant leaks.

items.name: Verify starter battery voltage above 12V
items.caution_notes: Use the combiner switch at the helm if necessary.

items.name: Start the main engine
items.caution_notes: Power the engine panel on, then press Start - it should crank and start easily. Verify raw water pumping from the exhaust. Verify positive oil pressure and that engine data is displaying. FAILED START - protect the engine from hydrolock. Follow the manual's cranking limit (commonly no more than 15 seconds, with about 15 seconds between tries). With a water-lift (waterlock) muffler, excessive cranking can fill it and push seawater into the cylinders: if the engine has not started after about 10 seconds of cranking, CLOSE the raw-water seacock and crank in short bursts until it starts. When it starts with the seacock closed, STOP the engine immediately, RE-OPEN the seacock, then restart and run normally - it must not run without cooling water (the impeller runs dry within seconds). If water in the cylinders is suspected (hard to turn, very slow cranking), do not crank - call a dealer. Check these numbers against your engine manual.

items.name: Start the generator
items.caution_notes: Start from the generator panel. Verify raw water pumping from the exhaust and positive oil pressure. Once running and stable, turn on the generator breaker at the AC panel. FAILED START - protect the generator from hydrolock: prolonged cranking without a start pumps raw water into the exhaust, which can then run back into the cylinders. If it will not catch: CLOSE the raw-water seacock, drain the exhaust muffler, and find out why it needs so much cranking. Once it starts, IMMEDIATELY re-open the seacock. If the generator runs its own automatic start sequence, learn how many crank attempts it makes; after any failed start, close the seacock before pressing Start again. Hydrolock damage is usually not covered by warranty.

items.name: Engine Room Blowers - Duct & Outlet Check
items.description: Check the duct intake opening has not slipped below the bilge waterline or collapsed. After the engine starts, confirm the engine-room blowers came on (they start automatically with the engine).
items.caution_notes: Check whether your engine-room blowers start automatically with the engine. On a diesel boat there is no need to pre-run them; once the engine is running, confirm they are on: you can hear them, and a hand over the exit hose confirms the outlet fan is moving air. (On a boat carrying gasoline, ALWAYS run the blowers before starting.) Confirm the blower voltage on the nameplate matches the circuit. Also check the intake duct has not slumped toward the bilge water.

items.name: Engine bay inspection (post-start)
items.caution_notes: Check for raw water, fuel, and coolant leaks. No smoke, fumes, or unusual noises. Confirm the blowers are pumping fresh air / removing excess heat.

items.name: Shutdown - main engine
items.caution_notes: A turbocharged engine needs a controlled cool-down: idle out of gear for 5-10 minutes first. Stop the engine, then switch off the engine panel.

items.name: Shutdown - GenSet
items.caution_notes: Turn the breaker off at the nav station to unload the motor; let it idle 5-10 minutes to cool via its built-in cooling. Use the Stop button on the genset control panel to stop it.

items.name: Engine room inspection (post-shutdown)
items.caution_notes: Check for leaks. Check the fuel filter bowl condition and clean if needed. Check strainer condition and clean if needed. Check for smoke or odors. Leave the fuel and raw-water systems configured for use, in case of an emergency restart.

items.name: Water Maker - System Pickling (Preservation)
items.description: Circulate a chemical matrix to preserve the dual membranes from microbial death during long structural absences.
items.caution_notes: Pickle at 0 PSI only - never lift the HP regulator with pickling solution in the lines or you rupture the membrane. Food-grade propylene glycol.

items.name: Black Water Tanks - Black Water Sludge Flush
items.description: Fill the holding tank halfway with fresh water and biodegradable laundry soap before moving the boat; the movement scours calcified scale away from the fiberglass tank walls.
items.caution_notes: Fiberglass tanks will not be eaten by the hydrogen sulfide from stagnant sewage, but it attacks the bronze fittings and any exposed metal over time, so don't let it sit. Inspect the sanitary hose, fittings and vent tubing for permeation/cracking on the same schedule as the pump hoses.

items.name: Secure loose items on deck
items.description: Stow or lash down anything topside that could shift, blow around, chafe, or walk off while the boat sits unattended for an extended period.

items.name: Evaluate: remove sails for storage vs. leave rigged and secured
items.description: Judgment call, not a fixed action. Factors: expected absence length, hurricane-season exposure at the layup location, the marina/yard storm plan (if on the hard). If leaving rigged: make sure every furled sail is secured (extra wraps, sheets tight, a lashing round the furled sail). If removing: follow the furler manual's unbend procedure.
items.caution_notes: Taking headsails off the furler before a storm reduces windage - treat this as a genuine storm-risk decision, not routine housekeeping.

items.name: Suspend main engine / generator Idle-Period Run scheduling while hauled out
items.description: No raw-water cooling available on the hard - do not run either engine. Defer the idle-period run due dates (and anything else that goes overdue) to the actual back-in-service date.

items.name: Notify marina/insurer of extended absence; arrange remote monitoring if available
Verify the seacocks: closable ones closed (A/C exceptions applied), scuppers left OPEN
items.description: Confirm every closable seacock is closed - except any feeding equipment deliberately left running (e.g. an A/C) - and that the cockpit scuppers are still OPEN. For an extended IN-WATER absence only - not applicable once hauled.
items.caution_notes: Cockpit scuppers stay open - the cockpit has to drain rain. A depth/speed transducer can be pulled and blanked with its plug (optional). Bilge-pump discharges above the waterline usually have no seacock. If an A/C is left running and drains condensate into the bilge, that bilge pump and its float must be known-good.

items.name: Shut down and secure all keel-cooled refrigeration
items.description: Covers every keel-cooled refrigeration unit. Do not run the compressor while hauled - with no water around the keel cooler it destroys the unit almost immediately.

items.name: Secure Salon AC and Berth AC - do not run while hauled
items.description: No raw water available for either unit's seawater side.
items.caution_notes: For a warm-climate haul, securing the unit and leaving the seawater loop dry is sufficient. Where freezing is possible, follow the A/C manual's winterising procedure (antifreeze through the water inlet -> strainer -> pump -> coil -> outlet).

items.name: Toilets out of service while hauled
items.description: No through-hull water available for the manual flush pump.

items.name: Do not attempt a watermaker production run while hauled
items.description: Pickling only (bucket-fed, works either scenario) - actual production needs a raw seawater feed that isn't available on the hard.

items.name: Portable floor A/C available for humidity control (optional)
items.description: In storage - a resource for a long yard stay, not a requirement. Deploy at your discretion.

items.name: Anode inspection/replacement - shaft, prop hub, strut, rudder stock
items.description: Haul-out is the easy access window instead of a dedicated dive.

items.name: Keel-cooler service - zinc/bonding audit + chemical descale
Feathering prop & line cutter service - grease, feathering test, backlash, anode, cutter
Review/activate any annual safety-gear send-out
items.description: PFD beacon battery overhaul, liferaft recertification, scuba cylinder VIP/hydro and regulator/BCD service. The gear is accessible and the boat is out of commission anyway - a natural window to send it out.

items.name: AC condenser/heat-exchanger descaling - all seawater-cooled A/Cs
items.description: Not haul-access-dependent, but the AC is already secured and not running during a haul - a natural window to do it.

items.name: Portable Fridge/Freezer - Off-Season Ventilation Latch
items.description: Prop the heavy lid open slightly whenever the box is powered down for long-term storage to prevent an anaerobic mold greenhouse from forming inside.
items.caution_notes: Layup: clean, dry, lid cracked on its vent latch, both DC and any AC cord unplugged. The thermal-fuse DC cord is a wear item - carry a spare.

items.name: Refrigerator - Off-Season Airing Lock
items.description: When shutting down the fridge for extended storage, prop the door open slightly using the built-in latch storage vent mechanism to prevent mold.
items.caution_notes: Layup: empty, clean, dry, and prop the door open on its retaining catch so the box airs - a closed damp box grows black mould on every surface in weeks. Kill the DC at the breaker.

items.name: Hot-water heater: breaker OFF (tank stays full)
items.description: Switch off the water-heater breaker at the panel. The tank stays full - do NOT drain it for a normal lay-up.
items.caution_notes: An electric water-heater element burns out in seconds if it is powered with no water around it. If the tank is ever drained or the boat is hauled, the breaker must already be off before anyone touches the tank.

items.name: Batteries stay ON: drop to the minimum-loads list
items.description: Leave the battery banks connected if solar (or shore power) keeps them up. Turn everything else off and leave only the minimum loads: e.g. bilge pumps, remote monitoring / telemetry, cameras, and (if the boat is afloat) air-cooled refrigeration and a dehumidifier. Keel-cooled refrigeration is covered by its own step and is never run while hauled. Edit this list to match what you actually leave running.
items.caution_notes: Check the bank state of charge before leaving and again on the first remote check-in; the charging source has to out-produce the standing loads in the worst weather expected.

items.name: Remove the canvas and the cockpit cushions
items.description: Take down and store below, dry: the canvas (bimini, spray hood and any other covers) and the cockpit cushions. Stow them so they are not touching the hull or a wet locker.
items.caution_notes: Canvas and cushions left up in the sun and storms wear out and go mouldy; canvas left up in a hurricane also adds windage.

items.name: Decide: anchor chain(s) - leave as is, or inspect / relocate
items.description: Judgment call. Decide whether to leave the anchor chain(s) stowed as they are, or take them out to inspect (and rinse, if galvanised) before leaving - galvanised chain left wet in a locker can rust into a solid pile. Record the decision and where each chain lives.

checklists.name: Getting Underway - From a Mooring Ball

items.name: Leaving - rope integrity scan
items.caution_notes: Visual check of the primary mooring painter line for pitting or structural chafe damage inside the bow chocks.

items.name: Leaving - secondary painter clearance
items.caution_notes: Cast off secondary safety lines from the buoy ring, leaving the vessel riding cleanly on a single, quick-release slip loop.

items.name: Leaving - standard helm calls (reference)
items.caution_notes: "Lines slack" - the slip line has no tension, safe to untie/pull. "Lines letting go" - crew actively casting off the ropes from the buoy. "Line clear"/"All clear forward" - rope fully out of the water and back on deck.

items.name: Leaving - secure the deck
items.caution_notes: Put away mooring snubbers.

items.name: Picking up - choose the ball
items.caution_notes: Pick a mooring ball.

items.name: Picking up - secure
items.caution_notes: Pick it up and secure with appropriate snubber rigging (dual line, one to each forward block).

items.name: Picking up - backup line
items.caution_notes: Confirm the secondary backup line is rigged with slack to catch only upon primary failure.

items.name: Picking up - monitor swing
items.caution_notes: Monitor swing diameter over the first 15 minutes to guarantee absolute clearance from shoals, obstructions, or neighboring hulls.

items.name: Picking up - anchor alarm
items.caution_notes: Activate the anchor alarm - confirm it transitions to the Engaged state.

items.name: Shore power disconnect
items.caution_notes: Shut off all internal 120V AC main distribution breakers BEFORE physically unplugging the shore power umbilical cord.

items.name: Mooring lines & fenders
items.caution_notes: Rig slip lines for short-handed release. Untie and stow all fenders into designated lazarette racks before clearing dock.

items.name: Standard helm calls (reference)
items.caution_notes: "Singling up" - crew removing extra lines, leaving one bow, one stern, and the springs. "Lines slack" - tension off the requested line, safe to untie/slip. "Letting go [line]" - crew actively casting off that line. "Lines clear" - line fully out of the water and on deck, helm free to use the engine without fouling the prop. Clearance calls: "Bow/Stern swinging [in/out]", "Hold turn", "[Distance] clear aft/forward", "All clear [Port/Starboard/Fore/Aft]".

items.name: Secure from clearing-out activities
items.caution_notes: Stow dock lines. Deflate and store fenders.

checklists.name: Initial Movement Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: The first few minutes after getting underway, before settling into the passage.

items.name: Bring the vessel to the planned route
items.caution_notes: Based on the chart plotter route.

items.name: Secure lines, fenders, etc. not needed during the passage
items.caution_notes: Once underway.

checklists.name: Post-Passage Cleanup Checklist
checklists.caution_notes: See the separate Putting Away the Sails checklist for rigging and sails.

items.name: Document maintenance tasks from passage events
items.caution_notes: Acquire the resources needed to deal with them.

items.name: Clean the boat - heads
items.caution_notes: Sanitation scale treatment: pump 1 cup of raw white vinegar into both manual heads, let sit 20 minutes to dissolve calcium scale before flushing.

items.name: Arrange return passage for crew members
Reprovision
items.caution_notes: Make the shopping list. Determine where items can be purchased, how to get there and back, and how to pay (local currency, credit card, etc.).

items.name: Reset internet access
items.caution_notes: Buy a local SIM / data plan if needed. Select cellular as the router's primary source. Pause the satellite internet plan.

items.name: Arch / Hardtop - Salt Water Spray Washdown
items.description: Flush the aluminum pipe frames, vinyl panels, and mesh nets with low-pressure fresh water to dissolve abrasive salt tracking.
items.caution_notes: Low-pressure fresh rinse of the frame, panels and nets after every offshore leg - salt under the panel-mount saddles and in the joints is where the anodizing gets undercut and the alu starts to pit.

items.name: Deck Hardware - Track & Car Washdown
items.description: Flush traveler tracks and genoa cars with low-pressure fresh water to dissolve salt deposits that lock up the cars.
items.caution_notes: Never mix ball types: brown Torlon (high-load genoa cars) with black/white Delrin (low-load traveler) - Delrin crushes instantly under genoa loads. No wet lubricant on the tracks.

items.name: Depth, Speed & Temp Transducer - Transducer Pull & Blanking
items.description: Pull the active sensor body out of its thru-hull housing and smoothly snap in your yellow blanking plug to stop water ingress while the boat sits stagnant.
items.caution_notes: Pull the transducer head before any long absence and fit the blanking plug - barnacles lock the paddlewheel and seize the sleeve. On refit, the moulded arrow points dead forward. Depower first.

items.name: Hatches & Port Holes - Salt Deposit Washdown
items.description: Flush all 6 deck hatches, 6 portlights, and the companionway assembly with fresh water to clear salt crusting from the hinge wells and drainage grooves.
items.caution_notes: Flush the hatch and portlight frames, hinge wells and drainage channels - dried salt in a hinge well is abrasive and wicks water past the gasket. Do the companionway assembly too.

items.name: Rigging - Rigging Rinse
items.description: Hose down the deck-level turnbuckles, chainplates, staysail quick-release levers, and roller furler drums with fresh water to clear micro-salt crystals.
items.caution_notes: New standing rigging stretches: track constructional stretch over the first ~50 miles and re-tune. On an older spar, watch the mast and boom for fatigue, not just the wire.

items.name: Running Rigging and Blocks - Freshwater Hardware Flush
items.description: Hose down all cockpit blocks, deck organizers, traveler cars, and rope clutches to clear crystalline salt that jams bearings and chews rope fibers.
items.caution_notes: No grease on Harken/Lewmar blocks - grease and WD-40 permanently flatten the Delrin/Torlon balls. Avoid fast loaded line releases; the friction melts Dyneema cores.

items.name: VHF Radios - Remote Mic Water-Clearing Flush
items.description: If a wave washes over the cockpit station, run the radio's water-clearing (speaker vibration) function, if it has one, to clear trapped water from the mic speaker grille.
items.caution_notes: Run it after every washdown. 303 Protectant on the coiled remote-mic cord - UV fissures in the jacket wick water into the DSC distress buttons.

items.name: Winches - Freshwater Washdown
items.description: Rinse the outer self-tailing arm, drum, and handle socket to dissolve salt crystals before they grind into the bearings.
items.caution_notes: Rinse the drum, self-tailer arm and handle socket before salt dries into the bearing races - the single biggest driver of winch wear. On the electric winch rinse around the base seal too.

items.name: Windlass - Freshwater Rinse
items.description: Clean after each use
items.caution_notes: Hose the gypsy, clutch cones and above-deck casting after every use - salt and grit in the clutch is what makes it slip or lock. Mild soap and a rag, then let it dry before the cover goes on.

items.name: Research arrival requirements
items.caution_notes: Departure paperwork; arrival fees; required permits/visas; communications requirements (satellite internet, cellular carriers); destination port arrival requirements; whether a local agent is needed; VHF channels in use (16/9, or something else); other local contact details (phone, WhatsApp); reprovisioning considerations on arrival - fuel/water availability, food availability, chandlery availability, sail loft availability, engine and generator repair facilities.

items.name: Preventative maintenance
items.caution_notes: Check the upcoming maintenance schedule and perform all PM expected to come due during the passage or shortly after arrival. Replenish spares/consumables used, if easily available. Clean the hull. Inspect the steering quadrant and cables. Shakedown cruise if the boat hasn't moved in several weeks - exercise the propulsion systems and familiarize new crew with the boat's operation.

items.name: Provisioning
items.caution_notes: Drinking water (bottles for the passage, jerry cans as spare). Precook meals and freeze/refrigerate for quick prep underway. Refill fresh water tanks from shore or the watermaker if able. Fill fuel tanks (+ jerry cans if the passage needs extra); treat with BioMuncher. Ensure power storage is at 100%. Charge all portable light sources.

items.name: Route planning
items.caution_notes: Macro: general planned route; need for additional crew; weather windows; arrange weather routing if desired; provisioning/menu required. Detailed: program the final route into the chart plotters; zoom in along the route to verify in-transit dangers/risks; send the float plan to your shore contact (cc crew designates if applicable).

items.name: Get familiar with the arrival port & surrounding waters
items.caution_notes: Update Active Captain data before departing. Below-water obstacles; local current and tide impacts; air draft considerations; temporary restrictions.

items.name: Decide where to keep the boat while in-country
items.caution_notes: Are permits required? Are reservations required? What fees are involved?

items.name: Retrieve the courtesy flag(s)
items.caution_notes: For the intended arrival country - and consider grabbing flags for potential safe havens along the planned passage.

items.name: Medical & physical disclosures
items.caution_notes: Privately ask crew to remind you of any severe allergies, medical conditions, or proneness to severe seasickness, and confirm where their personal meds are stored.

items.name: Bring out cockpit passage materials
items.caution_notes: Portable spotlight (charged); PFDs; binoculars; prepare the dodger / put away no-see-um netting.

items.name: Cabin preparation
items.caution_notes: Foul weather gear prepped in the salon; convert the salon table to a passage berth; put away/secure all loose items (at least a 40° heel); verify all cabinets/doors/hatches are latched/locked; double-check toolroom, port berth, and galley storage.

items.name: Prep fishing gear
items.caution_notes: Clean/rig rods and reels; fillet station; rod tethers; waist cup.

items.name: Prep the ditch bag
